messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multilevel serial dilution assay
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Multilevel serial dilution assay
messages.body_plain:
I seem to recall that this model has about 1 more parameter than can typically be estimated from data.  So you could well have some very weak identification.

> On Mar 30, 2016, at 12:16 PM, Jonathan Audet <jona...@hotmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> I think I figured where most of the issues were arising from. The 5-parameter form for the logistic curve adds an asymmetry factor to the equation. This asymmetry changes the location of the inflection point. The plot of the hyper-means of those two parameters (mu_log_Asym, mu_log_Inflec) looked much like the middle panel of figure 20.1 in the Stan manual (when you have 2 intercepts with proper priors). Removing the asymmetry reduced the divergent transitions to 46 (all in one chain, adapt_delta = 0.99) and the max_treedepth problems to 324 (shinystan says ~900; max_treedepth = 15) over 4 x 2000 post-warmup draws.
>
> If these two parameters are so correlated, would it help if the correlation was modeled explicitly? If so, how does the multivariate reparameterization work with multi-level parameters. (Also, instead of doing: cov_matrix Sigma; L <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma); , is it possible to do cholesky_factor_cov L; ?)

> CC: krzysztof...@gmail.com
> From: jona...@hotmail.com
> Subject: RE: [stan-users] Multilevel serial dilution assay
> Date: Tue, 15 Mar 2016 20:50:22 -0500
>
> Thanks for the tips!
> I have used non-centered parameterization in other models, but did not realize it would help here.
>
>
> I will try those changes out tomorrow.
>
>
> Re 4.6 GHz: It does worry me whenever I look at the temperature but that is from Asus’ OC utility… and it cools down pretty quick.

> Cc: krzysztof...@gmail.com
> Subject: Re: [stan-users] Multilevel serial dilution assay
>
>
> There were some neat adjustments in Wing Wong's dChip software
> (for genomic microarrays) for noisy chips (people putting fingers
> on them, getting contaminated, etc.).
>
> If you've increased adapt_delta and upped the max depth
> and are still having issues, you'll need to reparameterize.
> It's probably a good idea anyway if possible.
>
> Looking at the model, you definitely want to make the hierarchical
> parts of it non-centered (aka, use the "Matt trick");  there's
> a writeup in the language manual.
>
> The other thing you can do is separate the uId[i] == std_loc
> cases from the others so that you don't need a loop over N_unkn.
>
> You'll save some time with vectorizing those normals in the loop over
> n_unkn.  For instance, if log_x is just the std_loc versions, then you
> can convert this
>
>   log_x[i] ~ normal(log_ser_dilutions[i] + log(pred_std), sigma_x[uID[i]] * abs_log_ser_dilutions[i]);
>
> to
>
>   log_x ~ normal(log_ser_dilutions + log(pred_std),
>                  sigma_x[uID] .* abs_log_ser_dilution);
>
> Or, you can just build one big vector foo that for each i contains
> either log(pred_std) or log_theta[uID[i]] depending on the
> std_loc condition.  Then get rid of the original loop and use:
>
>   log_x ~ normal(log_ser_dilutions + foo,
>                  sigma_x[uID] .* abs_log_ser_dilutions);
>
> It may seem like extra work to populate foo, but the vectorization of
> normal() more than makes up for it.
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  Overclocked at 4.6 GHz?  Isn't that thing melting its case?
>
>
> > On Mar 14, 2016, at 4:56 PM, Jonathan Audet <jona...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Sorry for the long delay. Other important things came up. Also, I had time to think about the model and go over that paper again. When I finally tried to model it based on what is on page 411, it (mostly) worked.
> >
> > I had not realized that the data I was using to test this version had one standard point far out of range, which threw off the curve (well it was making sense given that data, but not given the rest of the data, e.g. the highest standard concentration was estimated at 10^4 instead of ~20). Making the model multilevel has solved the issue (although obviously not for a single plate).
> >
> > For example, the data (std in blue, unknowns in red, lines link serial dilutions of the same sample): (plate 12 was the one that threw me for a loop, everything but the top 2 dilutions is lower)
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > The regressions with 95% HDI on the calculated concentrations (std in red):
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > Overall, the model estimates the individual points (each replicate of each dilution of each sample) with a, imho, remarkable accuracy. The output is consistent with the previous results and makes sense given the background.
> >
> > I am still having issues with divergent transitions, hitting the max_treedepth, and major autocorrelation. From the little I understand about HMC, there are probably things in there that can be reparameterised to improve efficiency.
> >
> > Newest model and code (with the same data I was using) are attached.  **This model took about 1.75 hours to sample on a i7-6700K overclocked at 4.6 GHz with 32 Gb of RAM.
> >
> >
> > On Wednesday, 17 February 2016 09:48:42 UTC-5, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> >
> >
> > On Tuesday, February 16, 2016 at 6:52:42 PM UTC-5, Jonathan Audet wrote:
> > I think I am starting to figure out what the main issue is with this model. Normally, the curve parameters are dependent on the standard, i.e. P(Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope | x_std, OD_std), and the unknown concentrations are dependent on the curve parameters, i.e. P(theta | Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope, OD_unkn). In the current model, since everything is calculated at once we have P(Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope, theta | x_std, OD_std, OD_unkn) which implies that the curve parameters are also optimized as a function of the unknowns, this makes no logical or physical sense.
> >
> > I disagree that it makes no logical or physical sense.  The "unknowns" are run repeatedly so they have a known dilution and a known reading.  The fact the dilution level is known _should_ contribute because the reading should go down with the dilution in a sensible way, following the estimated curve.  I get that in practice this model is not working out as written but I wouldn't blame it on logical/physical inconsistency.  In BUGS people avoid this kind of problem using a function called (I think...) "cut", but Stan does not do that.  It's possible that dealing with this issue takes this project from "applying a model described in a paper" to "extending the paper" and if you don't want to do that using generated quantities is the right way  to go.
> >
> > Also, since there are 72 wells of unknowns (18 samples, 2 dilutions each, in duplicate) and 24 wells of standard per plate, the unknown overwhelm the standards.
> >
> > Yes, I think the most likely issue is that a level of noise is not being taken into account---e.g.-the variation inherent in the enzyme that leads wells to develop at different speeds.
> >
> > As I said earlier, one solution is to use inverse calculation in the generated quantities block. However that has two problems: 1) Artificial limits have to be placed on some parameters (so that Bottom < OD < Bottom + Span), even though OD readings above the top of the curve are possible due to measurement and enzymatic noise (this is an ELISA assay);
> >
> > These limits are not so much artificial as physical if you include the appropriate noise.  The true OD for a very low concentration sample can't be lower than the true instrument output with a negative control, but those things are all measured and recorded as averages.  The best data to go into a model like this would be a series of measurements (not averaged) or the sufficient statistics (mean measurement, measurement noise) and the equations for the curve would only be written for the "true" values not the measured values.  I think this is all possible in Stan just maybe more work that you want to put in at the moment.
> >
> > 2) In biological assays, in my experience, interpolated values do not quite scale across dilutions, i.e. simply multiplying to reverse the dilution can yield surprisingly different values, that is the strength (in theory) of the approach used in the paper, it can weigh different dilutions depending on the precision they yield.
> >
> > That's the aspect of the model I find most interesting as well but it might take more work on the model itself to get the benefits---especially since you mentioned divergent iterations in the previous post.  It's a good signal that part of the parameter space is difficult for the sampler to deal with.
> >
> > Is there a way to make the curve parameters independent of the unknowns' OD while keeping the multilevel unknown estimation? That issue did not seem to be a problem in the paper.
> >
> > This is what the "cut" function does in BUGS, there is no parallel in Stan.
> >
> > Sorry I can't be more helpful, I don't have time to dig in at the moment.
> >
> > Krzysztof
> >
> >
> > On Monday, 15 February 2016 16:23:20 UTC-6, Jonathan Audet wrote:
> > OK, I did what Andrew did and made an estimator for each plate, I did try to make some parameters multilevel but that makes for atrocious sampling and does not help with prediction. I think I figured out how unknown estimation is done in the paper, I was going to write "see above" but it appears my email failed me (which explains why no one reacted to it...). The advantage is that there is no need to deal with the beta1 < OD < beta1 + beta2 constraint. I added some generated quantities to keep track of the variation in coefficients between the plates and named the coefficients for their function.
> >
> > I only have one question left:
> >
> > Is there some vectorisation or optimization that I am missing, or something that can be reparameterized better? Every now and then (on the exact same data) I get a complete chain of divergent transitions (and the other 3 chains are quite fine) and the model takes 25 minutes (on my computer) to generate 4000 draws (including 1500 warmup). Using shinystan, I could not relate divergent transitions to any specific parameter. The chains also look a bit correlated.
> >
> > On Saturday, 13 February 2016 18:38:51 UTC-6, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> > On Saturday, February 13, 2016 at 5:45:37 PM UTC-5, Jonathan Audet wrote:
> > The model without the unknown, while still having sampling issues, actually retrodicts the curves quite well already.
> >
> > I am including a corrected script, I noticed some missing functions in the original one. Also, a version of the curve-only model with the cholesky decomposition.
> >
> >
> > That's great! Thanks for sharing the improved code.
> >
> > Regarding tau, I did make it half-normal, its values in the posterior are all 0.05-0.5 so right now I think I put a normal(0.25, 0.1) prior on it. Would it be better to model log_tau instead?
> >
> >
> > I wouldn't worry about modeling log_tau instead.  When you declare it as:
> >
> >  vector<lower = 0>[5] tau;
> >
> > Stan (hoping I get this right) internally uses log(tau) as a parameter (on the real line).
> >
> > If the posterior really looks a lot like the prior I would wonder whether there's much information about it in the data, or if it's not well identified.  Since you can do these models plate-by-plate there ought to be... making the prior tighter is not going to solve this issue so I would avoid normal(.25,.1) and try to understand the model better.  If you can currently fit the model (even without unknowns) I would run that version and look at the pairs plots of other parameters with tau and see if some are highly or non-linearly correlated with it.
> >
> > Also looks like the OD line (OD ~ normal(cOD, sigma_idiv);) and the parent cOD calculation makes a lot more sense now with the paper.
> >
> > Krzysztof
> >
> >
> >
> > Sent from Mail for Windows 10
> >
> >
> > From: Krzysztof Sakrejda
> > Sent: February 13, 2016 3:29 PM
> > To: Stan users mailing list
> > Subject: [stan-users] Re: Multilevel serial dilution assay
> >
> >
> > On Saturday, February 13, 2016 at 2:04:08 PM UTC-5, Jonathan Audet wrote:
> > I will try out your suggestions today.
> >
> > Regarding the unknown calculations, I have to admit I don't quite follow the reasoning of section 3.2 of the paper. In the context of least-squares fit, I would just isolate x instead of y and work from there. This is what I did here. But that method is only valid if "y" is between the bottom and top, each of which moves with the state of the sampler.
> >
> >
> > You need to place constraints on the parameters in the declaration to deal with this, it's the <lower=min(OD), upper=...>, since you have three parameters and two constraints it's not too straightforward but should be doable.
> >
> > When I pull out x I get:
> >
> > log(x) = log(beta_3) + 1/beta_4 * (log(y-beta_1) - 1/beta_4 * log(beta_1+beta_2-y))
> >
> > Based on your stated constraints: beta_1 < OD < beta_1 + beta_2, I think you need to change to something similar to:
> >
> > real<upper=min(OD)> beta_1;
> > real<lower=OD-beta_1> beta_2;
> >
> > Not checked for algebra/syntax but you get the idea.  It would be cool to see this model working well---I RA'd in an analytical chemistry lab for much of my undergrad and I kept thinking model-based calibration would be a great idea.  We did a lot of other quantitative stuff but never this.  Feel free to post more questions if there are other issues with it!
> >
> > Krzysztof
> >
> >
> >
> > On Saturday, 13 February 2016 08:40:31 UTC-6, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> > I looked through the model and here are the issues I noticed:
> >
> > - Use lkj_corr_cholesky instead of lkj_corr (section 51.2 in the 2.9 manual).
> > - It would help to figure out the appropriate scale for tau, and perhaps at least while you are figuring out the model make it half-normal.
> > - This:
> >
> > //Use the current parameters to calculate the interpolated concentration of each unknown value.
> > //The OD (Y value) must be higher than the bottom asymptote (beta[1]) and lower than the top asymptote (beta[1] + beta[2]) or RStan throws an error at the end (for RStan > 2.6).
> > //So any value outside the asymptotes gets the "marker value" of -50. Additional R-side commands deal with this afterwards.
> > for(i in 1:N_unkn){
> >   vector[5] beta;
> >   beta <- exp(logBeta[pID_unkn[i]]);
> >   if(Unknown[i] > beta[1] && Unknown[i] < (beta[1] + beta[2])){
> >     indiv_theta[i] <- log10((beta[3] / pow(pow((beta[1] - (beta[1] + beta[2])) / (beta[1] - Unknown[i]), 1 / beta[5]) - 1, -1 / beta[4])) * Dilution[i]);
> >   } else {
> >     indiv_theta[i] <- -50;
> >   }
> >
> >
> > This should be (?) generating a warning about using a non-linear transform on the LHS of a sampling statement, ultimately associated with the line:
> >
> >    indiv_theta[i] ~ normal(theta[uID[i]], sigma_unkn);
> >
> > So that's not quite the model you think it is.  I don't quite see how this version matches up with with the article so I won't try to make more detailed comments on it but it looks like you could simplify this a fair bit---I don't think the '-50' flag value should be necessary in this model.
> >
> > Krzysztof
> >
> > On Wednesday, February 10, 2016 at 5:45:35 PM UTC-5, Jonathan Audet wrote:
> > I think someone inquired about the code for the serial dilution assay in the paper here. I have also been trying to implement it. I seem to have been able to code the model overall, but some issues remain. I did modify it a bit: I included 5 parameters instead of four (but have faced the same issues with a 4-parameter model) and I adjusted the priors for my assay. Also, the model does not take days into account (the paper had 3 levels: individual plate -> plates on same day -> days).
> >
> > Two issues are beyond my math skills:
> > First, the model always runs into large numbers of divergent transitions even with adapt_delta = 0.95.
> > Second, (probably related) some of the R_hat's are terrible, especially for the correlation matrix Omega.
> >
> > Third, should I be worried about all the warnings regarding positive-definite matrices and other related issues?
> >
> > I also don't know if I am missing opportunities to vectorize (or otherwise speed up) the code...
> >
> > I included 2 models, an initial one (which has the above issues) which simply calculates the curves, and a second one (ends in "unkn") which is meant to include multilevel interpolation of samples based on the curve. I was very interested in using the multilevel prediction across dilutions of unknown samples but the paper is vague. As I understand Stan, making the prediction multilevel requires putting it in the "model" block since it is a sampling statement (rather than just in the "generated quantities" for normal interpolation, which has worked fine in other models without any multilevel aspects). However, including unknowns completely messes up the curve parameters for that plate; I have included unknown data for one of the plates. The inclusion of unknowns also slows sampling substantially, the 3000 samples in the script generally take far longer than the 6000 for the model without unknowns.
> >
> > I tried to comment the models as much as I could. I also included data and unknown data along with a script.
> >
> > I am currently using Microsoft R Open 3.2.3 on Windows 7 (and 10) x64 along with the MKL libraries it provides. The script calls on the Checkpoint package to ensure that all package versions are stable.

I am trying to install rstan on R 3.1.0 (using a mac). I have tried to do what is documented on the github page but it tells me that rstan won't work on R 3.1.0. The github page indicates that you just need to be using anything higher than R 3.0.2, so that doesn't really make sense to me. I have read the other threads here on this issue and have tried to use the approaches indicated but they wont work either.

Any ideas or am I out of luck?

Thanks!

pw

I ran into an unexpected behavior in RStan when I tried to
fit a model:

> fit <- stan("exon-diff-hier.stan", data=c("I", "J", "K", "N", "y"),
+             chains=1, iter=100, refresh = 1);
>

So I ran stan() and got no output whatsoever.

Then I quit R, restarted, ran the same script, and got this at the
same stage:

> fit <- stan("exon-diff-hier.stan", data=c("I", "J", "K", "N", "y"),
+             chains=1, iter=100, refresh = 1);
SYNTAX ERROR, MESSAGE(S) FROM PARSER:

ERROR at line 35

 33:    parameters {
 34:      matrix[I, J] logit_mu;        // exon expression level in group
 35:      matirx<lower=0>[I, J] sigma;  // replicate variability
          ^
 36:      real logit_psi_raw[I, J, K];  // exon inclusion level (non-centered)

PARSER EXPECTED: <one of the following:
  a variable declaration, beginning with type,
      (int, real, vector, row_vector, matrix, unit_vector,
       simplex, ordered, positive_ordered,
       corr_matrix, cov_matrix,
       cholesky_corr, cholesky_cov
  or '}' to close variable declarations>
Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  :
  failed to parse Stan model 'exon-diff-hier' due to the above error.

I believe I followed the directions to run in parallel (which does happen)
and to not recompile (which does not happen---it recompiles the model each time).

- Bob

messages.subject: How to deal with very slow warm up due to large tree depth?
messages.subject_clean: How to deal with very slow warm up due to large tree depth?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to estimate a hierarchical negative binomial regression

for multiply imputed data. Warm up is very slow (~75 samples after

72h, yes that’s hours!), which is partially due to the size of the data

(~190000 cases,  ~20 predictors, 22 groups) and the associated

large number of parameters.

However, I suspect that the main reason is the large tree depth value

 (around 14) during warm up, because if I run a non-hierarchical

model for the same data, that takes around the same time for the

gradient evaluation, 150 warm up iterations plus 500 samples are

done in 9h (tree depth during warm up is around 10 for this model).

I think the large tree depth is partially due to me setting the target

acceptance rate to .9, which I did because in earlier runs of a very

 similar model I found divergent iterations after warm up.

If I understood the section “58.2. HMC Algorithm Parameters” in the

stan reference correctly, one way reduce the tree depth is to increase

the step size, but I fear if I do this (via reducing the target acceptance

rate) I run the risk of getting divergent iterations again. Later under the

heading “” it reads:

“Poor behavior in the tails is the kind of pathology that can be uncovered

by running only a few warmup iterations. Looking at the acceptance

probabilities and step sizes of the first few iterations provides an idea of

how bad the problem is and whether it must be addressed with modeling

efforts such as tighter priors or reparameterizations.”

I scaled all predictor variables and have used non-centered parameterization

where I know this is possible, but I am uncertain what problematic acceptance

probabilities and step size are.

I am attaching diagnostic plots for a hierarchical and non-hierachical model,

the stan model for the hierarchical regression, and the output of the

stan-summary for the non-hierachical model as further information.

The parameters for sampling were

num_samples=500 num_warmup=150

algorithm=hmc engine=nuts max_depth=20 adapt delta=.90

init=0

I would be very thankful about any tips and/or pointers to where I do not

understand things correctly.

Best - Guido

PS: The variational method results in rather implausible parameter values, even if I use the parameters I get with the optimizing approach as inits. But I must say that I know very little about how one maybe could improve the results of the variational method. It does not seem to work as a black box approach for my model/data.

messages.subject: Re: sampling function with kronecker matrix
messages.subject_clean: sampling function with kronecker matrix
messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, April 3, 2016 at 4:46:32 PM UTC-4, Haoyan Sun wrote:
> Hi, I am new to Stan, and I am trying to write a hierarchical bayesian model in Stan.
> For my model, I would like to do a multivariate normal sampling with kronecker matrix, I saw some discussion about the kronecker matrix but I don't know whether it is feasible in Stan now?
> For example, can we call a function such as below ?
> y ~ multi_normal(vector mu, kronecker_matrix)
> where
> kronecker_matrix = matrix A (x) matrix B

Still not possible.

> If not, what would be a good way to write this function in Stan?

There is this R code that you could adapt to Stan code in the case where the Kronecker product is part of a quadratic form, as in the case of a multivariate normal

K <- 25L
D <- diag(1 + runif(K))
a <- runif(1)
W <- round(matrix(runif(K^2), K, K))
W[upper.tri(W, TRUE)] <- 0
W <- W + t(W)
Lambda <- Harman23.cor$cov[1:4,1:4]
y <- rnorm(K * ncol(Lambda))
mult <-
  function(D, a, W, Lambda, y) {
    temp <- Lambda %*% matrix(y, nrow = ncol(Lambda))
    # optimize this particularly if D - a * W is sparse!!!
    scalar <- t(y) %*% c(apply(D - a * W, 1, "%*%", t(temp)))
    return(scalar[1])
  }

all.equal(c( t(y) %*% kronecker(D - a * W, Lambda) %*% y ),
          mult(D, a, W, Lambda, y))

Ben

O([number of leapfrog steps] * [time to compute derivatives for a leapfrog step])

Is this the case? When sampler optimization is discussed here we usually focus on reparameterizations that make sampling "easier". Does the following mechanism explain why this works?

sampling easier -> fewer rejected proposals -> larger step size needed to achieve desired acceptance rate -> fewer leapfrog steps on average before u-turn -> faster iterations

Does this suggest that I could speed up sampling by reducing adapt_delta (as long as it didn't result in more than a few divergent transitions)?

Also, is vectorization the only way to decrease the derivative computation time?

Cheers
Sam

messages.subject: Fitting models of mixture distributions with continuous portions + discrete spikes
messages.subject_clean: Fitting models of mixture distributions with continuous portions + discrete spikes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Folks,

I'm trying to explicitly model some distributions that have very fat tails and a discrete spike at zero. The two tails can sometimes look very different to each other and I want to capture that. To give you some context: this is profit data at a household level from some developing countries. Some households in my data make positive business profits, some make negative, and some make zero or don't operate a business at all (which gets recorded as an exact zero). I need to keep all of these households in the sample because I want to study the distributional effects of a binary treatment variable on these people, which might include moving some people out of the spike into the tails or vice versa. I'm attaching some histograms as examples. The plots are zoomed in / truncated on both axes - the true spike is much higher and the true tails go much further out, but you get the idea.

After some discussions with econometrics and EECS folks around MIT, and using some prior information from economic theory that suggests income/profit/wealth variables typically follow power laws, I figured to start with a mixture model with a discrete spike at zero and 2 pareto distributions as the 2 tails (obviously the negative tail has to be a kind of "reverse" pareto). I want to do inference about the mixture assignment probabilities and the parameters that control the shapes of the tails. I know Stan can't do spike+slab models, so I wrote a Gibbs sampler. However, I don't like having to use conjugate priors on the pareto distribution parameters, and I eventually want to put all of these distributions into a big hierarchical model which might be a stretch of my Gibbs sampling abilities. The friendly person behind @mcmc_stan on twitter suggested there should be a workaround in stan, so I'm posting here to see what people think about this problem and/or if anyone has any suggestions.  I looked at the previous discussion topics for spike and slabs but they mostly seemed to be about discouraging people from using spike+slab priors -- and yes, I would absolutely never use spikes in my priors, but in this data there is a genuine discrete spike and I want to model it.

Thanks so much in advance for any input or advice you have!

Cheers
Rachael

messages.subject_clean: Fitting models of mixture distributions with continuous portions + discrete spikes
messages.body_plain:
Hey Rachael -

I have similar issues working with microfinance repayments data--lots of 0s, lots of due amounts, and different distributions on either side.

Ben Goodrich suggested a work-around that I'm finding works very nicely: have a model for the type of person, and then a model for profits within each person type. So you could have a categorical logit model for whether the person falls into a loss-making/zero profit/profitable category (use k-1 parameterisation with informative priors), and then model the loss or profit with and exponential or lognormal distribution or whatnot, conditional on the category. This should be a lot easier than mixture modeling, and won't have all the weird label-switching problems.

The disadvantage is that your parameters aren't as interpretable, so any treatment effects estimate will be the "derivative" of the posterior prediction with respect to the treatment. But that's not hard to simulate.

Jim

On Monday, April 4, 2016 at 1:43:15 PM UTC-4, Rachael Meager wrote:
> Hi Folks,
>
> I'm trying to explicitly model some distributions that have very fat tails and a discrete spike at zero. The two tails can sometimes look very different to each other and I want to capture that. To give you some context: this is profit data at a household level from some developing countries. Some households in my data make positive business profits, some make negative, and some make zero or don't operate a business at all (which gets recorded as an exact zero). I need to keep all of these households in the sample because I want to study the distributional effects of a binary treatment variable on these people, which might include moving some people out of the spike into the tails or vice versa. I'm attaching some histograms as examples. The plots are zoomed in / truncated on both axes - the true spike is much higher and the true tails go much further out, but you get the idea.
>
> After some discussions with econometrics and EECS folks around MIT, and using some prior information from economic theory that suggests income/profit/wealth variables typically follow power laws, I figured to start with a mixture model with a discrete spike at zero and 2 pareto distributions as the 2 tails (obviously the negative tail has to be a kind of "reverse" pareto). I want to do inference about the mixture assignment probabilities and the parameters that control the shapes of the tails. I know Stan can't do spike+slab models, so I wrote a Gibbs sampler. However, I don't like having to use conjugate priors on the pareto distribution parameters, and I eventually want to put all of these distributions into a big hierarchical model which might be a stretch of my Gibbs sampling abilities. The friendly person behind @mcmc_stan on twitter suggested there should be a workaround in stan, so I'm posting here to see what people think about this problem and/or if anyone has any suggestions.  I looked at the previous discussion topics for spike and slabs but they mostly seemed to be about discouraging people from using spike+slab priors -- and yes, I would absolutely never use spikes in my priors, but in this data there is a genuine discrete spike and I want to model it.
>
> Thanks so much in advance for any input or advice you have!
>
> Cheers
> Rachael
>

The main problems were
 Lack of a license.stan file in inst/chunks which tools/make_cpp.R is hard-coded to try to #include . I have added an empty license.stan but you should fill that in inside /* */
Declaring the refund package under Imports in DESCRIPTION (and also mistakenly adding an apostrophe to @imports refund in the .R file
Lack of #' @useDynLib mypackage, .registration = TRUE in a .R file (so Roxygen was regenerating the NAMESPACE without the useDynLib(mypackage, .registration = TRUE) line
Thanks for using rstan.package.skeleton, as it helps me figure out where the documentation / automation needs to be improved. Some tips:
Put ... as an argument to gfpcaBayes and pass that to sampling, rather than hard-coding the arguments
Using a multivariate non-centered parameterization (Matt trick) in the .stan file. This would require inverting the Cholesky factor of the precision matrices and multiplying by independent standard normals

Ben

parameters is fine for the likelihood.  See the zero-inflation models in the manual for an example.
These mixtures also tend to be well-identified and fit well; I use zero-inflation all the time.
It’s just a small jump to the three-component model you want to build.

messages.body_plain:
Regarding interpretable parameters:

I think it _is_ a good idea for parameters to be interpretable in the sense of having an understandable meaning within a generative model.

But I do _not_ think it necessary or often appropriate for parameters in a model to align with quantities of interest or relevant causal summaries.  For a simple example, consider a 2-part model which first has a logit probability of income exceeding zero, and then a log regression for income, conditional on it being zero (similar issues arise in survival-type models).  Then a total causal effect will be expressed as the difference in expected income, which tangles both parts of the model and is not a single coefficient.  And that’s fine:  people should abandon the idea that they have to set up their model so that a particular “beta” is the parameter they care about.

A

So you could have a categorical logit model for whether the person falls into a loss-making/zero profit/profitable category (use k-1 parameterisation with informative priors), and then model the loss or profit with and exponential or lognormal distribution or whatnot, conditional on the category. This should be a lot easier than mixture modeling, and won't have all the weird label-switching problems.
>
> The disadvantage is that your parameters aren't as interpretable, so any treatment effects estimate will be the "derivative" of the posterior prediction with respect to the treatment. But that's not hard to simulate.
>
> Jim
>
> On Monday, April 4, 2016 at 1:43:15 PM UTC-4, Rachael Meager wrote:
> > Hi Folks,
> >
> > I'm trying to explicitly model some distributions that have very fat tails and a discrete spike at zero. The two tails can sometimes look very different to each other and I want to capture that. To give you some context: this is profit data at a household level from some developing countries. Some households in my data make positive business profits, some make negative, and some make zero or don't operate a business at all (which gets recorded as an exact zero). I need to keep all of these households in the sample because I want to study the distributional effects of a binary treatment variable on these people, which might include moving some people out of the spike into the tails or vice versa. I'm attaching some histograms as examples. The plots are zoomed in / truncated on both axes - the true spike is much higher and the true tails go much further out, but you get the idea.
> >
> > After some discussions with econometrics and EECS folks around MIT, and using some prior information from economic theory that suggests income/profit/wealth variables typically follow power laws, I figured to start with a mixture model with a discrete spike at zero and 2 pareto distributions as the 2 tails (obviously the negative tail has to be a kind of "reverse" pareto). I want to do inference about the mixture assignment probabilities and the parameters that control the shapes of the tails. I know Stan can't do spike+slab models, so I wrote a Gibbs sampler. However, I don't like having to use conjugate priors on the pareto distribution parameters, and I eventually want to put all of these distributions into a big hierarchical model which might be a stretch of my Gibbs sampling abilities. The friendly person behind @mcmc_stan on twitter suggested there should be a workaround in stan, so I'm posting here to see what people think about this problem and/or if anyone has any suggestions.  I looked at the previous discussion topics for spike and slabs but they mostly seemed to be about discouraging people from using spike+slab priors -- and yes, I would absolutely never use spikes in my priors, but in this data there is a genuine discrete spike and I want to model it.
> >
> > Thanks so much in advance for any input or advice you have!
> >
> > Cheers
> > Rachael
> >

Hello,

[Background: I am trying to fit a model that is extremely slow
and I am now investigating the possibility to save time by reducing
the number of warm up iterations (which is slow due to a
small step size). Details here:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!category-topic/stan-users/general/KWzdLTVLILI)

Is it correct that the distribution of 150 warm up iterations is

75 iterations fast adaption
25 iterations slow adaptation
50 iterations fast adaptation

whereas if one uses 149 warm up iterations the distribution is

23 iterations fast adaptation
113 iterations slow adaptation
14 iterations fast adaptation
 ?

This seems to be implied by the default adaptation parameters
and stan's behavior if one specifies fewer than 150 warm-up
iterations.

It would also seem to me that if one specifies exactly 150 warm up
iterations, adaptation intervals for slow adaptation will not expand
as described in the stan language reference.  (I am not sure what
happens if one specifies e.g. 180 warm up iterations, so that the
total number of slow warm up iterations is not a multiple of 25.)

So it appears to me that if one uses relatively few warm up iterations,
one should better also set init_buffer, term_buffer, and window
(and not only the total number of warm up iteration.)
Is this correct?*

Finally:
How can I determine how many warm up iterations are needed,
or if adaptation was successful?

Best - Guido

* If yes, an immediate follow up questions is if I have e.g. 75
iterations for slow parameter adaption: Is it better to have one
75 iteration window, or is it better to set window=25 to get one 25
 and one 50 iterations wide window?

messages.body_plain:
Tweaking warmup isn’t going to help.

There are two possibilities for why your step size is small.
Either your posterior is really complex and the step size
needs to be small to report accurate results, in which case
warmup is working as it should, or your posterior has a
pathological region that causes adaptation to decrease
the step size to zero.  In the latter warmup is still doing
what it is supposed to do and tweaking it won’t make the
pathological region go away.

If you step size is small but nonzero, say around 1e-4 or 1e-5
then you just have a complex model and there’s not much
you can do besides decor relation parameters by implementing
your model in another way.

If your step size is equivalent to floating point zero, around 1e-15
or lower, then you have pathological regions and HMC isn’t
going to be able to do much of anything (nor is any other
algorithm).  This is often due to very bad nonlinear non-identifiabilties
and in this case you’ll definitely have to tweak your model.
You can play around with centering vs noncentering various
groups as well as the carful specification of priors.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Initial Value Rejection with CVODE
messages.body_plain:
Stan is like any other C++ program and can be run through GDB with enough
effort, although you’ll have to be careful because of all the templates.  Print
statements are typically much faster than trying to following GDB as it bounces
between Stan and CVODE.

The -1 error states that CVODE hit the max_num_steps threshold that you
specified (See Section B.2 of the CVODE manual), which is not uncommon
out in the tails of the parameters. You can increase the threshold from 1e6 to
1e8 or the like or find a better initial condition, but your model looks sufficiently
complex that I would step back and start with something simpler.  The bounds
are not helping anything — use soft contains with priors instead.  The 1e-11
in the ODE specification is a sure sign that you can rescale your parameters
so that they’re all O(1) which could make huge improvements.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speed of a single iteration
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Speed of a single iteration
messages.body_plain:
> I'm trying to get my head around how a single interation in NUTS proceeds. From the paper it seems like the running time of a single iteration should be approximately
>
> O([number of leapfrog steps] * [time to compute derivatives for a leapfrog step])
>
> Is this the case?

Yes.

> When sampler optimization is discussed here we usually focus on reparameterizations that make sampling "easier". Does the following mechanism explain why this works?
>
> sampling easier -> fewer rejected proposals -> larger step size needed to achieve desired acceptance rate -> fewer leapfrog steps on average before u-turn -> faster iterations

The causality is not quite correct.  Better model implementations have two effects.

Firstly they can make the optimal integration time (epsilon * number of leapfrog steps)
decrease, which means fewer leapfrog steps regardless of epsilon.

Secondly, they can lead to larger epsilon.  The step size has to match the
smallest length scale in the posterior, and better model implementations can
have larger smallest length scales.

Typically the integration time will scale with the longest length scale so the
number of leapfrog steps will scale as

number of leapfrog steps = integration time / step size \approx coefficient * longest length scale / shortest length scale.

Ideal posteriors have the same length scale in each parameter direction,
so that the ratio of length scales is unity, and decrease that leading
coefficient.

> Does this suggest that I could speed up sampling by reducing adapt_delta (as long as it didn't result in more than a few divergent transitions)?

Reducing from delta = 0.8 to anywhere above 0.6 may lead to marginally
faster execution, but below 0.6 is likely to be much worse.  In general you
want to stick to the interval [0.6, 0.8] unless there are divergences, and
if there are divergences look to larger values to decrease the step size.

> Also, is vectorization the only way to decrease the derivative computation time?

You can also try to reuse shared expressions and avoid unnecessary
computation (such as inverting a constant matrix).

On Mon, Apr 4, 2016 at 5:21 PM, WallSt <how...@zail.org> wrote:

> The results between the GP method and the GAM method look quite different on the right hand side tail of the first derivative plot,  The r-bloggers plot has the first derivative above 1% and your plot has the first derivative tending to 0%. Your graph suggests a slowdown in temperatures increasing, but not the r-bloggers post.

I wonder if this difference might be more trivially attributed to the mean-reversion behaviour at the edges induced by my re-scaling of the data and use of a 0 mean vector. I'm guessing that GAM prefers to just stay in the region of the local data.

> Also, your choice of priors seems worth investigating.  Perhaps changing the priors to something non-informative might make a difference.  Perhaps you could try cauchy priors?

I chose the priors to be fairly wide-yet-reasonably shaped defaults  (i.e. avoiding cauchy for poor sampling behaviour as noted in other threads here, and using a non-zero-mode for sigma & eta). Switching to cauchy(0,4) for all the hyperparameters (rho, sigma, eta) yields much slower sampling (lower ESS given constant time) but not particularly distinguishable posterior ribbons for the mean function.

> Finally, there could be a change point in the data.  Try splitting the data from 1950 onwards and see if the hyperparameters change.

Neat idea!

messages.body_plain:
Hi All.

I have been playing around with the dynamic model for a long time. It turns out that using weakly informative priors as specified by Gelman (2008) to anchor the dynamic parameters helps; I also had to tweak the max_treedepth, but now the model converges beautifully, and has some of the desired properties (i.e. strong correlation between beta_t and beta_(t-1) that wears off slowly deeper down the temporal chain (model below).

Two problems remain:

First, my division random effects have a very wide posterior distribution for divisions in which I have no data (specifically, Division 3 and Division 6; I can post posterior results if desired). From my understanding, the posterior here should be pretty much the same as the prior, i.e. have 95% of the probability mass between -0.9 and 0.9, but the estimated standard deviation is >10.

Second, I am trying to use the model results to get probability estimates for voting for specific demographic combinations, but I am unsure what metric to use to construct point estimates and credible intervals. My initial idea was to construct HPD intervals by doing something like

 params_dem<-extract(fit)
best_dem<-which.max(params_dem$lp__)

and do the same for the 2.5% and 97.5% percentile. The problem here is that different model runs yield very different point estimates, which I guess is attributable to the built-in strong correlative structure of the model. I guess alternatively I can construct n.draws probability estimates for each demographic combination and then take the empirical percentiles, but even this yields substantively different point estimates. Having said that, the model converges perfectly in terms of the Rubin-Gelman diagnostic. I can't quite wrap my head around this, and any suggestions as to how to construct reliable point-estimates of probability and credible intervals based on the below model are more than welcome!

Many thanks again,
Tobi

The Model:

data {
  int<lower=0> N;                                         // sample wave_size

  int<lower=0> n_age;                                     // number of age categories
  int<lower=0> n_race;                                    // number of race categories
  int<lower=0> n_edu;                                     // number of education catoegories
  int<lower=0> n_division;                                // number of Divisions
  int<lower=0> n_states;                                  // number of States
  int<lower=0> n_party_id;                                // number of party-categories
  int<lower=0> n_waves;                                   // number of Waves

  int<lower=0,upper=n_division> division[N];              // Division for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=1> gender[N];                         // Gender each respondent

  int<lower=0,upper=n_age> age[N];                        // age for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_edu> edu[N];                        // edu for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_race> race[N];                      // race for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_party_id> party_id[N];              // party_id for each respondent

  real vote_prev_state[N];                                // 2012 state-vote at the individual-level

  int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];                              // vote-choice

  int<lower=0,upper=N> in_wave[N];                        // wave of respondents
  int<lower=0>        wave_size[n_waves];                 // N individuals per Wave
 int<lower=0> wave_lims[n_waves,2];                       // first individual in wave and individuals per wave                                                              (5*2 matrix)
}
parameters {

  real beta [n_waves];                                    // coefficient-array for female; wave
  vector[n_age] a_age [n_waves];                          // coefficient-array for age; wave
  vector[n_edu] a_edu [n_waves];                          // coefficient-array for edu; wave
  vector[n_race] a_race [n_waves];                        // coefficient-array for race; wave
  vector[n_party_id] a_party_id [n_waves];                // coefficient-array for party_id; wave
  vector [n_division] a_division[n_waves];                // coefficient-array for division; wave

  real gamma;                                             // previous vote- slope
}

model {

  gamma~cauchy(0,2.5);                                    // embed 95% probability mass between 0.01% and 99.9%                                                           // (Gelman 2008)
  a_division[1]~ cauchy(0,0.425);                         // embed 95% probability mass between 70% and 30%
  beta[1]~cauchy(0,2.5);                                  // embed 95% probability mass between 0.01% and 99.9%
  a_age[1]~cauchy(0,2.5);                                 // embed 95% probability mass between 0.01% and 99.9%
  a_edu[1]~cauchy(0,2.5);                                 // embed 95% probability mass between 0.01% and 99.9%
  a_race[1]~cauchy(0,2.5);                                // embed 95% probability mass between 0.01% and 99.9%
  a_party_id[1]~cauchy(0,2.5);                            // embed 95% probability mass between 0.01% and 99.9%

  for (k in 2:n_waves) {

    beta[k] ~ normal(beta[k-1], 0.05);                    //  assume 5% shift per demographic per wave covers                                                            // 95% of probability mass
    a_age[k] ~ normal(a_age[k-1], 0.05);                  // assume 5% shift per demographic per wave covers                                                             // 95% of probability mass
    a_edu[k] ~ normal(a_edu[k-1], 0.05);                  // assume 5% shift per demographic per wave covers
                                                          // 95% of probability mass
    a_race[k] ~ normal(a_race[k-1], 0.05);                // assume 5% shift per demographic per wave covers                                                             // 95% of probability mass
    a_party_id[k] ~ normal(a_party_id[k-1], 0.05);        // assume 5% shift per demographic per wave covers                                                             // 95% of probability mass
    a_division[k] ~ normal(a_division[k-1], 0.05);

}
                                                          //Likelihood for each i in each wave
for(s in 1:n_waves){
      int obs_in_wave[wave_size[s]];

obs_in_wave<-segment(in_wave,wave_lims[s,1],wave_lims[s,2]) ;   // find observations in each wave
  for (i in 1:wave_size[s]) {
real y_hat;
    y_hat <-
    beta[s]*gender[obs_in_wave[i]]
    +a_age[s,age[obs_in_wave[i]]]
    +a_edu[s,edu[obs_in_wave[i]]]
    +a_party_id[s,party_id[obs_in_wave[i]]]

    +a_race[s,race[obs_in_wave[i]]]+gamma*vote_prev_state[i]
    +a_division[s,division[obs_in_wave[i]]];

    y[obs_in_wave[i]] ~ bernoulli_logit(y_hat);
  }
  }
  }

Extreme quantiles, including min and max, are extremely noisy.  Stick
to at least 5/95, if not 10/90, to get more stable results.

On Apr 5, 2016, at 4:43 PM, Tobias Konitzer <tobias....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Second, I am trying to use the model results to get probability estimates for voting for specific demographic combinations, but I am unsure what metric to use to construct point estimates and credible intervals. My initial idea was to construct HPD intervals by doing something like
>
>  params_dem<-extract(fit)
> best_dem<-which.max(params_dem$lp__)
>
> and do the same for the 2.5% and 97.5% percentile. The problem here is that different model runs yield very different point estimates, which I guess is attributable to the built-in strong correlative structure of the model. I guess alternatively I can construct n.draws probability estimates for each demographic combination and then take the empirical percentiles, but even this yields substantively different point estimates. Having said that, the model converges perfectly in terms of the Rubin-Gelman diagnostic. I can't quite wrap my head around this, and any suggestions as to how to construct reliable point-estimates of probability and credible intervals based on the below model are more than welcome!

messages.subject: parameter correlations in posterior?
messages.subject_clean: parameter correlations in posterior?
messages.body_plain:
My understanding is that HMC with unit mass matrix
is invariant to rotations of the posterior, but not scaling.
Gibbs is the opposite (invariant to scale, but not rotation).

But when we do adaptation of a diagonal mass matrix, we run
into the problem that we break rotational symmetry in the algorithm.
Is that why correlated parameters can be problematic for HMC?
If we adapt a dense mass matrix, do we regain rotation invariance
(up to the formidable issue of estimating that mass matrix).

I'm not worried (yet) in this discussion about varying curvature.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Whether you need a Jacobian depends on what you
do with pi_new.  If you have pi_new on the left
of a ~ (literally or conceptually through increment_log_prob),
then you need a Jacobian.

I discuss that approach to the label-switching problem
in the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual.  Ordering
changes the posterior; how dramatically depends on how close
your mixture components are to each other.

I didn't understand why you wanted to define pi_new the way
you did.  Why not just define pi_new as a parameter directly?

Also, if you don't need to save tmp, you could define this as:

>   transformed parameters {
>     positive_ordered[K] pi_new;
>     {
>        positive_ordered[K+1] tmp;
>        tmp <- cumulative_sum(theta); //going to discard this variable
     }
>     pi_new <- head(tmp,K)/tmp[K+1];

and then tmp is a local variable that won't be saved.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for bringing this up --- it's a very legitimate concern
that I keep bringing up myself.

Here's a complete list of the planned changes:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Stan-3-Density-Notation-and-Increments

Each plan change is clearly (I hope) laid out and distinguished
from the background discussion.  2.10 will have at least these changes:

  * = replacing <- for assignment

  * target += ... replacing increment_log_prob(...)

In both cases, the existing behavior is deprecated, so there'll be
full backward compatiblity.  I'm in the middle of adding the vertical
bar and _lpdf, etc. notation, but it probably won't make it until
2.11.

We're not going to break backward compatibility until we
release Stan 3, and that's probably at least a year out
at the pace we're going.  We hope to do that with automatic
translation scripts for models, but no promises (we're very
shorthanded for core Stan development below the interfaces
level).  And even with Stan 3, we might still support our
old syntax and not remove it until Stan 4.  I'm terribly worried
about running into a Python 2.x vs. 3.x problem. We can't
afford to fork our entire community because the core dev team
is too small.

- Bob

On Tue, Apr 5, 2016, 3:39 PM Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Tweaking warmup isn’t going to help.
>
> There are two possibilities for why your step size is small.
> Either your posterior is really complex and the step size
> needs to be small to report accurate results, in which case
> warmup is working as it should, or your posterior has a
> pathological region that causes adaptation to decrease
> the step size to zero.  In the latter warmup is still doing
> what it is supposed to do and tweaking it won’t make the
> pathological region go away.
>
> If you step size is small but nonzero, say around 1e-4 or 1e-5
> then you just have a complex model and there’s not much
> you can do besides decor relation parameters by implementing
> your model in another way.
>
> If your step size is equivalent to floating point zero, around 1e-15
> or lower, then you have pathological regions and HMC isn’t
> going to be able to do much of anything (nor is any other
> algorithm).  This is often due to very bad nonlinear non-identifiabilties
> and in this case you’ll definitely have to tweak your model.
> You can play around with centering vs noncentering various
> groups as well as the carful specification of priors.
>

>

> Basically what I am doing is to model random coefficient beta_i with individual predictors, say beta_i is i*3 matrix, Z_i is individual predictors data, a i*4 matrix

> beta_i ~ multi_normal(Z_i*delta, Vbeta)

it needs to be solved.

We prefer scaled LKJ to inverse Wishart.

messages.subject_clean: Reproducing a simple clustered-robust standard error OLS with Stan
messages.body_plain:
Corey's right! Include a cluster-specific random effect for the intercept. You can also do cluster-specific REs on the slopes. If your variables only vary at the cluster level the slopes correction may be harder but even then I think you might be able to do it as long as you constrain the functional form that governs the REs.

Cluster-Robust SEs actually do less controlling for intracluster correlation than cluster REs do. Once you have the cluster REs I don't think the cluster-robust SE makes any sense, there should be no residual correlation to pick up...

Like Bob said, Stan is really for fitting Bayesian models, and cluster-robust SEs are a specific kind of frequentist corrective to standard errors on a frequentist estimate. I don't think smushing these things together will produce anything coherent, let alone useful. It is an interest of mine to understand the relationship between these kinds of frequentist SE correctives and the bayesian modelling tools we use to combat the same problems, but there is not much work on it yet. If I were you I would first try to understand the relationship between these things before smushing them together, I suspect you'll find that it won't make sense to combine them, but I am willing to be shown a proof to the contrary. :)

Cheers
Rachael

(i)  Michael --- are you still running a zero-tolerance policy on
divergent transitions?

(iii) Philip --- that imputation should be OK if all the chains
converged.  100 imputations is probably overkill.   But I'm going to
post another question with a fresh subject to try to get Andrew's attention
to see what he thinks the impact on R-hat etc. would be.

(v) Cauchy posteriors are bad news because expectations aren't defined.
But Cauchy priors don't lead to Cauchy posteriors when there's more than
a few data points (get a theoretician or someone with experimental cycles
to answer more precisely).

Running with a higher adapt_delta (target acceptance rate) should answer
the question of whether the divergences matter here.

- Bob

> On Apr 1, 2016, at 1:52 PM, Philip Boonstra <ph...@boonstras.com> wrote:
>
> Hi, First, thanks to the development team for such a fantastic tool for practical Bayesian analysis. Count me a big Stan fan.
>
> Second, I'm in a bit of a conundrum. Session info is at the bottom. Here are the salient points.
>
> (i) I fit a logistic regression with a horseshoe (i.e. two-level, half-cauchy) prior, parametrized as follows:
> data {
>   int<lower=0> n_stan; // num obs
>   int<lower=0> p_stan; // num covariates
>   int<lower=0,upper=1> y_stan[n_stan]; // outcome
>   matrix[n_stan,p_stan] x_scaled_stan; //covariates (no intercept)
> }
> parameters {
>   real mu;
>   vector[p_stan] beta_raw;
>   real<lower=0> tau;
>   vector<lower=0>[p_stan] lambda;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>   vector[p_stan] beta;
>   beta <- tau*(lambda .* beta_raw);
> }
> model {
>   lambda ~ cauchy(0,1);
>   tau ~ cauchy(0,1);
>   beta_raw ~ normal(0,1);
>   y_stan ~ bernoulli_logit(mu + x_scaled_stan * beta);
> }
> (ii) I fit the data to about 1600 observations, 54 predictors (after transforming categorical to dummy and specifying my interactions)
> (iii) There were missing data - mostly sporadic. My strategy to handle this was as follows: construct 100 multiply imputed datasets, run the the sampler on each imputed dataset for a warmup of 400 and 300 additional iterations, and concatenate the results for posterior inference on the combined 100x300 = 30,000 draws.
> (iv) I originally did the analysis using rstan v2.5.0, so I did not see warnings about divergent iterations. Everything looked reasonable, e.g. Rhats < 1.02, reasonable traceplots, clinically sensible findings. And the covariates the model identified as most impactful co-coincided with my collaborator's clinical prior. Our model performed decently but not stellar. AUC in the training data of about 0.68; AUC in the validation data of about 0.64. Fairly well calibrated.
> (v) However, while doing some follow-up work (and having learned about the issues of sampling from the Cauchy distribution in Stan), and with the latest and greatest rstan (v2.9.0-3) in hand, I see now that about 1-2% of my iterations are reported as divergent, i.e. about 3-7 for each chain of 300 iterations. Looking at paired plots and shinystan, the divergent iterations do not jump out at me as inherently pathological. No funnel shapes, no divergent iterations near tails of the parameters or the posterior mode.
> My questions: The analysis is finalized at this point, with the results already in press. Much of the language in the RStan vignette and google discussions here suggests that observing any divergent iterations after the warmup is unacceptable. Is that a fair interpretation -- is it the presence of divergent iterations or the proportion of divergent iterations that matters more? Or is that too general of a question to ask? Is re-running the analysis with, a larger targeted acceptance rate and/or t_3 tails warranted here, at least for a sensitivity analysis?
>
> Thanks in advance,
> Phil

> Platform: x86_64-apple-darwin13.4.0 (64-bit)
> Running under: OS X 10.11.2 (El Capitan)

messages.body_plain:
> (i)  Michael --- are you still running a zero-tolerance policy on
> divergent transitions?

Yes with caveats for people who really know what they are doing (i.e. me*).
Basically if the divergences can be ignored then you should be able to
get rid of them by increasing adapt_delta by a small amount.  If that
doesn’t work then the divergences are meaningful.

*The only time I personally ignore divergences is when I can isolate
their origin to hierarchical effects that should be implemented with
a partially-centered parameterization, so not quite centered but not
quite noncentered.  But this requires a lot of expertise and I make
no guarantees of valid results if you ignore any divergences.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] parameter correlations in posterior?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] parameter correlations in posterior?
messages.body_plain:
There is a lot of confusion around these points, so let me
start from the beginning.

1)  In theory Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is fully geometric,
which means it is independent to whatever choice of
parameters we use.  Gibbs sampling does depend on
the parametrization, as the exact parametrization defines
the conditionals.

Operationally, if we change the parameters (potential
energy) then the momenta (kinetic energy) have to change
in the opposite way so that the Hamiltonian, and hence
the trajectories, remain invariant.

Provided that we transform the parameters and momenta
together then all versions of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo are
invariant to any well-behaved transformation, including
rotations and scalings.

Interestingly enough, Random walk Metropolis behaves
the same way!  When we transform the parameters we
also have to transform the proposal covariance or _we’re
specifying a different transition_!

2)  This is confusing because in practice people often
transform the parameters but leave the momenta (kinetic
energy) the same.  Because we’re not transforming them
together, this implies that we’re specifying a _different_
kinetic energy.

For example, a “unit mass matrix” is defined only relative
to a given parameterization.  If we transform the system
then both the parameters and momenta change, including
the mass matrix to something non-unit.  Forcing the
mass matrix to stay unit while changing the parameters
is implicitly defining a different kinetic energy.

The same thing happens with Random walk Metropolis.
If we keep the covariance constant but change the
parameters then we’re effectively defining a completely
different transition and can expect different performance.

3) All of this is complicated by adaptation.  If we define
the mass matrix to be the global covariance of the target
distribution then we have no freedom to transform the
parameters and momenta separately.  Change the
parameters and the form of the global covariance
changes, hence the mass matrix changes.  But this
leaves the total system invariant as in (1).

In summary, all of this is confusing because people often
talk about the invariance of the posterior _relative to a fixed
kinetic energy and mass matrix_.  But that’s an odd construction
because the parameters and momenta/kinetic energy/mass matrix
are supposed to transform together, so fixing the kinetic energy
and changing the parameterization is just a sneaky way to specify
an mass matrix.

The performance of HMC depends on how the target distribution
interacts with the kinetic energy.  If the target distribution is
correlated in a parameterization but the kinetic energy is defined
with a unit mass matrix then the trajectories will be highly
oscillatory and expensive to simulate.  If the parameterization
is fixed then rotating and scaling the mass matrix can define
a more optimal kinetic energy that reduces the oscillatory nature
of these trajectories.

Ultimately one can show that the optimal Euclidean mass matrix
is given by the global covariance of the target distribution, which
is invariant to any particular parameterization as discussed above.

Okay, that probably didn’t make any sense so we’ll have to iterate.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] pystan ADVI
messages.body_plain:
That doesn't solve your problem, it just masks it!

If you really have multiple modes, as in mixture models like K-means,
LDA, or unsupervised HMMs, nothing is going to solve your problem.
The technology doesn't exist to do full Bayesian inference in these
settings and the approximations (like taking a variational approximation
of a single mode) are a long way from the actual model people write
down in their papers.

The command-line version works and should be easy to call
from Python.  The output is CSV so it should be easy to read
back in.  The only hassle is the input data format, which is
an easy one to generate programatically.  And given that you don't
want any of the posterior analysis tools, I'd recommend just going
the command-line route.

- Bob

> On Apr 5, 2016, at 4:36 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> There is a lot of confusion around these points, so let me
> start from the beginning.
>
> 1)  In theory Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is fully geometric,
> which means it is independent to whatever choice of
> parameters we use.  Gibbs sampling does depend on
> the parametrization, as the exact parametrization defines
> the conditionals.
>
> Operationally, if we change the parameters (potential
> energy) then the momenta (kinetic energy) have to change
> in the opposite way so that the Hamiltonian, and hence
> the trajectories, remain invariant.
>
> Provided that we transform the parameters and momenta
> together then all versions of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo are
> invariant to any well-behaved transformation, including
> rotations and scalings.
>
> Interestingly enough, Random walk Metropolis behaves
> the same way!  When we transform the parameters we
> also have to transform the proposal covariance or _we’re
> specifying a different transition_!
>
> 2)  This is confusing because in practice people often
> transform the parameters but leave the momenta (kinetic
> energy) the same.  Because we’re not transforming them
> together, this implies that we’re specifying a _different_
> kinetic energy.
>
> For example, a “unit mass matrix” is defined only relative
> to a given parameterization.  If we transform the system
> then both the parameters and momenta change, including
> the mass matrix to something non-unit.  Forcing the
> mass matrix to stay unit while changing the parameters
> is implicitly defining a different kinetic energy.
>
> The same thing happens with Random walk Metropolis.
> If we keep the covariance constant but change the
> parameters then we’re effectively defining a completely
> different transition and can expect different performance.
>
> 3) All of this is complicated by adaptation.  If we define
> the mass matrix to be the global covariance of the target
> distribution then we have no freedom to transform the
> parameters and momenta separately.  Change the
> parameters and the form of the global covariance
> changes, hence the mass matrix changes.  But this
> leaves the total system invariant as in (1).
>
> In summary, all of this is confusing because people often
> talk about the invariance of the posterior _relative to a fixed
> kinetic energy and mass matrix_.  But that’s an odd construction
> because the parameters and momenta/kinetic energy/mass matrix
> are supposed to transform together, so fixing the kinetic energy
> and changing the parameterization is just a sneaky way to specify
> an mass matrix.
>
> The performance of HMC depends on how the target distribution
> interacts with the kinetic energy.  If the target distribution is
> correlated in a parameterization but the kinetic energy is defined
> with a unit mass matrix then the trajectories will be highly
> oscillatory and expensive to simulate.  If the parameterization
> is fixed then rotating and scaling the mass matrix can define
> a more optimal kinetic energy that reduces the oscillatory nature
> of these trajectories.
>
> Ultimately one can show that the optimal Euclidean mass matrix
> is given by the global covariance of the target distribution, which
> is invariant to any particular parameterization as discussed above.
>
> Okay, that probably didn’t make any sense so we’ll have to iterate.
>
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Determining impact of divergent transitions after warmup
messages.body_plain:
The answer is (iii) --- it's a computational issue.

There's not much out there to read!  Basically just what Michael's
written --- in papers (see arXiv), in our manual, and on this
list and the dev list.

It's almost always caused by areas of high curvature in the posterior
which are difficult to follow using only small steps along the gradient.
It almost always manifests as floating-point underflow or overflow in
the density or gradient calculations, which we report as "divergent"
iterations.

If the curvature (second derivative matrix) doesn't vary by position
in the posterior (as in the multivariate normal), then adaptation
is much easier.  When curvature varies a lot, as in a hierarchical
model (see the funnel example in the manual), adaptation to a single
step size/mass matrix isn't possible, and areas of the posterior become
hard to explore.

This also explains why reparameterization can help.  Again, see the
funnel example in the manual for an extreme example, or read Michael's
paper with Mark Girolami on hierarchical models for much more detail
and an explanation of how data can tame the funnel prior.

It's hard to quantify how much bias there might be without getting
a better handle on what's really going on in a paticular posterior.  Usually
it's not very big in the examples I've looked at.  You'll wind up getting
the same kinds of biases with Gibbs, Metropolis and ensemble samplers---these are
hard problems computationally;  we're just trying to be helpful in providing
diagnostics.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] parameter correlations in posterior?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] parameter correlations in posterior?
messages.body_plain:
Given a parameterization, the only unconstrained distribution
specified by a global covariance is the Gaussian,
so we can reduce this discussion to Gaussian targets.

The Hamiltonian in this case is given by

H = 0.5 * p^{T} M^{-1} p + 0.5 * (q - mu)^{T} Sigma^{-1} (q - mu)

Now we can apply an orthogonal transformation to rotate the q/mu,
but to maintain the same system we have to do the opposite
to the momenta,

q -> X q
p -> X^{T} p

which gives

H = 0.5 * p^{T} X M^{-1} X^{T} p + 0.5 * (q - mu)^{T} X^{T} Sigma^{-1} X (q - mu)

The optimal transform completely decouples this into N one-dimensional
(1 q + 1 p) systems.  We start by decoupling the potential energy — if
Sigma = L L^{T} then we want X = L so that

H = 0.5 * p^{T} L M^{-1} L^{T} p + 0.5 * (q - mu)^{T} (q - mu)

Then the kinetic energy decouples if M = Sigma.  In other words,
the only way to decouple a correlated Gaussian is to set the
mass matrix to the global covariance of the target distribution.

messages.body_plain:
Hello Michael,

I am attaching a figure with the evolution of step size and n leapfrog steps.
dotted vertical lines delineate warm up phases and the solid vertical lines
delineates the end of the warm up.

As you can see, up to ~65 000 leapfrogs are done per iteration during warm up,
before the the step size goes down in in the terminal buffer. Given that my machine
needs 2100s per leapfrog step (warm up took nearly 6 days!) I really would like to
further reduce the number of warm up iterations.

That is why i was asking for ways to assess if warm up was successful.
Intuitively I think that I should get away with a relatively short warm up, because
even if my model is complex, I still have lots of data.

best - guido

PS: I have already optimized the model by using non-centered parameterization of
regression coefficients and for cauchy distributed variables.

On Tuesday, April 5, 2016 at 3:39:43 PM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Tweaking warmup isn’t going to help.
>
> There are two possibilities for why your step size is small.
> Either your posterior is really complex and the step size
> needs to be small to report accurate results, in which case
> warmup is working as it should, or your posterior has a
> pathological region that causes adaptation to decrease
> the step size to zero.  In the latter warmup is still doing
> what it is supposed to do and tweaking it won’t make the
> pathological region go away.
>
> If you step size is small but nonzero, say around 1e-4 or 1e-5
> then you just have a complex model and there’s not much
> you can do besides decor relation parameters by implementing
> your model in another way.
>
> If your step size is equivalent to floating point zero, around 1e-15
> or lower, then you have pathological regions and HMC isn’t
> going to be able to do much of anything (nor is any other
> algorithm).  This is often due to very bad nonlinear non-identifiabilties
> and in this case you’ll definitely have to tweak your model.
> You can play around with centering vs noncentering various
> groups as well as the carful specification of priors.
>
>
> On Apr 5, 2016, at 10:02 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Hello,
> >
> > [Background: I am trying to fit a model that is extremely slow
> > and I am now investigating the possibility to save time by reducing
> > the number of warm up iterations (which is slow due to a
> > small step size). Details here:
> > https://groups.google.com/forum/#!category-topic/stan-users/general/KWzdLTVLILI)
> >
> >
> >
> > Is it correct that the distribution of 150 warm up iterations is
> >
> > 75 iterations fast adaption
> > 25 iterations slow adaptation
> > 50 iterations fast adaptation
> >
> > whereas if one uses 149 warm up iterations the distribution is
> >
> > 23 iterations fast adaptation
> > 113 iterations slow adaptation
> > 14 iterations fast adaptation
> >  ?
> >
> > This seems to be implied by the default adaptation parameters
> > and stan's behavior if one specifies fewer than 150 warm-up
> > iterations.
> >
> > It would also seem to me that if one specifies exactly 150 warm up
> > iterations, adaptation intervals for slow adaptation will not expand
> > as described in the stan language reference.  (I am not sure what
> > happens if one specifies e.g. 180 warm up iterations, so that the
> > total number of slow warm up iterations is not a multiple of 25.)
> >
> > So it appears to me that if one uses relatively few warm up iterations,

> > Is this correct?*
> >

> > * If yes, an immediate follow up questions is if I have e.g. 75

messages.subject: Creating Posterior Predictive Checks
messages.subject_clean: Creating Posterior Predictive Checks
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm in the middle of a series of workshops on Bayesian data analysis
and Stan as part of Dublin R. I gave them a few years ago but decided
to run it again and switch the inference engine to Stan.

The materials for the workshop are all available in a bitbucket repo

https://bitbucket.org/kaybenleroll/dublin_r_workshops

The relevant stuff is in the wsbda201603 directory for anyone
interested. It's all a bit rough and ready.

Anyway, while I probably won't be covering it this month, I also want
to talk a little about posterior predictive checks - most likely in
the workshop next month.

I am building a hierarchical model for coins, coin tosses and mints as
described by Kruschke in DBDA.

Here is a snapshot of the data:

!> inputdata.dt
       mint.id <http://mint.id> coin.id <http://coin.id> toss.count success
    1:       1       1        888     437
    2:       1       2       1034     524
    3:       1       3       1033     490
    4:       1       4        961     469
    5:       1       5        931     428
   ---
 2525:       5    2525        965     505
 2526:       5    2526        943     498
 2527:       5    2527        983     529
 2528:       5    2528       1026     588
 2529:       5    2529       1061     591

Thus, each datum contains an index for the mint and coin (each coin.id <http://coin.id>
is unique for the whole dataset). Each coin had an individual number
of trials, and the number of successes is also given.

I built a hierarchical model in the standard way, model the theta of
the coin as being drawn from a Beta distribution parameterised by mu
and K, with the mu and K being drawn from a higher Beta and a Gamma
distribution, each mint having its own prior.

I have kept the five mints separately for now, purely to keep things
simple, but figure now is a good time to introduce PPCs.

The idea is  to use the data to assess the quality of the mints. Which
of the 5 mints produces the 'best' coins, best being defined as toss
probability being closest to 0.5 with the lowest variance.

Anyway, I was thinking about the good ways to set this up via the
generated quantities block. I can use each sample to generate a mu and
K for each mint and then generate coins and tosses after that. With
that I could perhaps generate what the overall probability of a
success is across all the coins generated, but also track the min and
max theta for each mint as a way to assess variance.

I know all of this is a little contrived, but it keeps things simple
and allows the attendees to focus on what is going on.

My big question is over how to capture the variance of the coin counts
and toss counts in the data. They are directly supplied rather than
being modelled, so is there a way to sample those counts in the
generated quantities block (like the sample() function in R) or should
I be thinking about this differently and just go with a fixed number
of coins and tosses for this?

Thanks for all your help. All the code I'm using is in the repo, but
please let me know if I am leaving out some details - I'm still a bit
hazy on the best way to use PPCs which is part of the motivation for
covering it in the workshop (I'm selfish that way).

--
Mick Cooney
mickc...@gmail.com
