messages.subject: Random Effect Specifications
messages.subject_clean: Random Effect Specifications
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I have been trying to compare uncertainty estimates with various prior specifications of a simple varying intercept model (predicting Democratic vote). The baseline model (Bayes_0_100_uniform) is below.

data {
  int<lower=0> N;                                         // sample size
  int<lower=0> n_age;                                     // number of age categories
  int<lower=0> n_race;                                    // number of race categories
  int<lower=0> n_edu;                                     // number of education catoegories
  int<lower=0> n_party_id;                                // number of party-categories
  int<lower=0,upper=1> gender[N];                         // gender for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_age> age[N];                        // age for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_edu> edu[N];                        // edu for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_race> race[N];                      // race for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_party_id> party_id[N];              // party_id for each respondent
  real <lower=0,upper=1> vote_prev_state[N];              // 2012 statevote at the individual-level
  int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];                              // vote-choice
}
parameters {

  real beta;                                              // coefficient for female
  vector[n_age] a_age ;                                   // coefficient for age
  vector[n_edu] a_edu;                                    // coefficient for edu
  vector[n_race] a_race;                                  // coefficient for race
  vector[n_party_id] a_party_id;                          // coefficient for party_id
  real gamma;                                             // previous vote- slope
  real<lower=0> sigma_age;
  real<lower=0> sigma_edu;
  real<lower=0> sigma_race;
  real<lower=0> sigma_party;

}

model {                                                 // Prior specifications
sigma_age~uniform(0,100);
sigma_edu~uniform(0,100);
sigma_race~uniform(0,100);
sigma_party~uniform(0,100);

  gamma~normal(0,5);                                  // embed 95% of the probability mass between 0.1 and 99.9%
  beta~normal(0,5);                                   // embed 95% of the probability mass between 0.1 and 99.9%
  a_age~normal(0,sigma_age);                          // estimate sigma separately
  a_edu~normal(0,sigma_edu);                          // estimate sigma separately
  a_race~normal(0,sigma_race);                        // estimate sigma separately
  a_party_id~normal(0,sigma_party);                   // estimate sigma separately

for (i in 1:N) {                                        //Likelihood
real y_hat;
    y_hat <-
    beta*gender[i]
    +a_age[age[i]]
    +a_edu[edu[i]]
    +a_party_id[party_id[i]]
    +a_race[race[i]]+gamma*vote_prev_state[i];
    y[i] ~ bernoulli_logit(y_hat);
  }
  }

>From here, I change the prior specifications on the sigmas for the random effects to be truncated uniform on the 0-Infinity interval (Bayes_unbounded_uniform; the canned STAN prior if the variance-prior is not made explicit), and I remove the prior completely, bounding the random-effect coefficients such that 95% of their probability mass falls between -10 and 10, like so (Bayes_no_prior):

  gamma~normal(0,5);                                  // embed 95% of the probability mass between 0.1 and 99.9%
  beta~normal(0,5);                                   // embed 95% of the probability mass between 0.1 and 99.9%
  a_age~normal(0,5);                                  // embed 95% of the probability mass between 0.1 and 99.9%
  a_edu~normal(0,5);                                  // embed 95% of the probability mass between 0.1 and 99.9%
  a_race~normal(0,5);                                 // embed 95% of the probability mass between 0.1 and 99.9%
  a_party_id~normal(0,5);                             // embed 95% of the probability mass between 0.1 and 99.9%

All three specifications produce very different credible intervals (the last one even different point-estimates), see CIs.pdf (attached; also includes uncertainty estimates from Glmer and Glmer2Stan). All credible intervals are actually wider than the one produced by Glmer. I especially fail to understand why the no-prior-specification yields results that are fundamentally different. Help is appreciated! Data and reproducible code is attached.

Many thanks,
Tobi

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Bob

I tried to simplify my model down and build it up slowly. The problem went away until I added the parameter C (which is block covariance matrix for two time points). This parameter comes in here:

I have some latent variables, x and mu (both are vectors with N elements), with joint distributions

(x[t],x[t+1])' ~ multiNorm((mu[t],mu[t+1])',COV)

where mu is at some higher level and COV is of the form

Sigma C'
C  Sigma

and then

x[t+1] ~ multiNorm(mu+C*inv(Sigma)*(x[t]-mu[t]),Sigma-C*inv(Sigma)*C')

When the model ran I got a lot of errors saying that the new covariance parameter ("Sigma-C*inv(Sigma)*C'" above) was not positive definite when trying to find initial points and it eventually gave up. When I set the initial values I got the message

IMK Stall detected, *please Report* your user scenario in <rdar://problem/16792073> - (imkxpc_windowLevelWithReply:) block performed very slowly (2.74 secs)

many times again. A better way to do this may be to be to specify the whole matrix in the parameters ie.

parameters{
  cov_matrix [2*N] COV;
...
}

and then specify that

COV[N+1:2*N,N+1:2*N] <- COV[1:N,1:N]

I tried this in the transform parameters part but the same thing as above seemed to happen. Is this possible and if so where do I do it? If this did happen, am I right in thinking that it would never converge as the algorithm would just be wandering round the COV[N+1:2*N,N+1:2*N] space. Can anyone think of a better way of defining the parameters as described above?

Cheers
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Creating Posterior Predictive Checks
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Creating Posterior Predictive Checks
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the link and letting us know.

To save Andrew the trouble of responding, I'd use a more realistic
example than coins.  He even wrote a paper on why coins are a bad
example:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/diceRev2.pdf

For pedagogical purposes, I'd only use one level of hierarchy to keep
things simple.  That's what I did in my case study, along with
a range of posterior p-values, predictive checks, predictions, event
probability estimates, and calibration/sharpness tests for model comparison
(of complete pooling, no pooling, along with partial pooling with hierarchical
models:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/pool-binary-trials.html

You'll also see the log-odds parameterization with a comparison to
the beta (for which I used a different prior, following Gelman et al.s
Bayesian Data Analysis, chapter 5).

And yes, using the generated quantities for posterior predictive
checks is exactly what you want to do --- I give examples in the
case study and explain why you want to do it.

I can't tell if I keep pointing to this tutorial because I just wrote
it, or wrote it so I wouldn't have to keep repeating myself!

You don't need all this modeling to answer your "which is the best
mint" question --- to literally answer your question you could just pool
everything within the "mint" and evaluate log density with
binomial(N, 0.5) model.  But really the question for mints isn't
flippability, but weight and size.

But that's probably not the question you really want to answer in
a real application, where either 0 or 1 is usually the target (infant
mortality vs. free throws, say).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Cool.  Thanks.  I had no idea that the Gaussian was
the only distribution with global covariance.

I was thinking unit Gaussian (hence the unit mass matrix).
Clearly that is invariant to rotation because the density
doesn't change in Euclidean coordinates under rotations.
I hadn't quite put all the pieces together to realize how
limited the case was that I was considering.

- Bob

> On Apr 6, 2016, at 4:35 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Given a parameterization, the only unconstrained distribution
> specified by a global covariance is the Gaussian,
> so we can reduce this discussion to Gaussian targets.
>
> The Hamiltonian in this case is given by
>
> H = 0.5 * p^{T} M^{-1} p + 0.5 * (q - mu)^{T} Sigma^{-1} (q - mu)
>
> Now we can apply an orthogonal transformation to rotate the q/mu,
> but to maintain the same system we have to do the opposite
> to the momenta,
>
> q -> X q
> p -> X^{T} p
>
> which gives
>
> H = 0.5 * p^{T} X M^{-1} X^{T} p + 0.5 * (q - mu)^{T} X^{T} Sigma^{-1} X (q - mu)
>
> The optimal transform completely decouples this into N one-dimensional
> (1 q + 1 p) systems.  We start by decoupling the potential energy — if
> Sigma = L L^{T} then we want X = L so that
>
> H = 0.5 * p^{T} L M^{-1} L^{T} p + 0.5 * (q - mu)^{T} (q - mu)
>
> Then the kinetic energy decouples if M = Sigma.  In other words,
> the only way to decouple a correlated Gaussian is to set the
> mass matrix to the global covariance of the target distribution.
>

I'm not sure what Andrew's thinking, but part of the problem
is computational --- you need a lot of draws to estimate tail
quantiles (you can think of this as only 2.5% of the samples
coming into play to help estimate the lower bound of a 95%
interval).

than central intervals or posterior means.

You can see all this through simulation by rerunning with different
seeds and different priors and looking at variance in the 2.5%
vs. 50% quantile estimates.  More things to go in the book!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Distribution of warm up iterations over adaptation of fast and slow parameters?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Distribution of warm up iterations over adaptation of fast and slow parameters?
messages.body_plain:
You can see exactly what happens in the code:
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/develop/src/stan/mcmc/windowed_adaptation.hpp.

If you specify less than init_buffer + term_buffer + window iterations then
the partitions shrink to relative sizes, which should be indicated by a
corresponding output message.

You need the init_window to converge so that the mass matrix isn’t biased by
the tails of the posterior, a long enough intermediate window to get a good
estimate of the global (co)variances, and then a terminal window to let the
step size adapt to the final mass matrix.  We default to a long window to get
a robust estimate of the global covariance to maximize post-warmup
performance.  Any tweaking to try to get away with decent performance
with less warmup is entirely up to your judgment.

On Apr 6, 2016, at 11:16 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hello Michael,
>
> I am attaching a figure with the evolution of step size and n leapfrog steps.
> dotted vertical lines delineate warm up phases and the solid vertical lines
> delineates the end of the warm up.
>
> As you can see, up to ~65 000 leapfrogs are done per iteration during warm up,
> before the the step size goes down in in the terminal buffer. Given that my machine
> needs 2100s per leapfrog step (warm up took nearly 6 days!) I really would like to
> further reduce the number of warm up iterations.
>
> That is why i was asking for ways to assess if warm up was successful.
> Intuitively I think that I should get away with a relatively short warm up, because
> even if my model is complex, I still have lots of data.
>
> best - guido
>
> PS: I have already optimized the model by using non-centered parameterization of
> regression coefficients and for cauchy distributed variables.
>
> On Tuesday, April 5, 2016 at 3:39:43 PM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Tweaking warmup isn’t going to help.
>
> There are two possibilities for why your step size is small.
> Either your posterior is really complex and the step size
> needs to be small to report accurate results, in which case
> warmup is working as it should, or your posterior has a
> pathological region that causes adaptation to decrease
> the step size to zero.  In the latter warmup is still doing
> what it is supposed to do and tweaking it won’t make the
> pathological region go away.
>
> If you step size is small but nonzero, say around 1e-4 or 1e-5
> then you just have a complex model and there’s not much
> you can do besides decor relation parameters by implementing
> your model in another way.
>
> If your step size is equivalent to floating point zero, around 1e-15
> or lower, then you have pathological regions and HMC isn’t
> going to be able to do much of anything (nor is any other
> algorithm).  This is often due to very bad nonlinear non-identifiabilties
> and in this case you’ll definitely have to tweak your model.
> You can play around with centering vs noncentering various
> groups as well as the carful specification of priors.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] 2.5%/97.5% intervals are generally a bad idea
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] 2.5%/97.5% intervals are generally a bad idea
messages.body_plain:
Hi, beyond the computational issue, my argument is that for decision making we want to know roughly where the parameter is but there’s no need to be requiring 97.5% certainty or anytihng close to that.  Of course in prediction problems we might care about things like 100-year floods, but for basic parameter esitmation it seems to me that 50% intervals make more sense.  Depends on context, of course, and I’ve struggled to figure out exactly how to write this up (even for blog, let alone in a paper or book).
A

> On Apr 6, 2016, at 3:05 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> I'm not sure what Andrew's thinking, but part of the problem
> is computational --- you need a lot of draws to estimate tail
> quantiles (you can think of this as only 2.5% of the samples
> coming into play to help estimate the lower bound of a 95%
> interval).
>
> Another issue is that tails can be more sensitive to priors
> than central intervals or posterior means.
>
> You can see all this through simulation by rerunning with different
> seeds and different priors and looking at variance in the 2.5%
> vs. 50% quantile estimates.  More things to go in the book!
>
> - Bob

Covariance is the variance between _parameters_, which
depends on your chosen parameters.  A rotation is a change
of parameters which changes the covariance.

What’s staying the same in all of this is the latent probability
distribution — we’re just changing the sample space that we
use to represent that distribution.  This is why I had to go so
high-level in the intro draft.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] R-like subset selection
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] R-like subset selection
messages.body_plain:
You can easily write your own function to do this:

vector r_style_subset(vector x, vector cond) {
  vector[sum(cond)] y;
  int pos;
  pos <- 1;
  for (i in 1:rows(x)) {
    if (cond[i]) {
      y[pos] <- x[i];
      pos <- pos + 1;
    }
  }
  return y;
}

It should really test that the entries in cond are 0 or 1,
and that x and cond have the same number of rows.

But I'm guessing you really want it to work for all possible
container shapes and you want us to extend all of our comparison
operators to allow R-like idioms such as y[y > 10].

It's not that hard to do, but will require a different syntax
because we don't have a proper bool type.  Nobody has any time
soon to do it, though.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I don't know about PyStan, but an alternative would be
to redefine the variable in generated quantities.  Calculations
there are almost free compared to places where we need derivatives.
And you can use a function to remove cut-and-paste in many cases.

- Bob

> On Apr 7, 2016, at 4:34 PM, Sachinthaka Abeywardana <sachin.ab...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

>
> On 7 Apr 2016 11:12 pm, "Ben Goodrich" <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Thursday, April 7, 2016 at 2:51:26 AM UTC-4, Sachinthaka Abeywardana wrote:
> I have a HMM with forward-backward model as shown below. I wish to inspect the posterior p(z_n|Data) where z_n is the state assignment variable. However, considering that p[N,K] is local to the `model` block I won't end up seeing this as one of the output parameters. How do you go about ensuring this will get saved?
>
> Incase I don't really care about saving the entire chain but just want the mean of it, how would I cater for that case? Saving a NxK matrix for a large chain might not be the best idea.
>
> Side note: I've declared mu as a ordered variable in the hope that it solves/ masks the multimodal issue.
>
> If you are using rstan, you can
> 	• define p in transformed parameters
> 	• not save the draws of p by calling stan with pars = "p", include = FALSE
> 	• use get_posterior_mean() afterward to look at the posterior mean of everything, including p
> Ben
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchies in Seemingly Unrelated Regressions?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Hierarchies in Seemingly Unrelated Regressions?
messages.body_plain:
Sorry for letting this one slip through the cracks.  You (and
any other poster) should feel free to ping the list if we haven't
answered in a couple days.  If things go this long, it's just that
we missed it.

A program should have a positive density (finite log density)
for any paramters satisfying the constraints.

One problem you have is here:

parameters {
  vector <lower=-1, upper=1> [3] rho_sur;
  vector <lower=0, upper=10> [3] sigma_sur;
...

transformed parameters{
  cov_matrix[3] Sigma_sur;
  Sigma_sur[1,1] <- square(sigma_sur[1]);
  Sigma_sur[2,2] <- square(sigma_sur[2]);
  Sigma_sur[3,3] <- square(sigma_sur[3]);
  Sigma_sur[1,2] <- rho_sur[1]*sigma_sur[1]*sigma_sur[2];
  Sigma_sur[1,3] <- rho_sur[2]*sigma_sur[1]*sigma_sur[3];
  Sigma_sur[2,3] <- rho_sur[3]*sigma_sur[2]*sigma_sur[3];
  Sigma_sur[2,1] <- Sigma_sur[1,2];
  Sigma_sur[3,1] <- Sigma_sur[1,3];
  Sigma_sur[3,2] <- Sigma_sur[2,3];

That's not a sound way to build a covariance matrix, because
there are values for rho for which Sigma_sur will not be positive
definite.  You want to model the covariance matrix directly as
a parameter, or ideally use a Cholesky factor of a correlation
matrix and scale it.

Also, we don't generally recommend those interval-constrained priors
on scales --- we prefer <lower=0> and a weakly informative prior.

The program could also be sped up with more vectorization, but
I'd get it working first if it's not too slow already.  One thing
you can do to speed things up is tighten some of the priros.  Unless
g_a and g_b can take on values in the 100s, a normal(0, 100) isn't
reasonable.

- Bob

> On Mar 17, 2016, at 9:45 AM, Lindsay <lindsay...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Stan Users,
>
> I am struggling with modelling hierarchies in a seemingly unrelated regressions model. I am aiming at a SUR version of something very like Example 17.2 in Gelman and Hill,  but with the exception that instead of a single outcome variable I have three (by assumption) correlated outcome variables.
>
> The model I think I want to run is to be found in the attached file sur_mlm_1a. However, when I try to run it, although the model does compile and sample something goes wrong. For each of the parameters samples a single value (plus or minus a minimal amount of Monte Carlo error) rather than a distribution. Reading the discussion on this list (and having put in a query in the past) I am assuming that this may be a problem with the priors---a combination perhaps of having too tight a uniform prior, and also the fact that a uniform prior is perhaps not a great choice.
>
> After a hiatus on this, I decided to come back with fresh eyes, and starts again, taking the advice in the manual on weakly informative ljk priors for covariances (p, 78 of the Stan 2.9.0 reference manual). When I implement the example as is (with no hierarchies) everything runs fine (not surprisingly).
>
> So for the next stage I am trying to have a group level intercept and slope with (for now) no correlation, in essence, a SUR version of Gelman and Hill's example 17.1. When I try to run the model (as in file sur_mlm_1b) I get the warning error messages at the bottom of this page.
>
> I am not quite sure where I am going wrong. It may be something I don't understand very well about the cholesky decomposition of the covariance matrix, or it could be an even dumber coding error, but I thought I had better ask rather than beat my head against a brick wall. I do realise that the choice of priors on sigma_a and sigma_b may leave something to be desired, but I don't think that is the problem.
>
> Incidentally, although this is not the main issue I am also getting the following error sporadically when I try to run the model in rstan--it is the "Error in readRDS(file.rda) : unknown input format" which seems confusing,
>
> DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:Warning (non-fatal):
> Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
> If so, you need to call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
> Left-hand-side of sampling statement:
>     a[k, j] ~ normal(...)
> Warning (non-fatal):
> Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
> If so, you need to call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
> Left-hand-side of sampling statement:
>     b[k, j] ~ normal(...)
> Error in readRDS(file.rda) : unknown input format
>
> Any advice on this greatly appreciated.
>
> Lindsay

> On Mar 16, 2016, at 9:17 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi!
>
> @ Daniel: Thanks for the clarification; makes sense wrt to how normal_log is defined.
>
> @ Aki: Maybe I was imprecise. The unit normal CDF can be approximated with (according to the Stan user manual)
>
> Phi_approx„(x)… ƒ = logit^{-1}(0.07056 * x^3 ‚ + 1.5976 * x)…
>
> Now, this can be used for a much improved (approximate) version of normal_cdf_log, since it won't under- or overflow so quickly. Robustness via a student_t or any other distributions would be a different approach which I haven't tried back then, but the above works splendid (in particular with ADVI which does not like NaNs so much, at least in the past). All I wanted to say is that putting a note in the manual besides the normal_cdf (where you warn about the numerical issues due to over+underflow) would be helpful for users who wonder how they may get around these numerical challenges.
>
> Sebastian
>
> On Wednesday, March 16, 2016 at 1:40:48 PM UTC+1, Aki Vehtari wrote:
>
>
> On Wednesday, March 16, 2016 at 12:19:00 PM UTC+2, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> BTW, it would be nice for users to point out in the manual at the normal_cdf doc that you can actually approximate this function in log-space very well using the Phi_approx function approach (log_inv_logit). This gave me much better model runs for left-censored data due to the improved numerical stability.
>
> Using logit is close to using student_t_cdf with degrees of freedom nu=7. Switching from normal to something with thicker tails may also explain the improved stability.
>
> Aki

messages.body_plain:
I missed this followup.  Answering now.  See below.

> On Mar 12, 2016, at 2:58 PM, Daniel Berman <daniel....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> Stan also supports MLE calculations, by the way.  It's
> just called "optimizing" as it finds the posterior mode
> (which is the MLE if the prior is uniform).
>
> The problems near boundaries are just due to numerical
> stability of the transforms.  For instance, we log constrain
> positive values, but this only gives us an effective
> range of (-320, +320) or so in the unconstrained space,
> beyond which we overflow or underflow.  So we either have
> to take small steps, or deal with a lot of rejection because
> Stan's HMC is only using the gradient (first-order derivatives)
> with multiple steps to simulate the Hamiltonian, which has more
> curvature (higher-order derivatives).
>
> We need to get all this written up in a user-facing way.
>
> Is it possible that changing to a probit scale (changing [-1,1]->[0,1]->[-inf,inf]) would help at all?

Very unlikely.  But we do have the Phi_approx inverse unit-normal CDF
you could try if you think it might help.

> Which estimate from Stan are you talking about?  The optimization
> result?  Those should be the same, at least up to several digits,
> assuming you've coded the model properly.
>
> The estimates from Stan I'm talking about are the ones using the priors I set. Matlab's MLE results are better than Stan's Bayesian results and I'm not sure where I'm going wrong.

I'm not sure what you mean by "better" here.  The MLE isn't
going to match the posterior mean in many models, and in some
cases they can be very different.  What you want to check is that
your posterior intervals are calibrated (50% of the 50% intervals
contain the true parameter values under simulation).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Sorry for the long delay.  I'm just catching up with mail
nobody answered.

The problem you're having at the end is probably due to label switching.
Try rerunning with chains=1 and see if the problem goes away.
There's a discussion in the problematic posteriors section of
the manual.

And I would not try to get clever with the mixing proportions
the way you are looking at y < 0 and y > 0.  The model will
sort this out, so ps should be of length 3 and it should be
just as in the manual, replacing

>    if(y[n] > 0) ps[1] <- log_theta[1] + normal_log(y[n],mu_up,sigma); //either is positive or negative
>
>    else ps[1] <- log_theta[2] + normal_log(y[n],mu_down,sigma); //either is positive or negative
>
>    ps[2] <- log_theta[3] + normal_log(y[n],mu_nn,sigma_nn); //for central distribution

ps[1] <- log_theta[1] + normal_log(y[n], mu_up, sigma);

ps[2] <- log_theta[2] + normal_log(y[n], mu_down, sigma);
ps[3] <- log_theta[3] + normal_log(y[n], mu_nn, sigma_nn);

-Bob

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I think the discussion of the relationship of amount of data
and non-centered parameterization is important, but as I far
as I can tell it is not in the manual. It would be great if the
the stan dev team could add a few sentences about this issue*,
even if there is no time for a full discussion partial centering.

Guido

*in particular, when does one have "enough data so that
non-centered parameterization  isn’t ideal". This could explain
why I recently could not fit a non-hierarchical regression
with non-centered parameterization (with N = 45 0000)
whereas a hierarchical regression with ~20 group with ns between
5 and 10 000 worked.

On Wednesday, April 6, 2016 at 12:35:21 AM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Then you’ll probably get a sufficient fix by mixing centered
> and non-centered parameterizations by group.
>
> On Apr 5, 2016, at 11:27 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > These are all hierarchical logistic regressions with
> > mixed amounts of data by group.  For instance, I'm working
> > on a very unbalanced hierarchical binomial model now that has
> > a lot of 0/0 observations and some 30K/60K observations.
> >
> > Those 0/0 cases also dominate the hierarchical variance (basically
> > pegging it to the next level up's variance), so I've
> > got bigger problems for this model.  The ones I did for the
> > case study were well behaved enough I could get rid of all the
> > divergences with a low enough step size.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >> On Apr 5, 2016, at 5:17 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >> But divergences that persist even at adapt_delta = 0.999 would make me
> >> anxious.  I usually accept the occasional divergence only when I’m near
> >> the nominal adapt_delta = 0.8.
> >>
> >> On Apr 5, 2016, at 10:16 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >>> I’d look at the plots of the hierarchical effects vs the hierarchical variance.
> >>> My guess is that you have enough data where the non-centered parameterization
> >>> isn’t ideal which manifests as an inverted funnel with divergences in the tail.
> >>>
> >>> Sometimes certain groups are more informative than others and you can
> >>> switch centering/noncentering group by group.
> >>>
> >>> Once I get time I’ll start to play around with partial centering so that we
> >>> can play around with that, too.
> >>>
> >>> On Apr 5, 2016, at 9:56 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >>>
> >>>> That's roughly been the case for me up to a point.  That is,
> >>>> I can go from 10 or 20 divergences to 1 or 2 by monkeying with
> >>>> adapt_delta and stepsize, but when I'm at adapt_delta=0.999 and
> >>>> I've already moved to a non-centered parameterization, I often
> >>>> still get 1 or 2 divergent transitions with 1K iterations in each
> >>>> of 4 chains.
> >>>>
> >>>> - Bob
> >>>>
> >>>>> On Apr 5, 2016, at 4:10 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>>>>
> >>>>>
> >>>>>> (i)  Michael --- are you still running a zero-tolerance policy on

> >>>>> Yes with caveats for people who really know what they are doing (i.e. me*).

> >>>>> doesn’t work then the divergences are meaningful.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Zero-inflated Poisson with over dispersion
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Zero-inflated Poisson with over dispersion
messages.body_plain:
The typical solution for overdispersion in count data is
to use a negative binomial, which is a gamma-poisson
compound rather than the lognormal-Poisson you're going with.
I don't know if the lognormal form is important, but the gamma
version is available in marginalized form in a couple
negative-binomial implementations.

Also, I don't know why you'd use that mu in both the binomial
and in the Bernoulli and Poisson components.

If you do Poisson explicitly, I'd suggest

poisson_log_log(y, alpha)  = poisson_log(y, exp(alpha))

- Bob

> On Apr 6, 2016, at 10:33 PM, Eric Wang <ericwan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear list,
>
> I have this simple zero-inflated Poisson model with over dispersion, the model is as follows,
>
> ———————— model ————————
> if y[i] = 0,        p(y[i] | mu[i]) = theta + (1-theta)Pois(0| exp(mu[i]) )
> otherwise,      p(y[i] | mu[i]) = (1-theta)Pois(y[i]| exp(mu[i]) )
>
> where
>
> theta = inv_logit(-mu[i])
>
> and
>
> mu ~ normal(mu0,sigma)
> ———————— end of model ————————
>
> My inference interest is only on the log-mean mu0 and the over-dispersion parameter sigma and I don’t care at all about the values of the mu[i]’s. However, I cannot figure out a way to marginalize them out so I leave them in the model. Below is how I wrote the model in stan
>
> ———————— stan model ————————
> data {
>      int<lower=0> N;
>      int<lower=0> y[N];
> }
> parameters {
>    real<lower=0> sigma;
>    real mu0;
>    real mu[N];
> }
> model {
>       mu ~ normal(mu0,sigma);
>       for (j in 1:N){
>       	      if (y[j] == 0)
>       	 increment_log_prob( log_sum_exp( bernoulli_log( 1,inv_logit(-mu[j] ) ),
> bernoulli_log(0,inv_logit(-kappa*mu[j] ))
> + poisson_log( y[j],exp(mu[j]) ) ) );
>       	      else
> increment_log_prob( bernoulli_log(0,inv_logit(-mu[j] ))
> + poisson_log( y[j],exp(mu[j]) ) );
>   }
> }
> ———————— end of stan model ————————
>
> However, when N = 1000 the running time starts to become really long. I guess part of the reason is because stan tries to save all the mu[i]’s whose total number equals the sample size.
>
> So my question is: is there a way to hack stan and let stan not save these mu[i]’s? Any other comments are also welcome.
>
> Thanks for your time.
>
> Best,
> Eric Wang
>

for polynomials, say alpha1 x + alpha2 * x^{2}, become
strongly non-identified causing no end of fitting problems.

that used such a polynomial so I can’t just get rid of the
higher-order terms.

Are there any tricks to decorrelate the coefficients by
transforming the covariates?  The physicist in me wants
to do some kind of Gramm-Schmidt, but then that would
require a choice of kernel.

We have an option to do the QR of a design matrix in rstanarm, and it seems to work well (but we haven't studied it that systematically). messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am just trying to understand a few things a little better about the engine for Stan. I was wondering - I know that Neal's article on HMC says that the Leapfrog method is ''Volume conserving''. I am just wanting to check my understanding of exactly what this means.

I am assuming that we can think of probability mass as a type of incompressible flow: we want to avoid destroying or creating mass, so that we still have a valid density.

Therefore, we need a numerical algorithm that also conserves this flow. This means that as leapfrog steps, no mass is created nor destroyed; it is merely redistributed.

Is the intuition above right, or am I way off?

Best,

Ben

In this application, I wish to perform inference on the function values (under a GP prior) at the training points.  Since we marginalize out the function for posterior inference, I sample them from the posterior predictive in the generated quantities block.   I use ADVI to approximate the joint posterior and the subsequent time to generate samples is slowed relative to parametric priors (e.g., a truncated DP prior) because of the choleskys, but it is fast enough.
>
> The issue is that all of the choleskys - over the iterations to draw samples from the approximate posterior - are retained in RAM, no matter whether they are declared as temporary / local objects.   You will see that I have used local blocks to declare these objects as temporary/local.  I find doing such speeds up the time it takes ADVI to find the local optimum, but it has no impact on local memory storage of the choleskys - which I don't return.  The result is that when I increase the sample to N = 4000, the amount of local storage is over 64GB.    I wondered whether objects - even temporary objects -  are written to R memory from C++ on each sampling iteration.  It is possible - sometime in the future - to explicitly free memory at the C++ layer for local objects on each sampling iteration without transferring them to R?

messages.subject: Severe sampling problem (high rejection) with non-identifiable model
messages.subject_clean: Severe sampling problem (high rejection) with non-identifiable model
messages.body_plain:
I have recently encountered a severe sampling problem when trying to run stan on a model that I have developed. An example of what I'm talking about is in the attached traceplots. problem.obs.error.5.jpg is the traceplot for one parameter of the model. problem.lp.jpg and problem.acc.rate.jpg are the traceplots for the lp__ variable and the accept_stat__ variable
respectively. The model is in the model.stan file. You can see that at a certain point (around iteration 1500) the acceptance rate goes down significantly, the lp__ value goes up significantly,
and the value for the parameter becomes more constrained. This behavior is actually seen for all parameters in this run but I'm just showing the traceplot for one as an example. Also notice that after a while the acceptance rate goes back up and the parameter starts to sample a distribution similar to what it was sampling before the acceptance rate plummeted. The problem
started to present itself when I added a set of parameters to represent the observation error within the error model. These are the obs_error_var parameters that all have inverse gamma prior distributions. The likelihood for the model makes some parameters non-identifiable but all parameters have proper priors from what I can see. The problem mainly started to present itself when I added the obs_error_var parameters.

I really would like some assistance on this. Could this be a bug or problem with the sampling program itself ?

Roy

messages.body_plain:
I have this working too. The accuracies of the results are
impressive. Good job Stan devs! I have some questions.

1. I generated some data with known parameters. What integrator is being
used and what error control? I'm assuming RK4 but neither was I able
to see anything in the documentation and nor did searching the repo
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan for RK4 yield any results. I tried
another solver (RKf45) in a stand-alone program but got sufficiently
different results to make me feel I didn't understand enough of what
Stan was doing under the covers. If I get time I will try a pure RK4
but I feel I'm shooting in the dark a bit until I know what Stan
*actually* uses.

2. It's imperative to use

./examples/pkpdmodel/pkpdmodel sample algorithm=hmc stepsize=0.001 data file=examples/pkpdmodel/pkpdmodel.data.R init=0.25

If you don't specify the stepsize and the init then the running the model produces

Iteration:    1 / 2000 [  0%]  (Warmup)

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:

Exception thrown at line 50: integrate_ode_cvode: parameter vector[2] is inf, but must be finite!

If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,

but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

and nothing further (in a reasonable time).

I assume that the stepsize is specified as 0.001 as the parameters
being estimated are of that order? I was unable to find any clues as
to why init needs set to 0.25 in this case though.

3. The estimation took

Warmup took (469) seconds, 7.8 minutes total
Sampling took (717) seconds, 12 minutes total

Is this to be expected? It seems quite quite big to me given the state
update (solving the ODE) should really be quite cheap.

Thanks, Dominic.

>
> ```
> ./examples/pkpdmodel/pkpdmodel sample algorithm=hmc stepsize=0.001 data file=examples/pkpdmodel/pkpdmodel.data.R init=0.25
> ```
>
> If you don't specify the stepsize and the init then the running the model produces
>
> ```
> Iteration:    1 / 2000 [  0%]  (Warmup)
>
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> Exception thrown at line 50: integrate_ode_cvode: parameter vector[2] is inf, but must be finite!
> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
>
> but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
> ```
>
> and nothing further (in a reasonable time).
>
> I assume that the stepsize is specified as 0.001 as the parameters
> being estimated are of that order? I was unable to find any clues as
> to why init needs set to 0.25 in this case though.

It takes steps in stepsize * gradient, and that needs to be small enough
to follow curvature in the posterior.

init=0.25 means that parameters are randomly initialized in (-0.25, 0.25)
on the unconstrained scale.  All parameters are transformed to being
unconstrained (details in the manual).

>
> 3. The estimation took
>
> ```
> Warmup took (469) seconds, 7.8 minutes total
> Sampling took (717) seconds, 12 minutes total
> ```
>
> Is this to be expected? It seems quite quite big to me given the state
> update (solving the ODE) should really be quite cheap.

CVODES should be faster.  These runs can be slow because either the
solver hits a stiff region it can't deal with or because the posterior
parameter density is complicated, and we need small step sizes in the HMC
algorithm.  The algorithms and adaptations are also described in the manual.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Local variables are indeed local. They're translated to local
variables in C++.  But if they are declared anywhere other than
the transformed data block or generated quantities, they will create
variables on the autodiff stack that last until the derivatives are
evaluated.  That's why it's better to define variables in transformed
data if at all possible.

Recalculations in generated quantities are cheap because no derivatives
are involved.

- Bob

> If the memory is the problem, I guess then the next step is to make all NTxNT matrices local (Bob can verify how generated quantities works if only local variables are big). Currently L is not local. To make L local you need to recompute the covariance matrix in generated quantities. Even with additional computation, it is possible that saving memory makes it faster. If this doesn't work then you need to move generated quantities computations out of Stan.

> Aki

In this application, I wish to perform inference on the function values (under a GP prior) at the training points.  Since we marginalize out the function for posterior inference, I sample them from the posterior predictive in the generated quantities block.   I use ADVI to approximate the joint posterior and the subsequent time to generate samples is slowed relative to parametric priors (e.g., a truncated DP prior) because of the choleskys, but it is fast enough.
>
> The issue is that all of the choleskys - over the iterations to draw samples from the approximate posterior - are retained in RAM, no matter whether they are declared as temporary / local objects.   You will see that I have used local blocks to declare these objects as temporary/local.  I find doing such speeds up the time it takes ADVI to find the local optimum, but it has no impact on local memory storage of the choleskys - which I don't return.  The result is that when I increase the sample to N = 4000, the amount of local storage is over 64GB.    I wondered whether objects - even temporary objects -  are written to R memory from C++ on each sampling iteration.  It is possible - sometime in the future - to explicitly free memory at the C++ layer for local objects on each sampling iteration without transferring them to R?

messages.subject: PSIS-LOO for nested/hierarchical cross validation
messages.subject_clean: PSIS-LOO for nested/hierarchical cross validation
messages.body_plain:
I am doing nested (or hierarchical?) cross-validation.

Let's say that I have two model classes M1 and M2, and in each class there are several models with different number of discrete components k (e.g., components in a mixture model).
I want to infer what's the best model class for a given dataset.

I could just have two super-models and do full MCMC directly in the larger space (treating the number of components as discrete parameters), but that's not viable for various reasons.
So, I am computing the posterior, via MCMC, separately for each model class M and number of components k.

The question is, is it okay to use PSIS-LOO twice here?
As far as I understand, I should do something like two nested leave-one-out CV:
For each model class M,
For i = 1..N, where N is the number of data points:
remove the i-th data point from the full dataset.
Perform PSIS-LOO (or any other method) on the reduced dataset to choose the best number of components.
Take the best model and now compute the prediction on the left-out i-th data point via PSIS. This yields the i-th LOO-CV score for the model class.
The LOO-CV score of each model class is the sum (or mean) of 1..N LOO-CV scores from the N reduced datasets.
Compare the summed scores of the model classes.
Does this make sense, and is there a reference for an usage of this kind? Any non-obvious caveat?
(I was checking this <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf> but it does not seem to cover this case.)

Thanks,
Luigi

messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 8, 2016, at 1:09 PM, Eric Wang <ericwan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> Thanks so much for the reply.
>
> The typical solution for overdispersion in count data is
> to use a negative binomial, which is a gamma-poisson
> compound rather than the lognormal-Poisson you're going with.
> I don't know if the lognormal form is important, but the gamma
> version is available in marginalized form in a couple
> negative-binomial implementations.
>
>
> If I were to have just univariate count data then yes I can definitely use Negative-binomial distribution. But eventually I want to model multivariate count data and the log-normal form enables me to model the underlying variance-covariance structure which is my main inference focus. Is Negative-binomial (any other count distribution) capable of modeling the correlation structure of multivariate data?

Not directly, as it's only univariate.  You'd have to
introduce latent structure in the underlying linear predictor
(and/or overdispersion parameter) of the GLM.

> Also, I don't know why you'd use that mu in both the binomial
> and in the Bernoulli and Poisson components.
>
>
> This comes from our prior belief of the data. Is having mu in both Bernoulli and Poisson harmful to MCMC?

As long as the posterior is proper, it won't break HMC.  I'm used
to seeing scale parameters in both means and variances for negative
binomial, but not for Bernoulli.  But I don't have a huge amount of
experience in any of this.

- Bob

The lag times and times at which input rates change result in discontinuities in the ODEs. Perhaps my application could serve as a template of a simple case where one wants to estimate the covariance parameters.   since i estimate the parameters, i can't declare L as transformed data, but building L twice in order that i can be local in each block that is used seems like memory should prevent memory usage from accumulating at the C++ layer as L is computed on each iteration.

On Sat, Apr 9, 2016 at 4:39 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> Local variables are indeed local. They're translated to local
> variables in C++.  But if they are declared anywhere other than
> the transformed data block or generated quantities, they will create
> variables on the autodiff stack that last until the derivatives are
> evaluated.  That's why it's better to define variables in transformed
> data if at all possible.
>
> Recalculations in generated quantities are cheap because no derivatives
> are involved.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> On Apr 9, 2016, at 9:39 AM, terrance savitsky <tds...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > L can't be local because it's used in both the model step and for generated quantities.   I suppose i could generate L, twice, in order to make it local.  i hadn't been motivated to do this because i don't believe that the locally-declared covariance matrices are actually treated as local in memory management.  i'll try it, anyway, and let you know.
> >
> > On Sat, Apr 9, 2016 at 4:43 AM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:
> > If the memory is the problem, I guess then the next step is to make all NTxNT matrices local (Bob can verify how generated quantities works if only local variables are big). Currently L is not local. To make L local you need to recompute the covariance matrix in generated quantities. Even with additional computation, it is possible that saving memory makes it faster. If this doesn't work then you need to move generated quantities computations out of Stan.
> >
> > Aki
> >
> >
> > On Friday, April 8, 2016 at 6:41:04 PM UTC+3, tds151 wrote:
> > Hi Aki and Bob,
> >
> > I attach the .stan script version I used, below.  My experience is as Aki predicted (pun intended).   In this application, I wish to perform inference on the function values (under a GP prior) at the training points.  Since we marginalize out the function for posterior inference, I sample them from the posterior predictive in the generated quantities block.   I use ADVI to approximate the joint posterior and the subsequent time to generate samples is slowed relative to parametric priors (e.g., a truncated DP prior) because of the choleskys, but it is fast enough.
> >
> > The issue is that all of the choleskys - over the iterations to draw samples from the approximate posterior - are retained in RAM, no matter whether they are declared as temporary / local objects.   You will see that I have used local blocks to declare these objects as temporary/local.  I find doing such speeds up the time it takes ADVI to find the local optimum, but it has no impact on local memory storage of the choleskys - which I don't return.  The result is that when I increase the sample to N = 4000, the amount of local storage is over 64GB.    I wondered whether objects - even temporary objects -  are written to R memory from C++ on each sampling iteration.  It is possible - sometime in the future - to explicitly free memory at the C++ layer for local objects on each sampling iteration without transferring them to R?
> >
> > Terrance
> >
> > /*
> >   y[c] ~ N_{T}(u[c], sigma_y[c]),  where c = 1,..,NT are domain-time case. sigma_y[c] are known
> >   // squared exponential covariance function for NT x NT covariance matrix, Sigma
> >   Sigma[i,j] = 1/eta * sum_{c=1}^{NT}sum_{c'=1}^{NT}
> >                             sum_{p=1}^{P} exp(-1/rho[p](x[c,p] - x[c',p])^{2})
> >   u[1] ,..., u[NT] ~ * N_{NT}(0, Sigma),
> >   eta     ~ Gamma(1,1) - precision parameter of squared exponential covariance function
> >   rho[k]  ~ Gamma(1,1) - predictor indexed length-scale parameters
> >
> >   We may marginalize over the u to achieve
> >   y[c] ~ N_{T}(0, Sigma + diag(sigma2_y))
> >
> >   Marginalizing over u adds the known response variances, sigma2_y, to the diagonals
> >   which stabilizes the cholesky computation for Sigma (which is very high-dimensional).
> >   We use the properties of the Gaussian wrapper in which the nonparametric GP is parameterized
> >   to draw u as a post-processing step using sampled values of c(rho,eta)
> >
> > */
> >

> >   int<lower=1> P; // number of predictors

> >   vector<lower=0>[NT] sigma2_y; // known domain variances
> >   real<lower=0> jitter; // stabilizing constant to add to diagonals of GP cov, Sigma */
> > } /* end data block */
> >
> >
> > transformed data{
> >   vector[NT] zros_NT;
> >   zros_NT <- rep_vector(0,NT); /* vector of zeros for sampling Tx1 fixed effects, beta */
> > } /* end transformed data block */
> >
> > parameters{
> >   // parameters for squared exponential covariance function
> >   real<lower=0> eta; /* squared exponential formula precision parameter */
> >   real<lower=0> rho[P]; /* length-scale parameters, indexed by predictor, x[,p] */
> > } /* end parameters block */
> >
> > transformed parameters{
> >   matrix[NT,NT] K; /* GP covariance matrix for u */
> >   matrix[NT,NT] L; /* cholesky_decompose(Sigma) */
> >
> >   { /* local block */
> >     matrix[NT,NT] Sigma; /* GP covariance matrix for NT x 1, u */
> >     real covformula_ijp;
> >     real s_ij;
> >      // off-diagonal
> >     for( i in 1:(NT-1) )
> >     {
> >       for( j in (i+1):NT )
> >       {
> >         s_ij <- 0;
> >         for( p in 1:P )
> >         {
> >           covformula_ijp      <- inv(rho[p])* pow(x[i,p] - x[j,p],2);
> >           s_ij                <- s_ij + covformula_ijp ;
> >         }/* end loop p over dimensions of x to fill cells of Sigma */
> >         s_ij       <-  exp( -s_ij ) ;
> >         s_ij       <-  inv(eta) * s_ij;
> >         K[i,j]     <- s_ij;
> >         K[j,i]     <- s_ij;
> >       } /* end loop j over columns to fill upper triangular cells of Sigma */
> >     } /* end loop i over rows to fill upper triangular cells of Sigma */
> >
> >     // diagonal
> >     for( k in 1:NT )
> >     {
> >       for( p in 1:P )
> >       {
> >         K[k,k]     <- inv(eta) + jitter;
> >       } /* end loop p over dimensions of x to fill cells of Sigma */
> >     } /* end loop k over diagonal entries of Sigma */
> >
> >     /* add model noise on the diagonal to achieve the marginal distribution */
> >     /* of y */
> >     Sigma     <- K + diag_matrix( sigma2_y );
> >     L         <- cholesky_decompose( Sigma );
> >   } /* end local block for building Sigma */
> >
> >
> > } /* end transformed parameters block */
> >
> >
> > model{
> >
> >   // priors for mean and covariance cluster location
> >   eta       ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 );
> >   rho       ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 );
> >
> >
> >   // observed response likelihood
> >   y         ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zros_NT,L);
> >
> >
> >
> > } /* end model{} block */
> >
> > generated quantities{
> >
> >   vector[NT] u; /* GP function drawn from posterior predictive */
> >   /* compute MSE for fit evaluation */
> >   real<lower=0> TSE;
> >   real<lower=0> MSE;
> >   /* posterior predictive quantities */
> >   { /* environment to declare local variables */
> >     matrix[NT,NT] div_L_K; /* L^-1 * K */
> >     matrix[NT,NT] Tau; /* posterior predictive covariance matrix for u */
> >     matrix[NT,NT] L_u; /* cholesky of Tau */
> >     vector[NT] mu_u; /* predictive mean of NT x 1, u */
> >     div_L_K                <- mdivide_left_tri_low(L,K);
> >     mu_u                   <- div_L_K' * mdivide_left_tri_low(L,y);
> >     Tau                    <- K - div_L_K' * div_L_K;
> >     L_u <- cholesky_decompose(Tau);
> >     u   <- multi_normal_cholesky_rng(mu_u,L_u);
> >     TSE <- squared_distance(u,y);
> >     MSE <- TSE/(NT);
> >   } /* end local variable block */
> >
> >
> > } /* end generated quantities block */
> >

> > Hi,

> > Based on your description we can focus on generative quantities block and thus the slowness is not due to the covariance matrix computation nor gradients. I don't see anything which should take so long time to compute in generated quantities. In my computer Cholesky for 2500x2500 matric takes about 0.2s (using several cores). Other computations should not be slower than Cholesky, and thus overall I would guess that one iteration in generated quantities should be about order of 1s and then 1000 samples should be less than 30 minutes. However, you are generating and writing to the csv file 1000x3 matrices of size 2500x2500, which (is I can calculate these correctly) makes about 1.7e11 bytes, which may take some time to write to the file. So my guess is that this I/O problem, and I guess you can solve it but using locally declared variables not stored in the output.

messages.body_plain:
The dynamic peak memory use is almost always dominated
by the cost to evaluate the gradient of the log density.
Stan uses on the order of 40 bytes per subexpression, all of
which needs to be stored at once.  Plus another 24 bytes
per parameter (plus terms for Jacobian if it's constrained).
So -((a - b) / c)^2 has three variables and four subexpressions.

You can check out our arXiv paper on autodiff if you want
the gory details.

Also, generated quantities is only evaluated once per iteration,
not once per leapfrog step in HMC.  Everything there gets translated
straightforwardly into C++ code and will behave as you expect.

- Bob

messages.subject: intro to Stan for mathy programmers?
messages.subject_clean: intro to Stan for mathy programmers?
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'll be speaking with a group of people at work about Stan in a week,
and I want to suggest some reading for them (say, somewhere from 5 to
40 pages). Can anyone help me out?

All of these people are software engineers who are also strong in
machine learning. They have some basic stats knowledge but e.g. are
likely vaguely (but not deeply) familiar with MCMC.

The ideal reading would give them a sense for why and how someone
would use Stan, and also enough of a sense for the algorithms involved
to feel like they basically know what's going on. I'd also love to
give them (and get for myself) a sense of the various software design
designs involved in building Stan.

At this point, I'm thinking of:

1. Some basic intro to MCMC
2. The NUTS paper:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/nuts.pdf.
3. Some selections from the STAN manual.

Any suggestions?

Thanks!
David

--
David J. Chudzicki
http://davidchudzicki.com
dch...@gmail.com
(518) 366-7303

messages.subject: Re: PSIS-LOO for nested/hierarchical cross validation
messages.subject_clean: PSIS-LOO for nested/hierarchical cross validation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Luigi,

Yes, it is sensible to use nested cross-validation here (although
integration over k would be better).

You can't use nested PSIS, because in the inner loop you are
doing model selection (optimisation of k). Importance sampling in PSIS
can be used only when you have samples from the posterior.

I recommend using K-fold-CV (e.g. K=10) in the outer cross-validation.

Not also that, the inner optimisation of k will cause overfitting and
the outer cross-validation is only estimating the amount of
overfitting, but can't prevent the overfitting. In some cases the
overfitting can be really bad. See Piironen & Vehtari, Comparison of
Bayesian predictive methods for model selection, which has been just
published in Statistics and Computing
http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11222-016-9649-y

Aki

On Saturday, April 9, 2016 at 11:58:06 PM UTC+3, Luigi Acerbi wrote:
> I am doing nested (or hierarchical?) cross-validation.
>
> Let's say that I have two model classes M1 and M2, and in each class there are several models with different number of discrete components k (e.g., components in a mixture model).
> I want to infer what's the best model class for a given dataset.
>
> I could just have two super-models and do full MCMC directly in the larger space (treating the number of components as discrete parameters), but that's not viable for various reasons.
> So, I am computing the posterior, via MCMC, separately for each model class M and number of components k.
>
> The question is, is it okay to use PSIS-LOO twice here?
> As far as I understand, I should do something like two nested leave-one-out CV:
> For each model class M,
> For i = 1..N, where N is the number of data points:
> remove the i-th data point from the full dataset.
> Perform PSIS-LOO (or any other method) on the reduced dataset to choose the best number of components.
> Take the best model and now compute the prediction on the left-out i-th data point via PSIS. This yields the i-th LOO-CV score for the model class.
> The LOO-CV score of each model class is the sum (or mean) of 1..N LOO-CV scores from the N reduced datasets.
> Compare the summed scores of the model classes.
> Does this make sense, and is there a reference for an usage of this kind? Any non-obvious caveat?
> (I was checking this <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf> but it does not seem to cover this case.)
>
> Thanks,
> Luigi

messages.body_plain:
Hi Aki,

thank you for your reply.

> You can't use nested PSIS, because in the inner loop you are
> doing model selection (optimisation of k). Importance sampling in PSIS
> can be used only when you have samples from the posterior.

So, I can definitely use PSIS-LOO for model selection (choice of k) in the inner loop, since I have the posterior for each k.
I understand that I also need a full posterior for PSIS-LOO in the outer loop, but I guess I could still use an approximate posterior?

Possible approximations are:
I just keep the model I select (i.e., the posterior over k has collapsed onto a single model). This is probably bad...
As a possibly better alternative, I can build a rough estimate of the posterior over k based on the exponentiated PSIS-LOO CV score of each k (similar to what Burnham & Anderson suggest for AIC-weighted prediction). Then I can easily produce samples from this "pseudo-posterior". I understand that this is not correct -- it's not even a proper approximation of the marginal likelihood (the log is on the wrong side of the summation, and I am using the posterior over parameters as opposed to the prior). However, it looks like that this pseudo-posterior would have some desirable properties in common with the marginal likelihood (i.e., it punishes bad models, and applies some sort of Occam's razor to complex models).
Supposing that (2) is not insane, could I then proceed with PSIS?

> I recommend using K-fold-CV (e.g. K=10) in the outer cross-validation.

Yes, that's the alternative (and long) way to go that I had in mind.

> Not also that, the inner optimisation of k will cause overfitting and
> the outer cross-validation is only estimating the amount of
> overfitting, but can't prevent the overfitting. In some cases the
> overfitting can be really bad. See Piironen & Vehtari, Comparison of
> Bayesian predictive methods for model selection, which has been just
> published in Statistics and Computing
> http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11222-016-9649-y
>

Oh, this is very serendipitous, thanks!
I will start reading right now.

Thanks,
Luigi

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] ODE solver: initial or solution times that depend on parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] ODE solver: initial or solution times that depend on parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

There is no convenient solution right now to my knowledge. The best way to solve it at the moment is to use what is called a transit-cmt modeling approach. However, this is tedious if you have a multiple-dosing instead of a single dosing situation. Although, I have a plan in my head of how to make multiple-dosing with a transit-cmt work in Stan.

Another solution is to pass the lag time as parameter into the ODE RHS, but then the ODE solver has to deal with a discontinuity which is not a good idea to do (but should work).

A convenient solution for users would be an event handling mechanism for ODEs in Stan which is capable to allow events which happen at time-points which depend on data and parameters. I do not know if this is possible. The problem is that these dosing events cause discontinuous shifts in the state. However, often dosing occurs in cmt=1 while we observe another cmt such that for this case things maybe OK. Maybe Michael has a clear view on this.

messages.body_plain:
On the "why would you use Stan" side, the case studies are excellent. Interesting problems, lots of hand-holding, good discussion of the statistics, etc.

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies.html

On HMC, the Stan manual and the Betancourt and Girolami paper are very straightforward. Michael's video (from 57') made HMC extremely clear for me https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pHsuIaPbNbY

A bit self-promoty, but I've got a short tutorial on what I call "Bayesian Workflow" (writing out the probability model, simulating with known parameters, estimating the model on simulated data, model comparison, inference/posterior prediction etc.). It doesn't get into the technical detail of how the model is fit, but the idea is to get folks excited about why they should learn that stuff.

http://nbviewer.jupyter.org/github/khakieconomics/intro_to_stan_for_econs/blob/master/IntroToStan_basics_workflow.ipynb

Hope this helps,
Jim

My understanding is that ADVI estimates the ELBO from a few samples and so might scale well both in terms of time and memory. I can post the stan code for my model if needed.

Best,
Vivek.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vivek, Stan requires loading all data in RAM so that’s one bottleneck. Do you know how much memory that takes by itself? In ADVI, there are a few inefficient copies of the parameter vector that occur, which in this case is pretty massive as ADVI will treat all parameters including document-specific/word-specific parameters as global. You can try some hacks that do data subsampling, c.f.,  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/adsvi/how_to_ADSVI.md

Dustin

messages.body_plain:
The actual local variable acts just like a local variable.  It
goes off the stack when the local block is done executing.  But
in C++ terms, creating a variable has the side effect of adding
things to global memory that will not be freed until after the
derivative is calculated.

> As a possibly better alternative, I can build a rough estimate of the posterior over k based on the exponentiated PSIS-LOO CV score of each k (similar to what Burnham & Anderson suggest for AIC-weighted prediction). Then I can easily produce samples from this "pseudo-posterior". I understand that this is not correct -- it's not even a proper approximation of the marginal likelihood (the log is on the wrong side of the summation, and I am using the posterior over parameters as opposed to the prior). However, it looks like that this pseudo-posterior would have some desirable properties in common with the marginal likelihood (i.e., it punishes bad models, and applies some sort of Occam's razor to complex models).

It might work or not. I don't know.
LOO (and similar approaches) doesn't penalize complexity if the predictions are good.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] High autocorrelation on parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] High autocorrelation on parameters
messages.body_plain:
It's not unusual for the intercept and slope of a regression to
be correlated.  Centering the variable quiz should help;  if the
values are all positive or negative, the problem's much worse.

I would also recommend adding weakly informative priors; it can
help quite a bit when parameters are only weakly identified.

- Bob

P.S.

What you're calling "upsilon_normal" should be called
"logit_upsilon", because it's the log odds of upsilon.
And speaking of logit,

  1 / (1 + exp(-upsilon_normal[i]))

should be

 inv_logit(upsilon_normal[i])

All those ~ statements to increment the log density
should be vectorized.  It'll be *a lot* faster.

Also, given that Y_mid and Y_min are data, you don't need an
explicit truncation (it only contributes a constant to the log
density).  The constraint on alpha makes sure you're in support.

messages.subject: Using ANOVA with ELPDs to choose between models
messages.subject_clean: Using ANOVA with ELPDs to choose between models
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I have been following the method of Vehtari et al. (2015) to compare models; specifically eqn. 24.

At the moment I am using this criterion by computing (for models A and B) a statistic:

                L =   (total(ELPD_A) - total(ELPD_B))/se(ELPD_A-ELPD_B)

If this number is much greater than 1, then we prefer model A.

First, is this method correct? For example, consider the below estimated ELPDs:

ELPD_A = (-100,-200,-200,...,-300,-400)
ELPD_B = (-100,-201,-201,...,-300,-400)

where "..." is the same for these two models, and let's say, of length 95 for both models. In this case, I think (again correct me if I'm wrong) that the se(ELPD_A-ELPD_B) =sqrt(100 x var(ELPD_A-ELPD_B)) ~ 1.4.

The difference in total ELPD ~ 2 > 1.4. Therefore we prefer model A. Is this logic correct?

So, if the above is right, this method appears to sometimes mean that we 'prefer' one model over another because a small number of estimated ELPD scores are very slightly higher.

Second, if we were to use ANOVA to compare the means between groups A and B, would this be ok? I have tried this and it seems to give a more reasonable answer that A and B are indistinguishable. Moreover, could this method be used across a number (greater than 2) of models?

Perhaps I am getting mixed up on two different viewpoints for comparing A and B: the first is purely in terms of point by point prediction, in which case A wins; the second is asking if there is any practical difference in the fits. Forgive the ignorance!

Best,

Ben

Sorry for the slow reply. Thanks for the feedback. I understand why Bayes factors would be deprecated.

My problem is as follows:

I have interval-censored aggregate usage data and loss numbers for a number of fleets of aircraft. In general, the number of aircraft lost as a function of fleet usage (in flying hours) seems to track as a non-homogeneous Poisson process with a Weibull rate function. The fleets are of similar types of aircraft, but not exactly the same. I would like to make some inferences about this class of aircraft in general and thence about how one ought to plan purchases of additional aircraft. That is, how many spares should one buy? Right now, the variance of my individual fleet estimates are high, especially for the smaller fleets which are of the most interest to me. Since regressions on the individual fleet seem to show some general trends for the model parameters, I want to compare a hierarchical model that allows pooling of information to the non-pooled models. I hope that by doing so I can reduce the variance for the fleets of most interest to me, and create a basis on which to make educated guesses about how a fleet of some new aircraft type would perform.

 I also want to compare various levels and types of fleet pooling to account for various factors, such as relative technological development (old aircraft designs were less reliable) and user peculiarities (if the same aircraft type is used for crop dusting by one user and for mid-altitude long-distance flying by another, their accident rates are likely to be different).

I had been thinking of a model averaging approach, which is why I was looking at Bayes factors.

Gregory Hunter

>

With that difference P(A is better than B)~0.92. There are different views whether this probability is high enough to say "prefer".

> So, if the above is right, this method appears to sometimes mean that we 'prefer' one model over another because a small number of estimated ELPD scores are very slightly higher.

But yes, in this approach it is possible that small difference is enough to prefer one model if that model is consistently better (in this case equal or better for all loo cases).
It is an approach for answering the question which has better performance. It is good to think what is your prediction task and what utility (or cost) function you want to use. You can also look at the magnitude of the difference, but it is not so easy to decide what would be practical difference in log density scale. It might be helpful to then use some application specific utility (or cost) function where "practical difference" is calibrated by the expert knowledge. We are writing a paper illustrating some options.

>
> Second, if we were to use ANOVA to compare the means between groups A and B, would this be ok? I have tried this and it seems to give a more reasonable answer that A and B are indistinguishable. Moreover, could this method be used across a number (greater than 2) of models?

If you follow the logic that uncertainty is related to not knowing the distribution of the future data and we approximate it by the observed data, then the comparison has to be a paired comparison.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Cutpoint Priors
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Cutpoint Priors
messages.body_plain:
What about a truncated stick breaking prior? The size-biasedness of TSB priors will
(1) force an ordering for the cutpoints;
(2) make draws of cutpoints live on [0,1] which you can scale willy-nilly;
(3) reinforce what Ben said on adding prior information via pseudocounts in the parameters of a Dirichlet prior (here, use Beta stick-breaking priors, which is what Ben essentially does based on the running sum in the make_cutpoints function).

Dustin

> On Apr 13, 2016, at 11:43 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> HI, are you saying that a simple flat prior on the cutpoints won’t work?  Or a super-weak prior such as normal(0,10)?
>
> I’m surprised that you get “cutpoint collapse” if you’re doing full Bayes (as opposed to maximum likelihood).
>
> If you want to put some prior info as below, I recommend putting the normal priors on the _differences_ between the cutpoints, not the cutpoints themselves.  Otherwise you have this weird thing going on where the cutpoints are all being pulled toward each other.
>
> A
>
> > On Apr 13, 2016, at 9:38 AM, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Sorry to bring this up again. I am (still) facing the cutpoint-collapse problem when fitting an ordered-logistic model. After reading this thread and several others, I am still not sure (1) how to properly specify the prior of the cutpoint parameters, and (2) is there a way to model the cutpoint hierarchically like below? I tried something before but it seems that it doesn't guarantee that c[n,k+1] > c[n,k], hence it won't compile. I would highly appreciate any suggestions!
> >
> > ordered[K] c_mu;
> > vector<lower=0>[K] c_sd;
> > ordered[K] c[N];
> >
> > for (n in 1:N)
> >    for (k in 1:K)
> >        c[n,k] ~ normal(c_mu[k], c_sd[k]);
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Wednesday, May 20, 2015 at 8:27:28 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > Cool.  I like that idea.
> > >
> > > Just ordering obviously isn't enough for the uniform distribution
> > > on an ordered vector to be proper.
> > >
> > > What does happen for reasons I still don't fully understand is
> > > that
> > >
> > >   ordered[K] cutpoints;
> > >
> > >   cutpoints ~ normal(0, 5);
> > >
> > > provides the same distribution for cutpoints as
> > >
> > >   vector[K] cutpoints_raw;
> > >
> > >   cutpoints_raw ~ normal(0, 5);
> > >
> > >   cutpoints <- sort(cutpoints_raw);
> > >
> > > You can put a prior directly on the gaps with
> > >
> > >   vector[1] cutpoint0;
> > >   vector<lower=0>[K - 1] cutpoint_gaps;
> > >
> > >   cutpoint_gaps ~ normal(0, 2);
> > >
> > >   ordered[K] cutpoints;
> > >
> > >   cutpoints <- append_col(cutpoint, cutpoint + cutpoint_gaps);
> > >
> > > I'm not sure how to constraint the lowest cut point, cutpoint0.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > > On May 19, 2015, at 10:53 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > One of the reasons the paper is unwritten is because I think it is better to bring the prior information through the parameters of a Dirichlet prior on the conditional probabilities of being in each category given that the predictors are at the sample means. In code, it would look like
> > > >
> > > > functions {
> > > >   vector make_cutpoints(vector probabilities, real scale) {
> > > >     vector[rows(probabilities)-1] cutpoints;
> > > >     real running_sum;
> > > >     running_sum <- 0;
> > > >     for(c in 1:(rows(cutpoints))) {
> > > >       running_sum <- running_sum + probabilities[c];
> > > >       cutpoints[c] <- logit(running_sum);
> > > >     }
> > > >     return scale * cutpoints;
> > > >   }
> > > > }
> > > > data {
> > > >   int<lower=1> N;            # observations
> > > >   int<lower=1> K;            # predictors
> > > >   int<lower=3> C;            # outcome categories
> > > >   matrix[N,K]  X;            # "standardized" predictor matrix
> > > >   vector[K] xbar;            # vector of predictor means
> > > >   int<lower=1,upper=C> y[N]; # ordinal outcome
> > > >   vector[C] pseudocounts;    # prior value for concentrations in Dirichlet prior
> > > >   real<lower=0> nu;          # scale for Cauchy priors
> > > > }
> > > > transformed data {
> > > >   matrix[K,K] middle;
> > > >   middle <- xbar * transpose(xbar);
> > > > }
> > > > parameters {
> > > >   vector[K] beta_raw;        # coefficients
> > > >   simplex[C] probabilities;  # of falling in each category given xbar
> > > > }
> > > > transformed parameters {
> > > >   vector[K] beta;
> > > >   vector[C-1] cutpoints;
> > > >   for (k in 1:K) beta[k] <- nu * tan(pi() * (Phi(beta_raw[k]) - 0.5));
> > > >   cutpoints <- make_cutpoints(probabilities, sqrt(quad_form(middle, beta) + 1));
> > > > }
> > > > model {
> > > >   vector[N] eta;
> > > >   eta <- X * beta;                                          # linear predictor
> > > >   for(n in 1:N) y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(eta[n], cutpoints); # likelihood
> > > >   probabilities ~ dirichlet(pseudocounts);                  # our intuitive prior
> > > >   beta_raw ~ normal(0,1); # prior implies beta ~ cauchy(0,nu)
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > Ben
> > > >
> > > > On Tuesday, May 19, 2015 at 8:25:50 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > > > Hi, Ben and I actually have an (unwritten) paper on this.  The short answer is that we do think there’s a place for a weakly informative prior here.  One challenge is that the scale of the cutpoints themselves is hard to know ahead of time, so we were talking about setting up a prior by putting in a small bit (possibly a fractional bit) of pseudo-data in each bin.
> > > >
> > > > > On May 19, 2015, at 5:46 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > Is there a natural prior for cut points (specifically in
> > > > > an ordered logistic regression) or is the ordered constraint
> > > > > sufficiently strong that the uniform prior is well-posed?

Apologies if this has been asked before.

For a model I'm trying to fit, I need to set inits to 0 for sampling to not throw an error. Is my understanding correct that this means one can't use (or at least, must be cautious with) the Rhat statistic for assessing chain convergence? From Gelman & Rubin (1992):

Setting the chains to initialise at the same value would violate this starting point assumption, producing spurious evidence of convergence. Correct?

messages.body_plain:
Hi all -

Just a heads-up. A new R package, "needs" makes it significantly easier to load libraries and share code. It checks to see if you have a library already installed, and if not, downloads it and loads it. It also allows the user to prioritize namespaces after loading, so you don't call MASS::select() when you really want dplyr::select(). Simple and useful.

But it doesn't yet play nicely with Stan. Yesterday I was getting the following error when calling an exported Stan function from within mclapply:

Warning: namespace ‘rstan’ is not available and has been replaced by .GlobalEnv when processing object ''.

I let the author Josh know, and he's investigating. In the meantime, the following fix that he suggested worked fine:

cat(file = file.path(Sys.getenv("R_HOME"), "etc", "Rprofile.site"))

Cheers,
Jim

Hi Lei, see chapter 23 of BDA3. 23.1 explains the pseudo-counts in the discussion here, based on the basic notion of a Bayesian histogram. ‘Stick breaking construction’ in 23.2 explains the stick-breaking prior for Dirichlet processes, where the sticks are broken off based on a Beta distribution. By truncated stick-breaking prior, I mean rather than run this stick-breaking process until infinity, it is run until the number of cutpoints. (This is just another representation of a Dirichlet distribution.)

Dustin

Finally got around to playing with this again. I read up on calibration and see that indeed the model seems to be well-calibrated insofar as the 25%ile-75%ile band of the y2 samples indeed captures 50% of the data.

However, when I run the model on just the even years, then again on just the odd years, there's substantial non-overlap of the resulting 95%ile bands of the samples for mu2 (mean function), supporting my previous observation that the bands for the mean function seem overly narrow. Presumably I'm incorrect in my interpretation of those bands as reflecting the credible range for the mean function of the data-generating process (since you wouldn't expect the credible range of this property to vary dramatically between odd & even years), so any idea what these bands are? More importantly, any idea what I'd need to do to compute what I thought those bands were (credible range for the mean function)?

Mike
