messages.body_plain:
The main problem is that you are only going to get weak identification
using a K-dimensional parameterization of a K-way multinomial output.  Especially
if you include a hierarchical model with varying scale --- because the scale of
the predictors is not defined given that it's a K-dimensional parameterization.
You can move the K-1 dimensional parameterization, which makes the priors
asymmetric, but makes everything well behaved.  It's the only thing you'd see
in a max likelihood setting.

You can also vectorize this

> for (m in 1:M){
>   sigma[m] ~ cauchy(0,3);

by declaring sigma as a matrix and using to_vector(sigma) on the left.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Cutpoint Priors
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Cutpoint Priors
messages.body_plain:
The transform for the simplex uses stick-breaking.  but
there's no ordering --- what do you mean by ordering of
the cutpoints?  The usual thing to do here is take the
cumulative sums, so you get an increasing sequence to scale:

parameters {
  simplex[K] theta;     // gaps between cutpoints
  real<lower=0> kappa;  // scale for cutpoints

transformed parameters {
  ordered[K] cutpoints;
  cutpoints <- cumulative_sum(theta) * kappa;

model {
  theta ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(alpha, K));

Then if you put a Dirichlet prior on theta, with alpha >> 1, it'll keep
the cutpoints apart.  And it's best to define that vector as
transformed data.

- Bob

> On Apr 14, 2016, at 12:11 AM, Dustin Tran <dustinv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> What about a truncated stick breaking prior? The size-biasedness of TSB priors will
> (1) force an ordering for the cutpoints;
> (2) make draws of cutpoints live on [0,1] which you can scale willy-nilly;
> (3) reinforce what Ben said on adding prior information via pseudocounts in the parameters of a Dirichlet prior (here, use Beta stick-breaking priors, which is what Ben essentially does based on the running sum in the make_cutpoints function).
>
> Dustin
>> On Apr 13, 2016, at 11:43 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>
>> HI, are you saying that a simple flat prior on the cutpoints won’t work?  Or a super-weak prior such as normal(0,10)?
>>
>> I’m surprised that you get “cutpoint collapse” if you’re doing full Bayes (as opposed to maximum likelihood).
>>
>> If you want to put some prior info as below, I recommend putting the normal priors on the _differences_ between the cutpoints, not the cutpoints themselves.  Otherwise you have this weird thing going on where the cutpoints are all being pulled toward each other.
>>
>> A
>>
>>> On Apr 13, 2016, at 9:38 AM, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> Sorry to bring this up again. I am (still) facing the cutpoint-collapse problem when fitting an ordered-logistic model. After reading this thread and several others, I am still not sure (1) how to properly specify the prior of the cutpoint parameters, and (2) is there a way to model the cutpoint hierarchically like below? I tried something before but it seems that it doesn't guarantee that c[n,k+1] > c[n,k], hence it won't compile. I would highly appreciate any suggestions!
>>>
>>> ordered[K] c_mu;
>>> vector<lower=0>[K] c_sd;
>>> ordered[K] c[N];
>>>
>>> for (n in 1:N)
>>>    for (k in 1:K)
>>>        c[n,k] ~ normal(c_mu[k], c_sd[k]);
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> On Wednesday, May 20, 2015 at 8:27:28 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>> Cool.  I like that idea.
>>>
>>> Just ordering obviously isn't enough for the uniform distribution
>>> on an ordered vector to be proper.
>>>
>>> What does happen for reasons I still don't fully understand is
>>> that
>>>
>>>   ordered[K] cutpoints;
>>>
>>>   cutpoints ~ normal(0, 5);
>>>
>>> provides the same distribution for cutpoints as
>>>
>>>   vector[K] cutpoints_raw;
>>>
>>>   cutpoints_raw ~ normal(0, 5);
>>>
>>>   cutpoints <- sort(cutpoints_raw);
>>>
>>> You can put a prior directly on the gaps with
>>>
>>>   vector[1] cutpoint0;
>>>   vector<lower=0>[K - 1] cutpoint_gaps;
>>>
>>>   cutpoint_gaps ~ normal(0, 2);
>>>
>>>   ordered[K] cutpoints;
>>>
>>>   cutpoints <- append_col(cutpoint, cutpoint + cutpoint_gaps);
>>>
>>> I'm not sure how to constraint the lowest cut point, cutpoint0.
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> > On May 19, 2015, at 10:53 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>> >
>>> > One of the reasons the paper is unwritten is because I think it is better to bring the prior information through the parameters of a Dirichlet prior on the conditional probabilities of being in each category given that the predictors are at the sample means. In code, it would look like
>>> >
>>> > functions {
>>> >   vector make_cutpoints(vector probabilities, real scale) {
>>> >     vector[rows(probabilities)-1] cutpoints;
>>> >     real running_sum;
>>> >     running_sum <- 0;
>>> >     for(c in 1:(rows(cutpoints))) {
>>> >       running_sum <- running_sum + probabilities[c];
>>> >       cutpoints[c] <- logit(running_sum);
>>> >     }
>>> >     return scale * cutpoints;
>>> >   }
>>> > }
>>> > data {
>>> >   int<lower=1> N;            # observations
>>> >   int<lower=1> K;            # predictors
>>> >   int<lower=3> C;            # outcome categories
>>> >   matrix[N,K]  X;            # "standardized" predictor matrix
>>> >   vector[K] xbar;            # vector of predictor means
>>> >   int<lower=1,upper=C> y[N]; # ordinal outcome
>>> >   vector[C] pseudocounts;    # prior value for concentrations in Dirichlet prior
>>> >   real<lower=0> nu;          # scale for Cauchy priors
>>> > }
>>> > transformed data {
>>> >   matrix[K,K] middle;
>>> >   middle <- xbar * transpose(xbar);
>>> > }
>>> > parameters {
>>> >   vector[K] beta_raw;        # coefficients
>>> >   simplex[C] probabilities;  # of falling in each category given xbar
>>> > }
>>> > transformed parameters {
>>> >   vector[K] beta;
>>> >   vector[C-1] cutpoints;
>>> >   for (k in 1:K) beta[k] <- nu * tan(pi() * (Phi(beta_raw[k]) - 0.5));
>>> >   cutpoints <- make_cutpoints(probabilities, sqrt(quad_form(middle, beta) + 1));
>>> > }
>>> > model {
>>> >   vector[N] eta;
>>> >   eta <- X * beta;                                          # linear predictor
>>> >   for(n in 1:N) y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(eta[n], cutpoints); # likelihood
>>> >   probabilities ~ dirichlet(pseudocounts);                  # our intuitive prior
>>> >   beta_raw ~ normal(0,1); # prior implies beta ~ cauchy(0,nu)
>>> > }
>>> >
>>> > Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,
I am using stan to fit a multilevel logistic regression model that includes random effects for age and period (year). I would like to be able to do a prediction for some new observations with observed patterns of the covariates in the model, but for a future period. So this is a type of forecast in a very loose sense of the word. My model is attached, and a link to my data is here:

https://drive.google.com/open?id=0B7G5045BmRHzQkRjUEgzc1p1UUk

In the generated quantities block, I do prediction for some new cases, but I can only include values of my variable `year_pred` that lie within the observed range. The data have year ranges of 1 to 14, but I would like to get a prediction for year 19 (posterior predicted value). If, otherwise stan throws an error:

"accessing element out of range. index 19 out of range; expecting index to be between 1 and 15;"

I see that rstanarm has the capacity in its posterior_predict() function to include new levels of a group-level variable. My issue is that my model has an random walk term for one of the random effects that rstanarm can't handle. My question is, how can I get rstan to allow me to do this in the generated quantities block? Any suggestions would be appreciated.

-Corey

The Stan modeling language allows you to specify (possibly) conditional
probability distributions,

p( parameters | data),

and then estimates expectations

E[f] = \int f(parameters) p( parameters | data) d(parameters).

The names “parameters” and “data” are indicative of our usual Bayesian
applications but they could refer to anything.

I am hesitant that you are defining a well-posed target distribution,
but if that’s really want you want to do then just define that distribution
in the model block and Stan will do the rest.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Identifying Polynomial Coefficients
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Identifying Polynomial Coefficients
messages.body_plain:
The dimensions are screwing with me here.

Let’s say that we have N data points and M covariates, where
N >> M.  In this case our original problem is

matrix[N, M] X; // data
vector[M] beta; // parameters
vector[N] alpha; // parameters
y ~ normal(X * beta + alpha, sigma);

If the covariates are highly correlated then this can cause
problems, so instead we want to use a QR decomposition,
to write

X * beta = (Q * R) * beta = Q * (R * beta) = Q * beta_tilde

and then fit the model

matrix[N, M] X; // data
matrix[N, N] Q;
matrix[N, M] R;
vector[N] beta_tilde; // parameters
vector[N] alpha; // parameters
y ~ normal(Q * beta_tilde + alpha, sigma);
beta = R \ beta_tilde;

But doesn't this replace the M original parameters with N >> M
new parameters?  Is the cost of decor relating really the
introduction of so many new parameters?

In any case qr_R is seg faulting on me so it looks like there
are bigger problems...

On Apr 8, 2016, at 5:00 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Friday, April 8, 2016 at 11:45:21 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > Right.  So instead of
> >
> > y = normal( X* beta + alpha, sigma);
> >
> > you’d fit
> >
> > Q = qr_Q(X);
> > R = qr_R(X);
> > y = normal(Q * beta_tilde + alpha, sigma);
> >
> > then
> >
> > beta = mdivide_right_tri_low(beta_tilde, R); ?
>
> Yeah, basically. We actually multiply Q by sqrt(N - 1) and divide R by sqrt(N - 1) to make beta_tilde have a more reasonable scale in large datasets. A lot of times ADVI only works well with this transformation.
>
> Ben
>

In the "thin" QR decomposition of the "tall" NxM matrix X = Q * R, Q is supposed to be NxM and R is supposed to be MxM.

This should then be vector[M] beta_tilde.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
First of all, sizes have to be integers, so you
would have to have:

  int<lower=1> Mi[N];

But we don't have ragged arrays, yet, so you either have
to use a melted encoding and put vectors back together if
you need them as such, or you have to declare a bigger array
of vectors

   vector[max(Mi)] bP[N];

and then just ignore the unused vectors (you have to
slice them down manually when you use them).

We'll get ragged arrays eventually, but probably not this year.

- Bob

In other words, a Stan program defines an unnormalized log density
that is proportional to p(params | data), usually by defining
the joint density p(params, data) and relying on Bayes's rule that
says p(params | data) prop-to p(params, data) when data is fixed.

- Bob

> On Apr 15, 2016, at 4:38 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> The Stan modeling language allows you to specify (possibly) conditional
> probability distributions,
>
> p( parameters | data),
>
> and then estimates expectations
>
> E[f] = \int f(parameters) p( parameters | data) d(parameters).
>
> The names “parameters” and “data” are indicative of our usual Bayesian
> applications but they could refer to anything.
>
> I am hesitant that you are defining a well-posed target distribution,
> but if that’s really want you want to do then just define that distribution
> in the model block and Stan will do the rest.
>

messages.body_plain:
Won't only using even or odd years in the time series affect
the scale of any kind of moving average function, so that you'd
be fitting different models?

You have to be careful with 95% intervals as they're very noisy
without a large effective sample size.

By captures 50% of the data, you mean the posterior predictive
50% intervals contain the true values around 50% of the time?

The real issue is that unless you have the true model, you
don't get guarantees on matching the true data generating process
with your estimates.  This is the sense in which all stats, frequentist
and Bayesian, is subjective.  For example, if I make a complete
pooling assumption for some item-specific effect, I'll get narrow
posterior intervals compared to assuming no pooling.  But I am unlikely
to get good coverage if that complete pooling assumption is incorrect.

Another example is that if you assume normal noise and the noise
actually has fatter tails, then you can't get calibrated.  Similarly
if you assume a Poisson or binomial distribution for counts or
repeated trials and the data's actually overdispersed.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
One method I've found helpful is to define a pair of index vectors:

int N; // number of measurements
int nPat; // number of patients
vector[N] bP;  // measurements
int<lower=1,upper=N> start_Pos[nPat];  // the first position on bP for each patient
int<lower=1,upper=N> stop_Pos[nPat];  // the last position on bP for each patient

/// ...

bP[start_Pos[i]:stop_Pos[i]] ~ ... // select the measurements of patient i

This I suppose this could result in slightly more overhead, but I think it makes the code easier to write.

messages.body_plain:
Right.  That's what Ben was suggesting.  Usually you only
need a single index array though and can use

  bP[start_pos[i], start_pos[i + 1] - i]

But then you have to be careful to pad the start_pos index to size N + 1
and add the final endpoint if you want the loops to be easy.

Think of all the integer arithmetic as a freebie --- it can
almost all be parallelized efficiently in the CPU beside the
floating point calls.  In contrast, iterating over two arrays
is more expensive, because memory access can be more (or even much
more) costly than integer arithmetic.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: _NEW_ term when using stan_glmer
messages.subject_clean: _NEW_ term when using stan_glmer
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

We didn't put out any user-facing documentation for this because we didn't want people to focus on this too much, but perhaps it would be better to include something about this in the package documentation. I suppose the best place would probably be in the documentation for the posterior_predict function.

Following up on what Ben said, the reason we add the terms labeled _NEW_ is so that we can allow posterior_predict to accept data (the newdata argument) containing levels of grouping variables not present in the original data. We mostly try to hide these _NEW_ terms from the user because they're not really of direct interest but rather just used internally to be able to produce the predictions if necessary.

Essentially, we add extra parameters to the group-level parameters but we make sure they do not enter the likelihood. That way the estimates of the actual group-level parameters are the same as they would be if we didn't add the extra levels, but we can use the posterior distribution of the extra levels if we need them when making predictions. Even though they don't enter the likelihood their posterior will not be identical to their prior because the parameters for the new levels share common hyperparameters with the other group-level parameters and we learn something about these hyperparameters. So we're updating what we believe about the new levels based on what we've learned from the data we did observe.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

Those aren't the same models (at least not without
the appropriate Jacobian adjustments), because
of the change of variables.

model1:  uniform on 2 x 2 covariance matrics

model2:  independent uniform on correlation and scales

The map between the two isn't linear, so you need a Jacobian
to make them the same model.

Centering as well as scaling X would probably help with
fitting a and b, as would weakly informative priors on
all the parameters.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: circular parameter
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan users,

I would like to ask about estimating a parameter that for a circular quantity (e.g. time).

I have included a toy dataset/models in the attached file that runs in r.

I am trying to model some oscillating time series data - e.g. y[i,j] ~ normal(sin(time[I,[j]+pos[j]), sigma)
Different subjects have different phase shifts (pos[j]) in the range -pi to pi
I would like to estimate the phase shift parameter.

Initially I used a uniform prior over the range -pi to pi for offset (model 1 in attached file). This resulted in the posterior distributions of pos[j] near -pi or pi being poorly estimated, presumably as the optimization method has difficulties moving between -pi and pi.

Then I tried a von meis prior with a very small kappa (0 is not allowed) for offset (model 2 in attached file). The results were similar to model 1.

Then I tried using 2 parameters with uniform prior over the range -1 to 1 (model 3, xpos and ypos). I then took the atan of ypos/xpos to get the angle. Since there are multiple values of xpos and ypos that give the same angle, I set parameter sigma to be equal to sqrt(xpos^2+ypos^2)+0.1 , to make xpos and ypos identifiable. The seemed to work better than models 1 or 2, but had the disadvantage that each individual now had their own sigma.

By chance I noticed that if I neglected to index sigma in the likleyhood function (line 241, model 4), then the estimates for the angle were more precise . Whilst the print of the model indicated there were  still as many sigma as individuals, they were now all of the same value.

My questions are
- the way I used to estimate the offset/angle in model 3 or 4 seemed better than in model 1 or 2, but I could not find examples of others doing this, so I was unsure if this is a reasonable way to do it?

- What is going on in model 4 vs model 3? I would  have expected not indexing sigma to result in an error?

Thanks for any advice you may have

Hugh

Please see the attached modell/data  file.

messages.body_plain:
There's a large literature on circular statistics.

We'll finally have a working version of unit vector
parameters in Stan 2.10 (out soon).  And I wrote up a new
chapter for the manual (warning---I had to learn as I
went, never having done circular stats).  I'm attaching
it prior to release (comments welcome, as always).

Your diagnosis is accurate --- the sampler can't move
between -pi and pi if you treat it as a line.  Stan uses
an auxiliary variable parameterization somewhat like yours
(but unconstrained), and a unit normal regulaization
described in the attached chapter;  there aren't any free
parameters in that, though --- you just need to fix the
scale.

If you did this

  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ normal(mu[n], sigma);

and sigma is an N-vector, then it's equivalent to this

  for (n in 1:N)
    for (m in 1:N)
      y[n] ~ normal(mu[n], sigma[m]);

which is not what you want to do.  It artificially multiplies
data size by N and ties all the parameters sigma[n] together.

- Bob

> On Apr 17, 2016, at 1:55 AM, Sachinthaka Abeywardana <sachin.ab...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> The data that I am simulating is a mixture of Asymmetric hyperbolic distributions (laplace is a special case). This distribution can be generated as:
> w ~ gamma(1,alpha0)
> y ~ N(w*a,w*sigma^2)
>
> where a and sigma2 are constants.
>
>
> So I generate the mixture as such:
> for (t in 2:T){
>   z[t] = sample.int <http://sample.int>(K,1,prob = p)
>   w = rgamma(1,alpha0)
>   y[t] = muk[z[t]]+w*ak[z[t]]+sqrt(w*sigma2k[z[t]])*rnorm(1)
> }
>
> muk is a location parameter.
>
> And the corresponding stan segment is as follows:
> for (t in 2:N) {
>     w[t] ~ gamma(2.0,1.0); //alpha0 = 2
>     for (k in 1:K)
>         acc[k] <- log(theta[k]) + normal_log(y[t],mu[k]+a[k]*w[t],sqrt(w[t])*sigma[k]);
>     increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(acc));
> }
>
>
> The question is:
> 1. Do I need to declare a w[t] for each k? (and why? i.e. does it need to be w[t,k]~gamma(2.0,1.0))

Those are different models.

> 2. Can I speed this stan code by declaring w ~ gamma(2.0,1.0) outside the for loop

You need to write to_vector(w) ~ gamma(2, 1);   And it'll be more efficient
than looping (not because of loop, but because of reduced virtual function
calls during derivative calculations).

> 3. Does stan care if I use a float number 2.0 or can I write 2 inside that gamma()

Integers are automatically promoted to reals for function
arguments requiring real arguments and in arithmetic operators
when the other operand is real (e.g., 1 / 2.0 will evaluate to
0.5).

- Bob

Hi Bob,
Following your solution on slicing and indexing my matrices and vectors, I wrote my code.
I have to define some of my matrices and vectors in the model block as they both depend on parameters and data. In particular, in the model section, I define a matrix of the form below:

matrix[1,max(Mi)] K_transpose_div_SigmaPred;

As a reminder, Mi is a vector of number of measurements per subject. So if Mi[1] is 12, it means subject 1 has 12 within-subj measurements. Note that subjects may have different number measurements. So the idea is let's define a big row matrix and if a subject has fewer observations, let's slice this row matrix as K_transpose_div_SigmaPred[1, 1:Mi_i] where Mi_i <- Mi[i]

Later in my data block, I have a loop on subjects and in a statement in that loop, I compute K_transpose_div_SigmaPred as:

K_transpose_div_SigmaPred <- to_matrix((K[1:(Mi_i), 1])' * inverse(SigmaPred[1:Mi_i, 1:Mi_i]));

K_transpose_div_SigmaPred[1, 1:Mi_i] <- to_matrix((K[1:(Mi_i), 1])' * inverse(SigmaPred[1:Mi_i, 1:Mi_i]));

But the line above is not valid and leads to compile error. Also it's not possible to declare K_transpose_div_SigmaPred within the loop as it seems that all variable declaration should be done on top of the model block. What would you think I should do?

Also, I'm so grateful to your guidance and help and so sorry I'm asking a specific question. I tried to find a solution over the past 2 days but no success and decided to get some help here.

On Monday, April 18, 2016 at 2:28:32 AM UTC+7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> There's a large literature on circular statistics.
>
> We'll finally have a working version of unit vector
> parameters in Stan 2.10 (out soon).  And I wrote up a new
> chapter for the manual (warning---I had to learn as I
> went, never having done circular stats).  I'm attaching
> it prior to release (comments welcome, as always).
>
> Your diagnosis is accurate --- the sampler can't move
> between -pi and pi if you treat it as a line.  Stan uses
> an auxiliary variable parameterization somewhat like yours
> (but unconstrained), and a unit normal regulaization
> described in the attached chapter;  there aren't any free
> parameters in that, though --- you just need to fix the
> scale.
>
> If you did this
>
>   for (n in 1:N)
>     y[n] ~ normal(mu[n], sigma);
>
> and sigma is an N-vector, then it's equivalent to this
>
>   for (n in 1:N)
>     for (m in 1:N)
>       y[n] ~ normal(mu[n], sigma[m]);
>
> which is not what you want to do.  It artificially multiplies
> data size by N and ties all the parameters sigma[n] together.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Apr 17, 2016, at 3:50 AM, 'Hugh' via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Stan users,
> >
> > I would like to ask about estimating a parameter that for a circular quantity (e.g. time).
> >
> > I have included a toy dataset/models in the attached file that runs in r.
> >
> > I am trying to model some oscillating time series data - e.g. y[i,j] ~ normal(sin(time[I,[j]+pos[j]), sigma)
> > Different subjects have different phase shifts (pos[j]) in the range -pi to pi
> > I would like to estimate the phase shift parameter.
> >
> > Initially I used a uniform prior over the range -pi to pi for offset (model 1 in attached file). This resulted in the posterior distributions of pos[j] near -pi or pi being poorly estimated, presumably as the optimization method has difficulties moving between -pi and pi.
> >
> > Then I tried a von meis prior with a very small kappa (0 is not allowed) for offset (model 2 in attached file). The results were similar to model 1.
> >
> > Then I tried using 2 parameters with uniform prior over the range -1 to 1 (model 3, xpos and ypos). I then took the atan of ypos/xpos to get the angle. Since there are multiple values of xpos and ypos that give the same angle, I set parameter sigma to be equal to sqrt(xpos^2+ypos^2)+0.1 , to make xpos and ypos identifiable. The seemed to work better than models 1 or 2, but had the disadvantage that each individual now had their own sigma.
> >
> > By chance I noticed that if I neglected to index sigma in the likleyhood function (line 241, model 4), then the estimates for the angle were more precise . Whilst the print of the model indicated there were  still as many sigma as individuals, they were now all of the same value.

messages.body_plain:
You don't need a sampling statement.  For every parameter
type Stan has, the default distribution is uniform over
values satisfying the constraint.  In this case, the
uniform happens to be improper.

If you want to know how we represent it as unconstrained
parameters, transform, and calculate the Jacobian, there's
a chapter on all the transforms we use near the end of the
manual.  The unconstrained representation is a Cholesky factor
with log-transformed diagonals (Cholesky factors with positive
diagonals are a basis for the symmetric, positive-definite
matrices).  The Jacobian's in the chapter, and it gets applied
automatically behind the scenes (and differentiated) for
each leapfrog step.

- Bob

> On Apr 17, 2016, at 6:37 PM, Bee <ceiiino...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you. Yes, I understand model3 is better, but I'd like to know how Stan implement uniform over covariance matrices.
>
> parameters {
>   cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
>   ...
>
> Could you write the math formula for the above uniform using sampling statement?
>
> - Bee
>
> On Monday, April 18, 2016 at 4:40:30 AM UTC+9, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> That's not uniform and violates the basic Stan principle
> that all legal values for parameters should have support
> (not all the legal parameter values here produce positive
> definite matrices).
>
> If you really want uniform over covariance matrices, it has
> to be this:
>
> parameters {
>   cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
>   ...
>
> Of course, that's improper, so you need to make sure you
> have some data so the posterior's proper.
>
> But we recommend scaling a Cholesky factor of a correlation
> matrix with some prior concentration around the unit correlation
> matrix.
>
> - Bob
>

> >
> > Bob, thank you for your reply.

messages.subject: ADVI... log-lik worse than with NuTS
messages.subject_clean: ADVI... log-lik worse than with NuTS
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I am working with a large/complex model which I would like to address with ADVI due to speed. However, it seems that the variance components are not estimated so well. That is, the random effects are often not moved away from the initial and most importantly the residual error sigma_y is estimated with nuts as 4.3-4.5 while ADVI gives me around 5.3-5.5, i.e. giving much less weight to the data.

I found that doing the automatic eta tuning does not work well for me, i.e. it tends to choose a too large value of 1 while 0.1 seems to be a safe choice and ADVI gives me a nice CONVERGED message.

Any ideas what one could try?

Sorry to not share the model which is just too big. From my view the model has a problem with it's parametrization (correlation of 0.9 of two parameters), but for reasons out of my control I don't want to change this.

Best,
Sebastian

This originally came from an issue discussion.  We're trying to
keep our issues focused on actionable issues, not general discussion,
so I'm moving this here.

The only reason to run a single chain that I can imagine is when
there's persistent multimodality and you're happy with a single mode and
can't easily merge multiple chains because of things like index switching and
you want to do inference dependent on the mixtures, as in creating one
of those word clouds from an LDA model or something like that.

I believe Ben's the one who wrote the pairs() plot in RStan and I'm not
sure what his intent was.  Maybe he can clarify.

messages.subject: new case study: Jacobians and the MLE vs. Bayes
messages.subject_clean: new case study: Jacobians and the MLE vs. Bayes
messages.body_plain:
I finally got around to writing up the effects of Jacobians
on MLEs (breaks them) vs. Bayesian posteriors (preserves them),
which is why we say that Bayes is invariant to reparameterization
with appropriate Jacobian adjustments, but MLEs aren't.

  http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mle-params.html

The case study also talks about how not including the Jacobian
preserves the MLE, so they're invariant in another sense, leading
to potential terminological confusion.

Also, if anyone else wants to contribute case studies, we're ready
to receive them.

- Bob

P.S.  Here's the abstract from the case studies page:

Maximum Likelihood, Bayesian Posteriors, and Reparameterization
---------------------------------------------------------------

When changing variables, a Jacobian adjustment needs to be provided to preserve the probability distributions of quantities of interest, incuding Bayesian posteriors. With appropriate Jacobians, Bayesian inference is invariant to the parameterization. In contrast, applying the appropriate Jacobian adjustment leads to different maximum likelihood estimates, whereas skipping the Jacobians leaves them unchanged. In this note, we contrast three simple repeated binary trial models, varying only by parameterization: (a) direct probability parameterization, (b) log odds parameterization without Jacobian adjustment, (c) log odds parameterization with Jacobian adjustment. Models (a) and (b) provide the same MLE, whereas model (c) has a different MLE. In contrast, models (a) and (c) provide the same Bayesian posterior, whereas model (b) differs.

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mle-params.html

> Noted. Sorry and thanks.

No problem at all.  We'd much rather get feedback than no feedback,
even if we want to move channels.

>> The only reason to run a single chain that I can imagine is when
>> there's persistent multimodality and you're happy with a single mode and
>> can't easily merge multiple chains because of things like index switching and
>> you want to do inference dependent on the mixtures, as in creating one
>> of those word clouds from an LDA model or something like that.
>
> I should have said I do want multiple chains from the final model;  I’m just wondering if it can help debugging. In a case where initialization looks OK but the sampler is having trouble exploring the whole posterior with any one chain, does adding more chains make it easier or harder to isolate the problematic part of the model?

Yes, multiple chains can help you find multiple spots in the posterior that
may be problematic.  And problems won't show up on every chain in every model.
They'll also show when you're not converging, which can be hard to diagnose
with a single chain that's not moving well.

I've found the pairs() plots to be most useful, because you can see strong
dependencies and nasty banana shaped marginal posteriors for pairs of paramters.

>> I believe Ben's the one who wrote the pairs() plot in RStan and I'm not
>> sure what his intent was.  Maybe he can clarify.
>
> Sorry, I think I’m missing the connection here. The issues in my original report were with stan_diag() and stan_par() — as far as I can tell pairs() works nicely with any number of chains, including 1.

You're right --- pairs() works with one chain now.  I believe it used
to require more than one by default.

- Bob

How small is n_eff and what are the R-hat values?

If the R-hats don't all converge to 1, it means the model's
going to need to be reparameterized or rewritten.

If the n_eff is just very small compared to the number of
iterations, that's sometimes workable and sometimes not.
It can often help to reparameterize.

How did you set your expectations for posterior standard deviation?
Assuming the model converges, they should be correct (to within
MCMC sampling error).  There's no inherent overestimation bis
for posterior variance!

- Bob

hi sebastian,

could you expand a bit on what you mean when you say "the variance components"? do you mean the variance components of the model, or the (marginal) variances of the posterior estimates?

i don't have much to go on here, but i might recommend decreasing the `tol_rel_obj` parameter, such that you run ADVI for more iterations before it converges.

another option is to try the fullrank version of ADVI, which is considerably slower (depending on the number of parameters in your model).

a downstream idea is to find a way to specify which parameters should be modeled independently (computationally cheap) and which ones should be modeled together (more accurate).

i hope this helps.

cheers,

Yes, you should be fine.  You aren't getting divergent transition
warnings?

A simulated value is a single value.  How do you compare that
to the width of a posterior?

And the posterior mean isn't going to be exactly the same.
Consider the case where I have a normal(0, 1) and make 5 draws.
What do I get for the mean?

> y <- rnorm(10)

> mean(y)
[1] -0.1355454

That's way off the expected value of 0!  It's just sampling variation
and that's what confidence intervals and posterior intervals are
quantifying (in different ways).

What you want to check is calibration.  If you have 100 parameters,
are roughly half of them in posterior 50% intervals?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
OK, that was a bit fast off the cuff.  I went back and revised it,
so it should read more smoothly.  And it provides an example plot
of the change of variables in question with an R simulation.  The
link's the same:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mle-params.html

Comments are more than welcome.  It's a tricky subject given
the interplay of MLE, posterior modes, and expectations/quantiles
with and without Jacobians.

- Bob

> On Apr 18, 2016, at 6:12 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> I finally got around to writing up the effects of Jacobians
> on MLEs (breaks them) vs. Bayesian posteriors (preserves them),
> which is why we say that Bayes is invariant to reparameterization
> with appropriate Jacobian adjustments, but MLEs aren't.
>
>  http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mle-params.html
>
> The case study also talks about how not including the Jacobian
> preserves the MLE, so they're invariant in another sense, leading
> to potential terminological confusion.
>
> Also, if anyone else wants to contribute case studies, we're ready
> to receive them.
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  Here's the abstract from the case studies page:
>
> Maximum Likelihood, Bayesian Posteriors, and Reparameterization
> ---------------------------------------------------------------
>
> When changing variables, a Jacobian adjustment needs to be provided to preserve the probability distributions of quantities of interest, incuding Bayesian posteriors. With appropriate Jacobians, Bayesian inference is invariant to the parameterization. In contrast, applying the appropriate Jacobian adjustment leads to different maximum likelihood estimates, whereas skipping the Jacobians leaves them unchanged. In this note, we contrast three simple repeated binary trial models, varying only by parameterization: (a) direct probability parameterization, (b) log odds parameterization without Jacobian adjustment, (c) log odds parameterization with Jacobian adjustment. Models (a) and (b) provide the same MLE, whereas model (c) has a different MLE. In contrast, models (a) and (c) provide the same Bayesian posterior, whereas model (b) differs.
>
> http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mle-params.html
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] new case study: Jacobians and the MLE vs. Bayes
messages.body_plain:
The most recent draft looks good, in particular because it is careful
to compare proper expectations to posterior modes.  But I would
change the name of the case study to avoid referencing MLE
altogether which induces much pedantry and confusion.

On Apr 19, 2016, at 6:33 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> OK, that was a bit fast off the cuff.  I went back and revised it,
> so it should read more smoothly.  And it provides an example plot
> of the change of variables in question with an R simulation.  The
> link's the same:
>
> http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mle-params.html
>
> Comments are more than welcome.  It's a tricky subject given
> the interplay of MLE, posterior modes, and expectations/quantiles
> with and without Jacobians.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>> On Apr 18, 2016, at 6:12 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>> I finally got around to writing up the effects of Jacobians
>> on MLEs (breaks them) vs. Bayesian posteriors (preserves them),
>> which is why we say that Bayes is invariant to reparameterization
>> with appropriate Jacobian adjustments, but MLEs aren't.
>>
>> http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mle-params.html
>>
>> The case study also talks about how not including the Jacobian
>> preserves the MLE, so they're invariant in another sense, leading
>> to potential terminological confusion.
>>
>> Also, if anyone else wants to contribute case studies, we're ready
>> to receive them.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>> P.S.  Here's the abstract from the case studies page:
>>
>> Maximum Likelihood, Bayesian Posteriors, and Reparameterization
>> ---------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> When changing variables, a Jacobian adjustment needs to be provided to preserve the probability distributions of quantities of interest, incuding Bayesian posteriors. With appropriate Jacobians, Bayesian inference is invariant to the parameterization. In contrast, applying the appropriate Jacobian adjustment leads to different maximum likelihood estimates, whereas skipping the Jacobians leaves them unchanged. In this note, we contrast three simple repeated binary trial models, varying only by parameterization: (a) direct probability parameterization, (b) log odds parameterization without Jacobian adjustment, (c) log odds parameterization with Jacobian adjustment. Models (a) and (b) provide the same MLE, whereas model (c) has a different MLE. In contrast, models (a) and (c) provide the same Bayesian posterior, whereas model (b) differs.
>>
>> http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mle-params.html
>>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alp,

I was referring to random effects, so variance components of the model. To be specific, I have a model about patients (the patients are observed over time, longitudinal data) which are grouped into treatment arms and then I have multiple treatment arms grouped into different studies. Some parameters vary by patients and some by study and by patient (nested!). While the patient specific parameters are well informed by the data, I observe quite some shrinkage towards the population mean for the study specific parameters when I use NuTS; still I think I need those.

Now when I run the model with ADVI, then the patient-level parameters receive a somewhat increased between-subject variability and the between-study parameters don't move away from the initial (both in comparison to the NuTS result). It seems that ADVI can't deal well with random effects which have some shrinkage on them.

I will try your suggestion of playing with the tolerance, sounds reasonable.

Thanks!

Sebastian

On Tuesday, April 19, 2016 at 3:09:01 AM UTC+2, Alp Kucukelbir wrote:
> hi sebastian,
>
> could you expand a bit on what you mean when you say "the variance components"? do you mean the variance components of the model, or the (marginal) variances of the posterior estimates?
>
> i don't have much to go on here, but i might recommend decreasing the `tol_rel_obj` parameter, such that you run ADVI for more iterations before it converges.
>
> another option is to try the fullrank version of ADVI, which is considerably slower (depending on the number of parameters in your model).
>
> a downstream idea is to find a way to specify which parameters should be modeled independently (computationally cheap) and which ones should be modeled together (more accurate).
>
> i hope this helps.
>
> cheers,
> alp

Hello all,

I wrote a previous message regarding when model A has a better predictive capability than model B (using the Vehtari 2015 paper). I think I now understand why we need to use the paired comparison in ELPD between the two models.

However, I am also looking for a measure to quantify (in plain English) the predictive capability of the two models. Basically something along the lines of "model A explains X% of the variance, and model B explains Y% of the variance".

The problem is that, when I use simple R-squareds to compare the two models, I frequently get a contradiction with the ELPD results. In other words:

by ELPD: model A > model B
by R-squared: model A < model B

where '>' and '<' indicate 'better than' or 'worse than' respectively.

This isn't surprising to me, since they measure completely different things. However, it is quite unfortunate since I want to quantify (ideally via a percentage measure, or something that can be interpreted biologically), the improvement in model A relative to model B.

Does anyone have any ideas for what I could use that would give a consistent story? (Another measure would be something like % deviance explained, but am unsure how to estimate this.)

Best,

Ben

If foo(...) is the distribution (used on the right side of ~),
then foo_log(y, ...) is the log density function.  Some of the
distribution names end in _log so you get _log_log on the density
function.

Look at the definitions and use the appropriate one.
The _log version of negative binomial builds in the exp()
operation, so you don't want to do it twice.

In terms of "slow", you want to measure effective sample
size / second, and then only once everything's converged
and you know you are getting the right answers.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] change of variables for compound parameter
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] change of variables for compound parameter
messages.body_plain:
The density beta(2,2) is only defined for outcomes in (0, 1).
So you'd need to ensure log(A) / B in (0, 1).  Then you
run into the usual multiplicative identifiability issue, here
with a log in the middle:

  log(A) / B === log(A^N) / (B/N)

If N = -1, you get sign flipping and multimodality.

This also means your transform isn't invertible (the inverse is
one to many), and thus there's no way to calculate the Jacobian.
At least I'm pretty sure that's what happens --- someone else should
check my work here, because I still count Jacobians on my fingers
and toes.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Ok, apologies for the lack of detail in the previous message. I have a hierarchical model of within-host malaria (their viral load), and the different hierarchies correspond to different treatment groups.

I am using various host covariates to explain the viral load within a patient. I have a number of models for this, each representing different biological assumptions about the disease. I want the data to allow me to resolve a difference between these models.

As such, I have explicitly done k-fold cross validation to estimate the out-of-sample predictive performance of each model. This is the ELPD to which I was referring in my original question.

However, I would also like to state something in biological/numerical terms which allows a person to get a sense of just how much variation is being explained by each model. This is what I was referring to in my original question when I said, model A explains X% of the variance, and model B explains Y% of the variance (in viral load)".

The problem I have at the moment is that the two different metrics - ELPD vs % variance explained - are giving conflicting views. Part of me thinks that - if all I ultimately care about is % variance explained - then I should use this to compare the models (and forget about ELPD).

Does this sound reasonable, and the best approach?

Best,

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Quantifying the predictive capability of two models in a way consistent with ELPD

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

In general any model B that has more parameters than model A will "explain" (in a not very useful sense of the word) more of the variation in the outcome. It's unfortunate that "explain" is the traditional term used here because model B might not explain much of anything useful and will still have a higher R^2. Another way to say this is that comparing models based on proportion of variance "explained" is asking the question "which model explains more?",  but you're interested in a different question, that is "which model explains better?".

ELPD has its limitations, but it comes closer to answering the quevstion you will typically want. As you say, the cost of this is that it's less intuitive and less direct than "explained" variation because computed ELPDs only have meaning relative to other computed ELPDs.

Maybe there's a clever way to present it for your particular application (which sounds interesting by the way) but I still the a better method with more difficult presentation is preferable to inferior method with simple presentation.

Jonah

messages.body_plain:
Exceeding the maximum tree depth doesn't mean the model hasn't converged. It just means the sampler becomes less efficient as when max tree depth is reached it reverts to a random walk.

To check convergence you can look at the traceplots with rstan.
Another option (ideally you do both) is to look at the Rhats for each parameter. They need to be less than 1.1 to indicate convergence.
The other thing to look at is the effective sample size you are getting for each parameter. I tend to ensure that each parameter has at least 100 samples.

You might also want to consider decreasing the initial stepsize from the default of 1 to something smaller e.g. 0.5 (control(list(stepsize= 0.5)), especially if you are getting a lot of numerical issues during warmup.
I'm guessing you're not getting divergent iterations based on the error messages you're receiving.

Sorry haven't looked at your model.

For my first stan analysis, I wanted to extend the
censored regression model decribed in the stan_2.9.0
manual, pp. 108-109, to allow for covariates, ie to
implement what econometricians call the tobit model.
This is the model version that does not impute the
censored values.

My stan results are so different from the ML results
using the tobit estimator from the AER package that
I think I must be doing something wrong. (See
particularly the mean of the distribution of beta[2]).
With stan using by default uninformative priors,
one would expect the results to be close, no?

Could I  persuade someone to take a look at this
and see if they can diagnose what's going on?

Thanks!!

##### R session     (results below)
library(rstan)
library(AER)

load("c:/work/limdep/aasho/r/aasho.rdata")

U<-max(rigid25$ltrig)

model<-ltrig~lslabdd+laxles+lwta

# fit the tobit model
(summary(tobit(model,data=rigid25,right=U)))

# now set up the data for stan
id_cens<-rigid25$ltrig==U
mmx<-model.matrix(model,data=rigid25)

x_obs<-mmx[!id_cens,]

dd<-data.frame(dd) # convert to data frame
colnames(dd)[1]<-"ltrig" # name of dependent variable

(summary(tobit(model, data=dd,right=U)))
# this agrees with the earlier version

# now for stan: form the data list
data<-list(y_obs=y_obs, x_cens=x_cens, x_obs=x_obs,
                     K=K, N_obs=N_obs, N_cens=N_cens, U=U)

# re-running with iter=10000, warmup=2000

fit<-stan(file="aasho2.stan",data=data,

messages.body_plain:
Could you explain the purpose of the replication here? Are you currently working with the same model and the same data as it was originally applied to?  Simulated data? Another data set?  I think you already have ample evidence that this model will not work well for this data (comments on this below) and rather than fiddling with sampler parameters the density needs to be reparameterized.

On Wednesday, April 20, 2016 at 2:57:44 AM UTC-4, huiying wrote:
> Hi James,
>
> Thanks for the helpful explanation and guidelines.
>
> With 10000 iterations and 4 chains, the output for Rhats was > 1.1 and effective sample size for some samples were < 100. Traceplots clearly showed evidence of divergence.
>
> With 1000 iterations, it is even more poorly converged.

If 10000 iterations doesn't fix a problem visible at 1000 iterations you will likely never run enough iterations to get good results out of this model.

>
> Do I increase the number of iterations until the output shows desired Rhats and ESS? Is that the proper way of conduct?

Fix the model.  Look for strongly correlated parameters,  poorly identified sets of parameters, or parameters with correlations changing as a function of other parameters, look for parameters on boundaries, these are all things you can fix but they need to be found first.

>
> With 20000 iterations, 4 chains, Rhats were less than 1.1 and ess were above 100 (at borderline for some parameters), however I still get warning message concerning max_treedepth. Would it be appropriate to ignore the warning message? (I doubt so?)

Treedepth limits how many steps the integrator running HMC will take before giving up (whether it finds a u-turn or not).  I'm sure there are models where it's ok and you can live with the reduced efficiency but I haven't run into one yet.  Typically this means that in at least one direction in one portion of parameter space the scale the sampler needs to move on is much larger than whatever part of the space it was tuned in (during adaptation).  If it's not a practically relevant part of the parameter space then you can make it go away by setting tighter priors, or transforming parameters or something similar.

>
> However, with further increased # of iterations (tried with 30,000 and 40,000), some parameters had very low ESS, while some had way above 100.

The 20k iteration chains missed pathologies in the model---not surprising since they had less time to find them.

>
> What are the possible reasons for increased number of iterations required to converge and also for exceeding max treedepth?
>
> Can rstan run on multiple thread (in case I really have to run 60,000 iterations!)?

You could run many chains in parallel but each one would still have to run until convergence so this is not likely to be helpful.

>
> I've also tried decreasing initial stepsize to 0.5, but that did not seem to improve performance. What does this do actually?

>
> :(
>
> Huiying

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Imposing consistency and sparsity in Transition matrix
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Imposing consistency and sparsity in Transition matrix
messages.body_plain:
In general, we don't recommend hard constraints.
Instead we prefer to let the data determine what the values
should be.  The problem you'll run into with hard constraints
is that the data may not be consistent with them and you'll
be trying to estimate parameters right up against boundaries,
which is problematic both statistically and computationally.

You can, if you really want to, set the Dirichlet prior to
be high enough to guarantee that the value is greater than 0.9,
because you can exploit the conjugacy to figure out what the
parameter needs to be.

If you really insist on doing what you suggest, then you
either need to do what Michael says and reparameterize, or
you need to do something like the following

parameters {
  simplex[K] theta_raw;

transformed parameters {
  simplex[K] theta;
  theta <- 0.1 * theta_raw;
  theta[k] <- theta[k] + 0.9;

Then theta will have theta[k] > 0.9.  But it's going to be very
poorly behaved if the data's not consistent with theta[k] > 0.9.

- Bob

> On Apr 20, 2016, at 7:58 AM, Sachinthaka Abeywardana <sachin.ab...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> The prior option wouldn't help me ensure that it is greater than a certain amount would it? Just feel like I have to guess the parameter for the k-th element in that case.
>
> On 20 Apr 2016 8:52 pm, "Michael Betancourt" <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Not unless you construct the simplex from some latent space where
> you can impose the constraint exactly.  But for this purpose a soft
> constraint will just work as well, which is easily implemented by adding
> a Dirichlet prior to each simplex with the kth hyperparameter significantly
> larger than the rest.
>

messages.subject: Re: beginner requests help: censored regression
messages.subject_clean: beginner requests help: censored regression
messages.body_plain:
The Stan code from the manual at the bottom of pg. 108 (and top of 109) is just for right censoring so it wouldn't be equivalent to your use of the tobit function, which I think defaults to left censoring at 0. That is, I'm pretty sure the default in AER::tobit is left = 0 so your formula

tobit(model,data=rigid25,right=U)

is really equivalent to

tobit(model,data=rigid25,right=U, left=0)

If you only want right censoring then I think you need to set left = -Inf.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

If I understand the responses correctly, I could choose my two transformed parameters to be:
  1.   log(A)/B
  2.   B

Then my Jacobian matrix is d[log(A)/B, B]/d[A,B], which has determinant 1/(A*B), so my change-of-variables adjustment is:
    increment_log_prob(-log(A) - log(B))

But, as Bob points out in his 2nd message, I could have arbitrarily chosen otherwise (here, let's say that A and B are both constrained to be positive, and n is an arbitrary nonzero real):
  1.   log(A)/B
  2.   B^n

And then my Jacobian is d[log(A)/B, B^n]/d[A,B], which has determinant n*B^(n-2)/a, so I would do:
    increment_log_prob( (n-2)*log(B) - log(A) )

I guess this can be correct: You can shift the log-prob by (any multiple of) log(B) and still end up with the quantity of interest (log(A) / B) correctly distributed, since this is just like putting different priors on the single-variable distributions... It just strikes me as a very strange result...

messages.body_plain:
See:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_matrix_and_determinant#Jacobian_determinant

The point is that densities are derivatives (of cumulative
distributions) and that changing the variables affects the rate
of change.  The Jacobian's there to compensate for the differential
change in volume of the transformed space compared to the original
space.  The transform has to be an invertible function.

The problem here is that even if we know how log(A) / B is
distributed, we can't invert that into a distribution over A and B,
because f(A, B) = log(A) / B isn't invertible (it's many to one
as I indicated in the first message).  So you might as well just
use a single parameter C instead of log(A) / B.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: beginner requests help: censored regression
messages.body_plain:
Ok I've figured out the issue. It's one of those annoying ones that's so simple but takes a while to actually spot. You just need to get rid of the multiplication by N_cens in the increment_log_prob line. Here's why:

In the example in the Stan manual mu is a scalar parameter so, since there are N_cens censored observations, in the line

increment_log_prob(N_cens * normal_ccdf_log(U, mu, sigma))

you need the multiplication by N_cens. However, when you go from mu to x_cens * beta you have a vector instead of a scalar and the call to normal_ccdf_log becomes vectorized. The vectorized call to normal_ccdf_log obviates the need to multiply by N_cens since x_cens * beta contains a value for each of the N_cens censored observations. So you just want

increment_log_prob(normal_ccdf_log(U, x_cens * beta, sigma)) ;

Anyway, when you make that change you should get the correct estimates.

On another note, I would run at least 4 chains. You also shouldn't need more than the default number of iterations per chain (2000) for a model like this, and you probably don't even need close to that many (I would double check that though).

Best,

Jonah

You'll have to choose the model.  And then it's possible it'll do
what you want (though I still don't see why you'd want this
over-parameterization in terms of A and B in this case).

We do something similar with unit vectors.  In 2D, there's really only
one degree of freedom (angle around circle).  But that wraps, so is
no good for sampling near the wrap point.  So instead we use 2 points
(x, y), and then project onto the unit circle.  That's over-parameterized,
and if we did just that, would not be identified.  So we put a unit normal
on x and y, and that identifies the scale and now everything's OK.  See:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-sphere#Generating_random_points

- Bob

> binomial_coefficient_log is used in view of unknown est_in and also non-informative/weak prior of est_if (risk of death), defined as having a beta distribution (0.5, 0.5) which is rather random?

It's probably someone trying to write out all the of
terms in a density like the binomial.

Is "rather random" a meta-comment?

> I'm sorry if this doesn't make sense.
>
> Could I have used the number of death, D ~ binomial(est_in, est_if)?

binomial requires a count as first argument and probaiblity in (0, 1)
as the second one.  It's just the usual binomial.

>
> theta gets a lower bound 0.0000015625 based on the knowledge that 20 cases were observed in the population of size 12.8e6.

You should just remove that lower bound.

> theta0 takes a prior beta(0.5, 1129.5) based on the knowledge that the 0 out of 1129 samples was found positive

This isn't the same as the 20 out of 1e7?

But if you started from a uniform beta(1, 1), the posterior
after 0 out of 1129 samples would be beta(1, 1130).

If that study's the same as this one, you can either combine
the data, or start with that posterior if nothing else is going on.

> in a previous study and alpha for beta distribution has to be >0.

beta(1, 1) is uniform;  beta(0.5, 0.5) is very U-shaped, with density
going to infinity as variate approaches 0 or 1.

> It is also set to bound between 0 and 1 because it is a parameter for baseline cumulative incidence, which is a proportion.

Yes, you need that constraint.

> if prior for pi is known to be beta(0.5, 193.5), can I incorporate this into the model when at the same time, pi is defined as theta0 + theta*x1?

You should think about priors on theta0 and theta rather
than a function of them.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I went back and looked at that model and there are all kinds
of problems with it, I'm afraid.

This:

 for (i in 1:W)

   pi_0[i] <- theta0 + theta * x1[i];

 for (i in 1:W)

   pi[i] <- fmin(pi_0[i], 1);

It doesn't make sense to truncate like this.  Instead, you
want to do a logistic regression and do this:

  pi[i] <- inv_logit(pi_0[i]);

But rather than doing that, you can just use binomial_logit.
But little steps first.

And you don't want to put a prior on pi_0;  you want to
express the priors on theta0 and theta.  If x is centered,
you can put the informative prior on theta0 (on the logit
scale).

I don't like the variables names "est_is" for estimated severity
risk;  the variable is just the severity risk and you estimate
it conditional on data.

Then I'm not sure why the code has the binomial spelled out
the way it is.

I'd suggest trying to write the model down mathematically first
as a GLM with appropirate priors, then simulate data and fit it,
then apply it to real data.

- Bob

On Wednesday, April 20, 2016 at 6:18:58 PM UTC-4, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> Ok I've figured out the issue. It's one of those annoying ones that's so simple but takes a while to actually spot. You just need to get rid of the multiplication by N_cens in the increment_log_prob line. Here's why:
>
> In the example in the Stan manual mu is a scalar parameter so, since there are N_cens censored observations, in the line
>
> increment_log_prob(N_cens * normal_ccdf_log(U, mu, sigma))
>
> you need the multiplication by N_cens. However, when you go from mu to x_cens * beta you have a vector instead of a scalar and the call to normal_ccdf_log becomes vectorized. The vectorized call to normal_ccdf_log obviates the need to multiply by N_cens since x_cens * beta contains a value for each of the N_cens censored observations. So you just want
>
> increment_log_prob(normal_ccdf_log(U, x_cens * beta, sigma)) ;
>
> Anyway, when you make that change you should get the correct estimates.
>
> On another note, I would run at least 4 chains. You also shouldn't need more than the default number of iterations per chain (2000) for a model like this, and you probably don't even need close to that many (I would double check that though).
>
> Best,
>
> Jonah

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, April 18, 2016 at 2:29:31 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> You don't need a sampling statement.  For every parameter
> type Stan has, the default distribution is uniform over
> values satisfying the constraint.  In this case, the
> uniform happens to be improper.

A bit more background on this in case it's helpful: Stan works by starting with a log probability variable (lp__) initialized to zero and then adding to it when a sampling statement or increment_log_prob() is used. Therefore if you declare a parameter and then don't give it a prior nothing will be added to the log probability and you get a uniform prior by default. Anyway, just wanted to make clear that it's not that Stan sneaks in a call to uniform() under the hood if you don't specify a prior or anything like that.

Jonah

>

> > See:
> >
> > https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_matrix_and_determinant#Jacobian_determinant
> >
> > The point is that densities are derivatives (of cumulative
> > distributions) and that changing the variables affects the rate
> > of change.  The Jacobian's there to compensate for the differential
> > change in volume of the transformed space compared to the original
> > space.  The transform has to be an invertible function.
> >
> > The problem here is that even if we know how log(A) / B is
> > distributed, we can't invert that into a distribution over A and B,
> > because f(A, B) = log(A) / B isn't invertible (it's many to one
> > as I indicated in the first message).  So you might as well just
> > use a single parameter C instead of log(A) / B.
> >
> > If you augment with the second equation as Daniel is suggesting it
> > is no longer many-to-one.  Major identifiability problem if you don't
> > observe one of the "components", sure, but it's no longer many-to-one.
>
> You'll have to choose the model.  And then it's possible it'll do
> what you want (though I still don't see why you'd want this
> over-parameterization in terms of A and B in this case).

I've only ever used this for models where the meaningful parameters
were not identified in the final model but it was useful to visualize
(via sampling)  how the particular model made them confounded.
This comes up a lot in ecological models with observation processes
where people observe, for example, only population counts  and mortality but they
want to model survival and immigration/emigration (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1541-0420.2010.01465.x/abstract
and associated elaborations).  A lot of those models are hopeless
if applied in rote fashion (i.e.-the original paper says it works, let's use
it for our data!) but they can be great if you augment the data by measurements
to resolve the non-identifiability.  Running the model (successfully) in
the original formulation is a useful way of identifying what data would
be most helpful.

K

>
> We do something similar with unit vectors.  In 2D, there's really only
> one degree of freedom (angle around circle).  But that wraps, so is
> no good for sampling near the wrap point.  So instead we use 2 points
> (x, y), and then project onto the unit circle.  That's over-parameterized,
> and if we did just that, would not be identified.  So we put a unit normal
> on x and y, and that identifies the scale and now everything's OK.  See:
>
> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-sphere#Generating_random_points
>
> - Bob

> On Apr 21, 2016, at 4:41 AM, Herra Huu <heikki.uu...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> As Aleksandar suspected, the current model doesn't correspond to MV Poisson distribution. In the current form it's just the product of marginal distributions, ie. defining joint density of form P(X1,X2,X3) = P(X1)P(X2)P(X3) and therefore missing the dependency structure.
>
> The correct joint density (for M=3) is given in page 36. Basically what you have to do is:
>

> take a sum over product of p(y1)p(y2)p(y3)p(y4)p(y5)p(y6), where each term is Poisson density, for all possible combinations of (y1,y2,y3,y12,y13,y23) such that:
> x1 = y1+y12+y13
> x2 = y2+y12+y23
> x3 = y3+y13+y23
>
> From there, it's easy to generalize for higher dimensions/different dependency structures, but it's also awfully computationally expensive if M/counts are high. Here is a simple example code for the M=3 case,

>
> data generation:
>
> library(rstan)
>
> N <- 500
>
> l1 <- 1.4; y1 <- rpois(N, l1)
> l2 <- 0.8; y2 <- rpois(N, l2)
> l3 <- 3; y3 <- rpois(N, l3)
>
> l12 <- 1.2; y12 <- rpois(N, l12)
> l13 <- 0.1; y13 <- rpois(N, l13)
> l23 <- 0.5; y23 <- rpois(N, l23)
>
> X <- matrix(0, N, 3)
> X[,1] <- y1+y12+y13
> X[,2] <- y2+y12+y23
> X[,3] <- y3+y13+y23
>
> model <- stan_model("MV_poisson.stan")
> samples <- sampling(model, list(X=X,N=N), chains=1, iter=100)
>
> Stan model code:
>
> data {
>   int N;
>   int X[N, 3];
> }
>
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0> lambda[6];
> }
>
> model {
>   for(n in 1:N) {
>       real lp[(1+min(X[n,1], X[n,2])) * (1+min(X[n,1], X[n,3])) * (1+min(X[n,2], X[n,3]))];
>       int n_used;
>       n_used <- 0;
>       for(y12 in 0:min(X[n,1], X[n,2]))
>        for(y13 in 0:min(X[n,1], X[n,3]))
>           for(y23 in 0:min(X[n,2], X[n,3]))
>             if((y12+y13) <= X[n,1] && (y12+y23) <= X[n,2] && (y13+y23) <= X[n,3]) {
>               n_used <- n_used + 1;
>             lp[n_used] <- poisson_log(X[n,1]-y12-y13, lambda[1]) +
>                           poisson_log(X[n,2]-y12-y23, lambda[2]) +
>                           poisson_log(X[n,3]-y13-y23, lambda[3]) +
>                           poisson_log(y12, lambda[4]) +
>                           poisson_log(y13, lambda[5]) +
>                           poisson_log(y23, lambda[6]);
>             }
>
>       increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp[1:n_used]));
>   }
>
>   lambda ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
> }
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question on varying-intercept and varying-slope model using multi_normal
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Question on varying-intercept and varying-slope model using multi_normal
messages.body_plain:
What Stan sneaks in under the hood is the Jacobian
of any constraints.  All of our underlying calculations in
sampling are after we unconstrain parameters.

So if you write

  parameters {
    real<lower=0> sigma;

Then we log-transform to unconstrained scale and sample over log(sigma).
But then we need to exp()-transform back and add the Jacobian to get
a uniform distribution for sigma over (0, infinity).

So it works out to the same thing (including what the lp__ value
is going to be) as

  parameters {
    real sigma_raw;
    ...
  transformed parameters {
    real<lower=0> sigma;
    sigma <- exp(sigma_raw);
    ...
  model {
    // Jacobian adjustment, log(abs(d/d.u exp(u))) = log(exp(u)) = u
    increment_log_prob(sigma);

Now sigma has an improper uniform distribution over (0, infinity)
and sigma_raw is the log transform of sigma.  And it's not just
virtually identical, it's really identical down to the operations
being run in the generated C++ code.

- Bob

> On Apr 21, 2016, at 11:16 AM, Jonah Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

The reason you want to run multiple chains is to make
sure that diffuse initializations converge to the same
region of the posterior.  So it's important to do it
before you do a final run.

- Bob

> On Apr 21, 2016, at 10:15 AM, vit...@osu.edu wrote:
>
> Thanks very much! (And the explanation wqs a bit of an embarrassment for me - I really should have noticed).  Your advice as to chains is well taken, though at this stage, given that this was my first attempt, I wanted to be confident that the model was right before working on production runs.
>

> On Wednesday, April 20, 2016 at 6:18:58 PM UTC-4, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> Ok I've figured out the issue. It's one of those annoying ones that's so simple but takes a while to actually spot. You just need to get rid of the multiplication by N_cens in the increment_log_prob line. Here's why:
>
> In the example in the Stan manual mu is a scalar parameter so, since there are N_cens censored observations, in the line
>
> increment_log_prob(N_cens * normal_ccdf_log(U, mu, sigma))
>
> you need the multiplication by N_cens. However, when you go from mu to x_cens * beta you have a vector instead of a scalar and the call to normal_ccdf_log becomes vectorized. The vectorized call to normal_ccdf_log obviates the need to multiply by N_cens since x_cens * beta contains a value for each of the N_cens censored observations. So you just want
>
> increment_log_prob(normal_ccdf_log(U, x_cens * beta, sigma)) ;
>
> Anyway, when you make that change you should get the correct estimates.
>
> On another note, I would run at least 4 chains. You also shouldn't need more than the default number of iterations per chain (2000) for a model like this, and you probably don't even need close to that many (I would double check that though).
>
> Best,
>
> Jonah
>

messages.subject: On using multivariate priors for non-varying parameters
messages.subject_clean: On using multivariate priors for non-varying parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

A conceptual question: how should I think about using multivariate priors for parameters that do not vary (across groups, time periods, etc)? For example, in a linear regression y = XB + e, giving a multi-normal prior to B. At school I was taught to use multivariate priors, and in many papers I see it done. But a) I've run some experiments with known parameters, for simple models, and using multivariate priors doesn't appear to improve inference. And b) I have difficulty seeing why someone would use a multivariate distribution when there is only one group. The posterior summarizes covariance between my parameters even if my priors don't have any explicit covariance.

Would appreciate any thoughts.

Jim

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] On using multivariate priors for non-varying parameters
messages.body_plain:
If you have a vector of parameters b, you’d put a correlated prior on b if this reflects your uncertainty about the parameter.  What I will usually like to do is transform the elements of b so that I am comfortable with independent priors on the transformed space.  For example, suppose the X’s are 5 different economic indicators.  Then you might want to parameterize b_k = a*gamma_k, for k=1,…,5, where a is some shared scale parameter that gets a prior, and gamma_1,…,gamma_5 have independent priors.

Even more than that, I’d like to put X_1,…X_5 on a common scale so that gamma_1,…,gamma_5 can have priors that are identically distributed as well as being independent.

A

no good way to convert a real to a rounded integer --- it breaks
all the derivatives in the systems).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] On using multivariate priors for non-varying parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] On using multivariate priors for non-varying parameters
messages.body_plain:
My _guess_ is that multivariate priors were a response to not standardizing
the continuous covariates in the design matrix.  For example, if you include
both x_{1} = chi and x_{2} = chi^{2} and chi is entirely positive or negative
then we know a priori that beta_{1} and beta_{2} will be strongly correlated,
and that a priori knowledge can be incorporated into a multivariate prior.
As Andrew notes, once the covariates have been standardized then an IID
prior is much more natural.

These is one of the reasons why reading economics papers makes me sad.  :-p

On Apr 22, 2016, at 4:10 AM, James Savage <jav...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks Andrew - that makes sense.
>
>
>
> On Thursday, April 21, 2016 at 11:01:04 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > If you have a vector of parameters b, you’d put a correlated prior on b if this reflects your uncertainty about the parameter.  What I will usually like to do is transform the elements of b so that I am comfortable with independent priors on the transformed space.  For example, suppose the X’s are 5 different economic indicators.  Then you might want to parameterize b_k = a*gamma_k, for k=1,…,5, where a is some shared scale parameter that gets a prior, and gamma_1,…,gamma_5 have independent priors.
> >
> > Even more than that, I’d like to put X_1,…X_5 on a common scale so that gamma_1,…,gamma_5 can have priors that are identically distributed as well as being independent.
> >
> > A
> >
> > > On Apr 21, 2016, at 10:50 PM, James Savage <jav...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi all,
> > >
> > > A conceptual question: how should I think about using multivariate priors for parameters that do not vary (across groups, time periods, etc)? For example, in a linear regression y = XB + e, giving a multi-normal prior to B. At school I was taught to use multivariate priors, and in many papers I see it done. But a) I've run some experiments with known parameters, for simple models, and using multivariate priors doesn't appear to improve inference. And b) I have difficulty seeing why someone would use a multivariate distribution when there is only one group. The posterior summarizes covariance between my parameters even if my priors don't have any explicit covariance.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] On using multivariate priors for non-varying parameters
messages.body_plain:
Wasn't Andrew making the point <http://andrewgelman.com/2016/03/25/28321/> the other week that if we scale covariates and then select a prior,
the prior is actually conceived with knowledge of the data, and isn't really a prior? This is a part of
my confusion. In any case, I think Andrew's point above is about scaling the parameters, not the
covariates.

What would make sense to me is if using a multivariate prior helped old-school samplers better
explore the parameter space.

In any case, does a model with no group-level varying parameters contain any identifying information
about the covariance terms of the multivariate distribution/the scaling matrix `a` in Andrew's example above?
To my mind, all the covariation for a single group's parameters will be captured in the joint posterior of the
means (as we get when we use univariate priors), and we'd only be able to draw inference about the
covariance matrix of a multivariate distribution if we have multiple groups. Is my intuition way off here?

Cheers,
Jim

On Friday, April 22, 2016 at 4:12:20 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> My _guess_ is that multivariate priors were a response to not standardizing
> the continuous covariates in the design matrix.  For example, if you include
> both x_{1} = chi and x_{2} = chi^{2} and chi is entirely positive or negative
> then we know a priori that beta_{1} and beta_{2} will be strongly correlated,
> and that a priori knowledge can be incorporated into a multivariate prior.
> As Andrew notes, once the covariates have been standardized then an IID
> prior is much more natural.
>
> These is one of the reasons why reading economics papers makes me sad.  :-p
>
> On Apr 22, 2016, at 4:10 AM, James Savage <jav...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Thanks Andrew - that makes sense.
> >
> >
> >
> > On Thursday, April 21, 2016 at 11:01:04 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > > If you have a vector of parameters b, you’d put a correlated prior on b if this reflects your uncertainty about the parameter.  What I will usually like to do is transform the elements of b so that I am comfortable with independent priors on the transformed space.  For example, suppose the X’s are 5 different economic indicators.  Then you might want to parameterize b_k = a*gamma_k, for k=1,…,5, where a is some shared scale parameter that gets a prior, and gamma_1,…,gamma_5 have independent priors.
> > >
> > > Even more than that, I’d like to put X_1,…X_5 on a common scale so that gamma_1,…,gamma_5 can have priors that are identically distributed as well as being independent.
> > >
> > > A
> > >
> > > > On Apr 21, 2016, at 10:50 PM, James Savage <jav...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hi all,
> > > >
> > > > A conceptual question: how should I think about using multivariate priors for parameters that do not vary (across groups, time periods, etc)? For example, in a linear regression y = XB + e, giving a multi-normal prior to B. At school I was taught to use multivariate priors, and in many papers I see it done. But a) I've run some experiments with known parameters, for simple models, and using multivariate priors doesn't appear to improve inference. And b) I have difficulty seeing why someone would use a multivariate distribution when there is only one group. The posterior summarizes covariance between my parameters even if my priors don't have any explicit covariance.
> > > >
> > > > Would appreciate any thoughts.
> > > >
