messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] On using multivariate priors for non-varying parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] On using multivariate priors for non-varying parameters
messages.body_plain:
> Wasn't Andrew making the point <http://andrewgelman.com/2016/03/25/28321/> the other week that if we scale covariates and then select a prior,
> the prior is actually conceived with knowledge of the data, and isn't really a prior? This is a part of
> my confusion. In any case, I think Andrew's point above is about scaling the parameters, not the
> covariates.

Yeah, there is a certain empirical Bayes feel here, but it’s subtle because the corrections
are done on the data and in some sense aren’t different from any of the other preprocesing/
cleaning that is done to measurements.  By the way, this is a really nice example of why
in practice it is nearly impossible to actually choose priors before seeing the data, and hence
why marginal likelihood-based techniques can be so fragile.

> What would make sense to me is if using a multivariate prior helped old-school samplers better
> explore the parameter space.
>
> In any case, does a model with no group-level varying parameters contain any identifying information
> about the covariance terms of the multivariate distribution/the scaling matrix `a` in Andrew's example above?
> To my mind, all the covariation for a single group's parameters will be captured in the joint posterior of the
> means (as we get when we use univariate priors), and we'd only be able to draw inference about the
> covariance matrix of a multivariate distribution if we have multiple groups. Is my intuition way off here?

They are very much different models, and so they will have different performance.

Because we’re considering just the continuous covariate term, X * beta, there’s
always going to be some subtle ambiguity between covariance between the covariates
and the slopes.  For example, if we can implement a N(0, Sigma) prior on the beta as

X * L * beta_tilde,

where the beta_tilde are IID gaussians and L is the Cholesky decomposition of Sigma.

But we can achieve nearly the same model by instead taking

(X * L) * beta_tilde

which can be implemented by standardizing the data, or using the QR decomposition
a la rstanarm.

Now these are technically different models, L is variable in the former and constant in
the latter, but they do achieve similar results of decorrelating the covariates and hence
making the model easier to fit.  Indeed, one could reasonable make the argument that
taking L from the empirical covariance of the data is an empirical Bayes approximation
to giving the beta a multivariate gaussian prior with unknown covariance that must be
learned from the data.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Speeding up Dynamic Regression Model with many time-periods and big sample size
messages.body_plain:
Moving to non-centered parameterizations will probably help for
group-level parameters where you don't have many elements.

  So instead of

    gamma ~ foo(loc, scale);

use

    gamma_raw ~ foo(0, 1);
    gamma <- loc + scale * gamma_raw;

where gamma_raw is the parameter and gamma is a local variable.

Also, these:

> for (k in 2:n_day) {
>     beta[k] ~ cauchy(beta[k-1], sigma_beta_evo);

are much more efficient as:

  beta[2:n_day] ~ cauchy(beta[1:(n_day - 1)], sigma_beta_evo);

This:

> for (i in 1:day_size[s]) {
>       real y_hat;
>       y_hat <- alpha
>         +beta[s]*female[obs_in_day[i]]
>       +a_age[s,age[obs_in_day[i]]]
>       +a_edu[s,edu[obs_in_day[i]]]
>       +a_party_id[s,party_id[obs_in_day[i]]]
>       +a_race[s,race[obs_in_day[i]]]+gamma*vote_prev_dma[i]
>       +a_dma[s,dma[obs_in_day[i]]];
>       y[obs_in_day[i]] ~ bernoulli_logit(y_hat);
>     }

can be vectorized as:

  y[obs_in_day] ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha
                                  + beta[s] * female[obs_in_day]
                                  + ...);

If you make female a vector.

If female[...] is an indicator, then it's acutally more efficient to
build up that linear predictor using conditionals to avoid the unnecessary
multiplication by zero and useless derivative propagations.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
You almost always want to put everything in a single joint
model.  There's no good way to chain models together without
doing that.

- Bob

> On Apr 25, 2016, at 5:44 AM, huiying <hyc.t...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I've tried to run two different models. The first is to estimate age-specific cumulative incidence, theta.
>
> data {
>   int N; // Number of weeks samples were collected
>   int n[N]; // Number of serum samples collected at week i (n will be a vector of length W)
>   int y[N]; // Number of positive serum samples at week i
>   int S; // Total number of severe infections
>   int D; // Total number of deaths
>   real x1[N]; // Number of expected scaled seroprevalence
>   int M; // population size for each age group
>   real ub; //Upper bound for age-specific prior theta0
> }
>
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0, upper=1> theta; // Cumulative incidence of infection in each age group
>   real<lower=0, upper=1> theta0; // Baseline cumulative incidence in all age group
> }
>
>
> transformed parameters {
>   real<lower=0, upper=1> p[N]; // Probability of being infected
>
>   real est_inf;// Estimated number of infections
>
>   for (i in 1:N)
>   p[i] <- inv_logit(theta0 + theta * x1[i]); // binomial_logit to transform p to values in the interval [0,1]
>
>   est_inf <- theta*M; // M is to be replaced by general population size of each age group
> }
>
>
> model {
>   theta ~ beta(0.5, 0.5); // Noninformative prior on theta
>   theta0 ~ beta(0.5, ub); // Prior information on age-specific theta_0
>
>   for(i in 1:N)
>   y[i] ~ binomial(n[i], p[i]); //Binomial likelihood of a positive serum sample
> }
>
>
>
> The output from the first model will be used to calculate population cumulative incidence and the estimated total number of cases, est_inf.
>
> Est_inf will then be used as an input for the 2nd model, as below, to estimate infection-severity risk (est_isr) and infection-fatality risk (est_ifr).
>
> data {
>   int est_inf; // Estimated number of infected cases
>   int S; // Number of severe cases
>   int D; // Number of deaths
> }
>
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0, upper=1> est_isr; // infection-severity risk
>   real<lower=0, upper=1> est_ifr; // infection-fatality risk
> }
>
> model {
>   est_isr ~ beta(0.5, 0.5); // prior for est_isr
>   est_ifr ~ beta(0.5, 0.5); // prior for est_ifr
>   S ~ binomial(est_inf, est_isr); // binomial likelihood of severe cases
>   D ~ binomial(est_inf, est_ifr); // binomial likelihood of fatal cases
> }
>
> Doing two models do not seem to be very ideal. However, with my limited knowledge, I guess this is one way I can get around with the limitations I obtained when attempting to everything in one model.
>
> Please let me know what you think of this approach. I'm sorry if this seems stupid.
>
> Thanks !
>
> Huiying
>

messages.body_plain:
vector[] is an array of vectors.  So you need either one
more level of looping or you need to apply to_vector if
they have the same dims:

  vector[5] y[3];
  vector[5] mu[3];

  y ~ cauchy(mu, 1.0)

gives the error you see.

But if you do this:

  matrix[3,5] y;
  matrix[3,5] mu;

  to_vector(y) ~ cauchy(to_vector(mu), 1.0);

it'll work.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Dear STAN-group,

I am trying to implement in STAN a zero-inflated beta regression following Ospina and Ferrari 2012 (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1103.2372.pdf). I used the equation 2.2 to develop the attached model which surprisingly worked, compiled and gave reasonable estimates on a simulated dataset. However as I am pretty new to STAN and bayesian data analysis in general I would like to get feedbacks from people with higher level of expertise than me.

Sincerely yours,
Lionel

PS: Here is the R code used to generate the simulated data and the model

set.seed(20160427)
dat<-data.frame(x=runif(100,-2,2))
mm<-model.matrix(~x,dat)
coefs<-c(-1,2)
mus<-invlogit(mm%*%coefs)
phi<-3
dat$y<-rbeta(n = 100,shape1 = mus*phi,shape2 = (1-mus)*phi)
#count how many 0s or 1s
length(which(dat$y==0 | dat$y==1))
#STAN models
m_zoib<-stan(file = "STAN/ZOIB_1.stan",data = list(N=nrow(mm),K=ncol(mm),y=dat$y,X=mm))

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] avoid bi-modal posterior distribution for Phi_approx(normal)?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] avoid bi-modal posterior distribution for Phi_approx(normal)?
messages.body_plain:
Point estimates are pretty much always lousy summaries of multimodal densities.

For example, if you take a beta(0.01, 0.01), there is a lot of mass around 0 and
1 and not much elsewhere.  It's not multimodal per se, because there are no modes,
but clearly no point estimate gives you a good summary of the behavior.

Averaging across the modes using full Bayes is exactly what you want to do.
That is, integrate over the posterior.

The usual problem is that it's hard to sample from a bimodal posterior unless
you can get a single chain to move among the modes.

- Bob

messages.subject: Hierarchical Multivariate Normal Models for Quantile Estimation: Inference Problems!
messages.subject_clean: Hierarchical Multivariate Normal Models for Quantile Estimation: Inference Problems!
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I'm working with hierarchical multivariate normal models and having trouble getting them to recover the parameters from test data. This might be because I'm unwittingly simulating weird test data, or because I'm dealing with too little data, or a weak identification problem, or maybe I am just poorly parameterising the model so the sampler is ill-conditioned. The R and stan files are attached here.

I'm simulating a 10-dimensional multivariate normal variable which realises across 5 different sites, once in each site. I am mimicking the situation in which I have estimates of 10 empirical quantiles and their standard errors from 5 different data sets of the same outcome. I have the realisations and their standard errors, so using the result in Koenker & Basset 1978 I can therefore construct the entire variance-covariance matrix of sampling error in each site. I want to estimate the hyperparameters: the grand mean vector, and the variance-covariance matrix that governs the variability of the realisations of empirical quantiles across sites.

I tried 2 models in stan: (1) allow a fully general hyper-variance-covariance structure with LKJ priors (on cholesky factors, of course), and (2) parameterise the covariance matrix by a scale vector and a correlation matrix that has an AR(1) structure, so it only has 11 unknown parameters, the 10 scales and the 1 "rho" from the AR(1). messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Zero Inflated Beta Regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Zero Inflated Beta Regression
messages.body_plain:
That's more like a hurdle model than a zero-inflated one.
You should check out the examples in the manual.

You declare the mixing ratio as

  real<lower=0,upper=1> a; //the zero-inflation parameter

but then have

 for(i in 1:N){
   if(y[i] == 0)
    increment_log_prob(a);
   else
    increment_log_prob((1 - a) * beta_log(y[i],alpha[i],beta[i]));
 }

The first line should be increment_log_prob(log(a)) or 1 ~ bernoulli(a).
And the second should be log1m(a) + beta_log(...).

Also, y[i] == 0 is odd for a continuous parameter in (0, 1).  Sounds
like a data collection defect, or something you should be modeling with
counts rather than proportions.

Having the alpha and beta vary by data point probably won't work
very well, either.  It also leaves the alpha[i] and beta[i] ungrounded
in cases where y[i] == 0.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I didn't understand your matrix construction in either transformed
data or transformed parameters --- maybe someone else will be more
familiar.

I wouldn't define sigma_sq and then take square roots --- go the
other way around and just model sigma.

Are you getting excptions that Sigma isn't positive definite?

Also, you want to stay with Cholesky factors through the whole
process;  it's way more efficient.

There are other efficiency gains to be had here, but let's get
the model working first.

How are you measuring reconstruction?  Are your posteriors not
calibrated in the sense that roughly 50% of the parameters don't fall in
their posterior 50% intervals?  You won't get exact reconstruction of parameters
except in the limit of increasing data sizes.

The prior on rho expects strong positive correlation throughout (2.5 standard
deviations just to get to correlation = 0).

You probably aren't going to be able to fit a multilevel model with
a fresh covariance matrix for each observation:

  for(k in 1:K){
    y[k] ~ multi_normal(beta_0_k[k], Sigma_y_k[k]);

The problem is that you only have a single observation y[k] with which to fit
an entire covariance matrix Sigma_y_k[k].

- Bob

Hi!

Thanks again. It took me a while to figure out how to arrange the random-effect matrices etc., but here is the model I came up with. I am not sure about my implementation of the non-centered parametrization and would love a quick comment! Apart from that, this settles it for me. I will keep you in the loop wrt run-time (650,000 N sample, 48 waves)!

data {
  int<lower=0> N;                                         // sample wave_size
  int<lower=0> n_age;                                     // number of age categories
  int<lower=0> n_race;                                    // number of race categories
  int<lower=0> n_edu;                                     // number of education catoegories
  int<lower=0> n_dma;                                     // number of dmas
  int<lower=0> n_party_id;                                // number of party-categories
  int<lower=0> n_day;                                     // number of party-categories

  vector <lower=0,upper=1> [N]female;                       // female each respondent

  int<lower=0,upper=n_age> age[N];                        // age for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_edu> edu[N];                        // edu for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_race> race[N];                      // race for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_party_id> party_id[N];              // party_id for each respondent
  int<lower=0,upper=n_dma> dma[N];                        // party_id for each respondent

  vector[N] vote_prev_dma;                                // 2012 state-vote at the individual-level

  int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];                              // vote-choice
  int<lower=0,upper=N> in_day[N];                         // wave of respondents
  int<lower=0>        day_size[n_day];                    // N individuals per Wave
  int<lower=0> day_lims[n_day,2];                         // first individual in wave and individuals per wave
}

parameters {

  real beta[n_day] ;                                      // coefficient-array for female; wave

  matrix[n_day,n_age] a_age_raw;                          // coefficient-matrix for age; wave
  matrix[n_day,n_edu] a_edu_raw;                          // coefficient-matrix for edu; wave
  matrix[n_day,n_race] a_race_raw;                        // coefficient-matrix for race; wave
  matrix[n_day,n_party_id] a_party_id_raw ;               // coefficient-matrix for party_id; wave
  matrix[n_day,n_dma] a_dma;                              // coefficient-matrix for DMA; wave

  real gamma;                                             // previous vote- slope
  real alpha;                                             //intercept
   real <lower=0> sigma_dma;
  real <lower=0> sigma_age;
  real <lower=0> sigma_edu;
  real <lower=0> sigma_race;
  real <lower=0> sigma_party_id;
  real <lower=0> sigma_beta_evo;
  real <lower=0> sigma_dma_evo;
  real <lower=0> sigma_age_evo;
  real <lower=0> sigma_edu_evo;
  real <lower=0> sigma_race_evo;
  real <lower=0> sigma_party_id_evo;

}

transformed parameters{
  matrix[n_day,n_age] a_age;                            //efficient non-centered paramterization
  matrix[n_day,n_edu] a_edu;
  matrix[n_day,n_race] a_race;
  matrix[n_day,n_party_id] a_party_id;
  a_age[1]<-a_age_raw[1]*sigma_age;
  a_edu[1]<-a_edu_raw[1]*sigma_edu;
  a_race[1]<-a_race_raw[1]*sigma_race;
  a_party_id[1]<-a_party_id_raw[1]*sigma_party_id;
for (i in 2:n_day){
  a_age[i]<-a_age_raw[i];
  a_edu[i]<-a_edu_raw[i];
  a_race[i]<-a_race_raw[i];
  a_party_id[i]<-a_party_id_raw[i];
}
}

model {
  sigma_dma ~normal(0,2.5);                             // within_DMA variance can move from 0.1% and 99%
    sigma_age ~normal(0,2.5);                           // within_Age variance can move from 0.1% and 99%
    sigma_edu ~normal(0,2.5);                           // within_edu variance can move from 0.1% and 99%
    sigma_race ~normal(0,2.5);                          // within_race variance can move from 0.1% and 99%
    sigma_party_id ~normal(0,2.5);                      // within_party variance can move from 0.1% and 99%
    sigma_beta_evo ~normal(0,2.5);                      // Evolution Variance for Female
    sigma_dma_evo ~normal(0,2.5);                       // Evolution Variance for DMA
    sigma_age_evo ~normal(0,2.5);                       // Evolution Variance for Age
    sigma_edu_evo ~normal(0,2.5);                       // Evolution Variance for Edu
    sigma_race_evo ~normal(0,2.5);                      // Evolution Variance for race
    sigma_party_id_evo ~normal(0,2.5);                  // Evolution Variance for Party

  gamma~normal(0,5);                                    // embed 95% probability mass between 0.01% and 99.9%
  alpha~normal(0,5);                                    // embed 95% probability mass between 0.01% and 99.9%                                                           /

  beta[1]~normal(0,5);                                  // embed 95% probability mass between 0.1% and 99%

  a_dma[1]~ normal(0,1);                                // embed 95% probability mass between 70% and 30%
  a_age[1]~normal(0,1);                                 // embed 95% probability mass between 0.01% and 99.9%
  a_edu[1]~normal(0,1);                                 // embed 95% probability mass between 0.01% and 99.9%
  a_race[1]~normal(0,1);                                // embed 95% probability mass between 0.01% and 99.9%
  a_party_id[1]~normal(0,1);                            // embed 95% probability mass between 0.01% and 99.9%
                                                        // Evolution Sampling:

 beta[2:n_day] ~ cauchy( beta[1:(n_day - 1)], sigma_beta_evo);
 to_vector(a_age[2:n_day]) ~  cauchy( to_vector(a_age[1:(n_day - 1)]), sigma_age_evo);
 to_vector(a_edu[2:n_day]) ~  cauchy(to_vector( a_edu[1:(n_day - 1)]), sigma_edu_evo);
 to_vector(a_race[2:n_day]) ~ cauchy(to_vector( a_race[1:(n_day - 1)]), sigma_race_evo);
 to_vector(a_party_id[2:n_day]) ~ cauchy( to_vector(a_party_id[1:(n_day - 1)]), sigma_party_id_evo);
to_vector(a_dma[2:n_day]) ~ cauchy( to_vector(a_dma[1:(n_day - 1)]), sigma_dma_evo);

  for(s in 1:n_day){                                    // Likelihood for each  each wave vectorized
   int obs_in_day[day_size[s]];
                                                        // find observations in each wave:

    obs_in_day<-segment(in_day,day_lims[s,1],day_lims[s,2]);

                                                        // Likelihood:
    y[obs_in_day] ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha
        +beta[s]*female[obs_in_day]
      +to_vector(a_age[s,age[obs_in_day]])
      +to_vector(a_edu[s,edu[obs_in_day]])
      +to_vector(a_party_id[s,party_id[obs_in_day]])
      +to_vector(a_race[s,race[obs_in_day]])
      +gamma*vote_prev_dma[obs_in_day]
      +to_vector(a_dma[s,dma[obs_in_day]]));
  }}

Might the solution be (in part) to remove the parameters from the transformed block, declaring all of the parameters in the parameter block, and writing the following in the modeling block:

model {

   for (m in 1:M){

      mum[mid[m]] ~ normal([itemplate[mid[m]]] + bd*display[mid[m]],sigmam[mid[m]]);
   }

   for (p in 1:P){
      mup[fid[p]] ~ normal(mum[imodel[fid[p]]] + bkc*kc[fid[p]],sigmap[fid[p]]);
   }

   for (k in 1:K){
      betai[iid[k]] ~ normal(mup[parent[iid[k]]],sigmai);
   }

   for (j in 1:J){
      uj[j] ~ normal(0,1);
   }

// response model

   for (n in 1:N){
      score[n] ~ bernoulli_logit(uj[pid[peeps[n]]]-betai[iid[item[n]]]);
   }

That was helpful, thanks.  I don't understand the full model but I see that the disc parameters are transformed parameters so the parameters themselves are not biomodal and the sampler should have no trouble working correctly.

>
> The concern I have is that, is such a bimodal posterior distribution a stable estimate of the parameter?

I'm not sure what stable means in this context but some models just have multi-modal posteriors so if the model
is right that's what you're stuck interpreting.

> If so, does this mean a parameter value of nearly 0 or 1 is more plausible than other parameter values?

That's the right interpretation.

> As we are also interested in the posterior mean (to correlate with fMRI data later), averaging across such a bimodal distribution doesn't seem good to us in this particular scenario.

Yes in this case a posterior mean will not be a useful summary if this is supposed to correlate with a measurement of this process later.  That said, the reason for the bi-modality is that disc_sd is large.  Have you thought about taking the disc_sd ~ cauchy(0,5) to something less extreme?  Given that this is a random effect plugged through Phi_approx I think a disc_sd ~ normal(0,1) would be a good start.  It might get rid of the bi-modality if the main issue is that disc_sd is just poorly informed from the data. stan_fit4linexpgastro_1b_mod in package gastempt

....

RcppModules: stan_fit4linexpgastro_1b_mod

>  I'd like to do something like... "y[1:ND] ~ normal(a[study[1:ND]] + b[study[1:ND], treatment[1:ND]], se[1:ND]);"

This doesn't make sense as there's only two arguments to normal.  And if
"se" is for "standard error", you probably don't mean that.  The std err
is a measure of estimator accuracy.  We just use sigma or tau.

To answer your question, yes you can do what you want to do:

I'm going to ignore that treatment thing because I don' tknow what it is,
but you can program a model with two varying intercepts as

  y ~ normal(a[study] + b[study], sigma);

assuming y, study, and sigma are all the same size N, so that it's equal to

  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ normal(a[study[n]] + b[study[n]], sigma[n]);

It'll also work if sigma is a scalar (in which case sigma[n] becomes sigma above).
You don't usually have a varying scale for each observation because you can't
can't be fit with a single observation.

> and "w[study[1:ND], treatment[1:ND]] <- delta[study[1:ND],treatment[1:ND] - d[treatment[1:ND]];" where ND is the number of data points and study and treatment are vectors containing the corresponding study and treatment for each data point, but I suspect that won't quite work... an array like b[study[1:ND], treatment[1:ND]] will not behave like a vector b[1:ND], right?  Any idea if I can do something different to vectorize?

See the indexing section of the manual for full details.
If a is a vector and nn is an array of integers, then
a[nn] is a vector of the same size as the array nn.  And so
on for other types.

- Bob

I see.  No, there's no good way to vectorize that as a one-liner.

The basic idea is that if you have multiple indexes, Stan's indexing
works as:

  b[study, value2][i,j] = b[study[i], value2[j]]

So b[study, value2] is of the same type as b (e.g., real[,] or matrix).

That's the same way that R works, by the way:

> a <- matrix(1:6, 2, 3)

> a
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    3    5
[2,]    2    4    6

> a[c(1,2), c(2,3)]
     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    3    5
[2,]    4    6

Now if it's a square matrix, you could use

  diag(b[study, value]),

but it wouldn't be efficient.  Just use loops to define the value you want.

    real b[N];

    ...
    for (n in 1:N)

      b_sv[n] <- b[study[n], value[n]];

    ... use b_study_value ...

- Bob

 to_vector(a_edu[2:n_day]) ~  cauchy(to_vector( a_edu[1:(n_day - 1)]), sigma_edu_evo);

checks, you'll go way way way out into the tails with a Cauchy.

messages.body_plain:
I can't follow what you're trying to do, but it's unlikely test1.stan
is right.

All this does in generated quantities:

 real<lower=0, upper=1> est_ifr;

  est_ifr <- beta_rng(0.5, 0.5);

is to assign est_ifr a random beta(0.5, 0.5) draw.  So the posterior
mean should always be 0.5.

Almost any conversion you do from real to integer in Stan outside
a piecewise approximation of a function with smooth knots is
going to be wrong.

- Bob

> On Apr 26, 2016, at 9:24 PM, huiying <hyc.t...@gmail.com> wrote:

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multi-level and cross-classified model... and fixed effects are being pulled toward zero?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Multi-level and cross-classified model... and fixed effects are being pulled toward zero?
messages.body_plain:
Sorry

> On Apr 26, 2016, at 9:43 PM, Shauna Sweet <shauna...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Bob,
>
> Thank you so much for your reply.
>
> Why do you restrict this parameter to be between 0 and 1?
>
>   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[4] kc[P];                //key content characteristics
>
> kc is a vector of zeros and ones, essentially a set of dummy/design variables which activate effects that are captured by bkc, in the parameters block.

You don't want to do this this way.  It's much more efficient
to declare it as an int and use a conditional rather than multiplying by 0 (drop) or
1 (include).  But I'd misparsed it as a parameter, not data.

So instead of kc[p,i] * x, use if_else(kc[p,i], x, 0).  But even
better, just drop the term if kc[p,i] == 0.

>   for (m in 1:M){
>   mum[mid[m]] <- mut[itemplate[mid[m]]] + bd*display[mid[m]];
>   }
>
> The same problem's repeated throughout.  So this might give mum two
> priors:
>
> for (m in 1:M){
> mum[mid[m]] ~ normal(mut[itemplate[mid[m]]],sigmam[mid[m]]);
> }
>
> Regarding the two priors, I will look back at my code, because what I'm trying to specify are regressions at multiple levels, and I'm not sure how/where to specify the residuals. So for example, the mean difficulty of item models (mum) is decomposed into the difficulty of the template which is used to generate that model (which has a mean difficulty mut), and a set of effects (bd). sigmam is supposed to be the residual variance, so what is not explained by the fixed effects... Does this make sense?

I get confused with fixed vs. random effects terminology.

The point is that you almost always want to give every
parameter a distribution (that is, all mum[k]), and you
almost never want to give a parameter two distributions.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Question about Wiener Diffusion Model Distribution in rstan_2.7.0-2
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Question about Wiener Diffusion Model Distribution in rstan_2.7.0-2
messages.body_plain:
The behavior is OK. It was just that the JAGS version used a more
intuitive coding that was less error-prone. The Wiener process
produces two variables. One indicates response choice and is binary
(correct/error, or left/right, or whatever), the other indicates
response duration (or response time: rt) and is continuous. In the
JAGS code, these bivariate outcomes were captured in a single number
by using the sign. So .313 indicates an rt of 313 ms that ended up at
the upper bound, and -.400 indicates an rt of 400 ms that ended up at
the lower bound.

In the Stan code, the negative sign was eliminated and only positive
numbers can be used. Confronted with lower bound responses, the user
now needs to invert both the starting point and the drift rate. This
doubles the Stan code length and increases the probability of making
an error.

I can understand that the original idea was "what the hell are these
negative times good for?", but they were there for a very good reason.
The code still works, but reverting to the old input procedure (the
one with the negative rts) would be a good idea, imo.

Cheers,
E.J.

Bob,

Thank you so much!

All of these changes seem to both improve running time, and the model does run.

I think that now my question has to do with correctly parameterizing a draw of parameters when those parameters are essentially drawn from independent distributions. In this case, I have a hierarchical 2 PL IRT model, with a regression at levels two and three with factors that contribute to both alpha (or log gamma) ad beta, but I need to specify the residuals for those regressions of the fixed effects on alpha and beta as independent. I was attempting to specify a covariance matrix with 0's on the off-diagonals, but I frequently got warnings about the factorization of that covariance matrix being negative. For example, I attempted to specify a covariance matrix Sigma, and then draw from a multi normal distribution as follows:

  transformed parameters {

  cov_matrix[2] Sigmap[P];

  for (p in 1:P){

     Sigmap[p,1,1]<-taup[p,1];
     Sigmap[p,1,2]<-nocov;
     Sigmap[p,2,1]<-nocov;
     Sigmap[p,2,2]<-taup[p,2];
    }

and then in the model block I had:

  for (p in 1:P){

  mup[p] ~ multi_normal(mum[p] + if_else(X1[p], kc1, 0) + if_else(X2[p], kc2, 0), taup);
  }

I read several posts about restricting tau to be less than 1, and this fixed the covariance matrix warnings, but I wondered if it wasn't causing other problems, namely it was inappropriately bounding tau, causing problems elsewhere... So then I attempted the following in this example, and the chains are not converging for taup. You'll see your suggested changes in the code implemented below! (I am sure it could be more elegant... :)

  for (p in 1:P){

    mup[p,1] ~ normal(mum[p,1] + if_else(X1[p], kc1[1], 0) + if_else(X2[p], kc2[1], 0), taup[1]);
    mup[p,2] ~ normal(mum[p,2] + if_else(X1[p], kc1[1], 0) + if_else(X2[p], kc2[2], 0), taup[2]);

  }

Should I return to bounding tau between 0 and 1, and returning to the multi_normal draw?

Again, I greatly appreciate your help!

Best,
Shauna

messages.body_plain:
Shouldn’t the transition matrix be built up generatively?
I.e. using simplices for each row of the eigenvector
matrix, Q, and positive values for the eigenvalues, lambda,
then reconstructing the transition matrix as Q * lambda * Q^{T}?

Then you can put whatever priors you want on the eigenvectors
and eigenvalues directly.

Besides, doing anything else would require a Jacobian of the
eigendecomposition which is super ugly (it’s used in the softabs
RHMC implementation).

messages.subject: Sampling speed on mac vs ubuntu
messages.subject_clean: Sampling speed on mac vs ubuntu
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I've built a fairly complex hierarchical model (600 + parameters) parameterised from N = 180,000 +.
I'm not having issues with getting the model to converge and I've implemented all the tricks to speed it up.
On my iMac it takes about 60 hours to complete 4000 iterations (iMac: 4 GHz Intel Core i7, 16 GB RAM).

What I have found odd though is when I put this model onto a AWS EC2 optimised compute instance (e.g. c4.2xlarge; https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/instance-types/) using linux docker containers the model takes over 200 hours to complete. This is despite using the same initials.
Sure the processor on my iMac is slightly faster then what is available on c4.2xlarge (3.5 GHz) but the difference in processor speed doesn't look like it explains this much of a difference.
I know there are differences in how the models are compiled and sampled between different operating systems could this be the discrepancy in wall time?

Cheers
J

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Rstan is running too slowly, seeking advice on ways to improve speed.
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Thanks for explaining!

What I'm trying to do can be divided into 3 parts:

Part 1: to estimate posterior distribution of theta (cumulative incidence).

----Part 1 is pretty straight forward, and is expressed from data and parameters block to model block, as in test1.stan.

Part 2: Then, using posterior theta to estimate est_inf (number of infection), using this equation: est_inf = theta x population size.

Part 3: Then, with est_inf, estimate est_isr (infection-severity risk) and est_ifr (infection-fatality risk), which are expressed as binomial likelihoods in the following equations:

S ~ binomial(est_inf, est_isr) and D ~ binomial(est_inf, est_ifr), where S and D are known.

Part 2 and 3 are written in generated quantities block because they take posterior estimate of theta (from part 1) as input (we say they are conditional on theta?).

It is mainly the part 3 that I'm struggling with, because,
1. est_inf has to be integer. From what I gathered from the mailing list discussion, a while loop can convert it from real to integer, if I really need to? I do understand the limitations associated with converting real to integer.
2. I can't write the usual format D ~ binomial(est_inf, est_ifr), as ~ is only allowed in the model block.
3. it seems like est_ifr <- beta_rng(0.5, 0.5) is not the right way to specify a prior beta distribution for est_ifr? If so, how should I write?

Is my understanding correct? If you have any solutions to the challenges I'm facing, please kindly advise.

Huiying

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, April 27, 2016 at 8:35:39 PM UTC+2, Eric-Jan Wagenmakers wrote:
> In the JAGS code, these bivariate outcomes were captured in a single number
> by using the sign. So .313 indicates an rt of 313 ms that ended up at
> the upper bound, and -.400 indicates an rt of 400 ms that ended up at
> the lower bound.

How do you represent missing values? How do you represent situation in which only one of the two variables is missing? How do you represent censored values? How do I know whether a value is an observed score or an upper or lower threshold of a censored score?

I use the negative response time values to flag the special cases and hence I'm in favor of the two-vector representation. In addition, it's consistent with the representation used by generalized linear models of response time-accuracy trade-off in IRT (e.g. van der Linden, W. J. (2007). A hierarchical framework for modeling speed and accuracy on test items. Psychometrika, 72(3), 287-308.) Sure, I and the IRT folks can translate our code to fit the specification used by response-time modelers. Sure I can add a vector or two that encodes thresholds. But then I have to complain that  this "doubles the Stan code length and increases the probability of making an error".

messages.body_plain:
There really is a single canonical solution; at least as far as the diffusion model is concerned. It's a bivariate model so the likelihood should be bivariate. I certainly understand that people are uncomfortable with the negative-RTs hack, and it's not good coding practice. But neither is implementing a bivariate distribution as two conditional univariate distributions.

Since there is a concern with breaking backward compatibility, I second Bob's suggestion of introducing a new distribution, suggest we explicitly label it bivariate and call it the "double Wiener distribution" and I can provide code to implement ~dwiener() if someone can help me translate it to the correct C prototypes and whatnot.

I think that will satisfy everyone involved.

Joachim

messages.body_plain:
> Q1. Any idea why we are getting 0 values for likelihood?

ADVI does not compute the log probability. Instead it evaluates the ELBO, which you can store using the diagnostic output file.

> Q2. With stan-ADVI we get an ELBO value of around -1100000 for the 1500 document dataset, whereas with the classical LDA implementation using VI(mean-field), we get a log likelihood value of around -890000. Is this an expected behaviour?

Yes. ADVI uses a general variational approximation. Details are here (http://www.proditus.com/papers/KucukelbirTran_2016.pdf).

I suspect what you call "classical LDA" uses a different variational approximation, custom tailored for LDA.

Thus, the ELBOs (at convergence) are different by definition.

Final comment: ADVI is not the best tool for fitting LDA and there are many excellent packages out there that implement fantastic algorithms for LDA specifically.

Cheers,
Alp

We don't recommend the uniform(1, 100) priors because the
100 is artificial.  Is it perhaps running up against a boundary
with 1 here in this?

  real<lower=1, upper=100> bias_magnitude;

  for(b in 1:num_batches) perturbation[b] ~ gamma(bias_magnitude, bias_magnitude-1);

For efficiency, you can vectorize the loop as

  perturbation ~ gamma(bias, bias - 1);

But when you do this:

  for(k in 1:K) phi_hat_no_bias[k] <- phi_given[k] .* perturbation;
  for(k in 1:K) phi[k] <- softmax(phi_hat_no_bias[k]);

you have a problem in that perturbation isn't going to
be identified here.  Given that phi_given is data (which I don't
understand, but that's another matter), you'll be able to induce
different scales in perturbation that lead to the same phi.  You
really need to fix one of the dimensions, like setting one of the
phi_given to 0.

- Bob

Matt and I were thinking about doing something like BUGS for variational inference (i.e. VIBES specifically), so that we could take advantage of the graphical model structure. This is useful in the case described here about specifying a variational approximation whose mean-field factors have the same exponential family form as the conditionally conjugate posterior’s exponential family. It’s also useful more importantly for a faster and stabler algorithm.

This would have to be done outside Stan of course because Stan (as far as I know) only has access to the “model” via the log joint density on a fixed data set and its gradient. I think expressive variational families is a solved problem even in this setting though; see my papers with Rajesh and Dave. There’s also a useful connection to ADVI in that the choice of distribution doesn’t matter so long as you use the right transformation from constrained to unconstrained (or unconstrained to unconstrained).

Dustin

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the reproducible bug report.

There's nothing wrong with

> Yfit <- X    ./ (1.0   / Prod   + X   / Cap);

because we have these signatures:

  operator/(vector, real) : vector

  operator+(real, vector) : vector

But there is a bug in the Stan code generator for this:

> Yfit <- X    ./ (1.0   / Prod   + X  ./ Cap);

Whenever the C++ fails to compile, it's a bug on our
end.  I filed an issue and assigned it to myself for 2.10:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1883

When it's fixed, (X ./ Cap) will produce the same value
as (X / Cap), so you can just go with the latter for now.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I hope you were kidding about reinstalling the OS.  I
don't think that's ever going to be the problem.

When you tried to install Stan, did you set dependencies,
as in:

> install.packages("rstan", dependencies = TRUE)

I think that's the magic incantation, as indicated here:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started#how-to-install-rstan

As far as I know, there's no way to have install.packages() indicate
a problem if the "dependencies = TRUE" bit is missing.  But I'm not
an R expert and suggestions for making the installs more reliable are
more than welcome.

- Bob

> On Apr 28, 2016, at 10:52 PM, Scott Akenhead <sc...@s4s.com> wrote:
>
> I am grateful that you fought your way through this and reported what worked. I had the same problem (rstan was missing RcppEigen) and was baffled by the voluminous output from a crashing stan_model.  Went through the usual ritual: reinstall OS, Xcode, R. Start R, update all, install rstan, wave an amethyst  crystal.  Still kablooey.  Found this thread just before sacrificing a chicken.  After installing RcppEigen, then installing rstan, then restarting R, it worked. I guess it is a simple as: RcppEigen is a dependency for rStan.  Anyway, thanks!

If it's a known quantity whose value is given to the program,
it goes in the data block.  If it's an unknown you're trying to
estimate, it goes in the parameter block.

But if you're asking that question, you may want to study some
other Stan programs before trying to write your own.  Especially if
you're tyring to fit an ODE-based model.  (We'll be rolling out
much better solvers soon, but it doesn't look like they'll get into

messages.subject_clean: Sampling for a local variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am using Stan to implement an algorithm for a novel model.  What I need is a temporal categorical variable generated from  a distribution.
Apparently, integer variables are not supportive in parameters block. The only choice left is to create a local variable in model block.

To show my intention, here is code.

Then I tried to sample for a local variable s in the model block

fit <- stan(file = 'localVar.stan', iter = 1, chains = 1)

I got the error:

left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
If so, you need to call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
Left-hand-side of sampling statement:

It seems that it is impossible to sample for a local variable in model block, except for the variables defined in the data block and parameters block.
If it is the case, is there alternative to save a temporal value generated from a distribution in model block?

Any ideas will be highly appreciated.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling for a local variable
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Sampling for a local variable
messages.body_plain:
You might want to have a look at the manual and other models
in Stan before attempting to write one yourself.  It doesn't
work like BUGS.

The warning you cite is just that --- a warning.  But
your code is missing parameter declarations, so there's nothing
that would be saved even if it did run.   The ~ doesn't do
random number generation; it just increments the log density.
Also when it is called in that Stan program, s wouldn't be defined.

Stan does not support integer parameters directly.  You
need to marginalize them out.

If the temporal categorical variable is finite, you probably
have something like a hidden Markov model (aka state-space
model).  There's a chapter in the manual explaining how to do HMMs
and the latent discrete parameter chapter explains how to deal with
a custom ecology state-space model.

- Bob

messages.subject: Sub-Hessians with STAN math autodiff library
messages.subject_clean: Sub-Hessians with STAN math autodiff library
messages.body_plain:
I'm using the STAN math autodiff library for a modeling problem with a large, sparse Hessian.  I know the sparsity structure in advance.  In order to efficiently compute the Hessian, I will need to compute sub-matrices of the Hessian.  AFAIK, this isn't supported in the current STAN libraries.  There are two ways I can think of to do this without substantially modifying my objective function, and a minimal example of both is attached.  I'd like to ask for feedback or other suggestions.

The easiest is to compute sub-rows of the Hessian by simply changing the range of the outer loop in hessian.hpp.  This is what I've done in the attached sub_hessian.hpp.

In order to compute sub-matrices on the diagonal, I created a functor that takes a smaller input vector than the full input vector, copies the values of the smaller vector into their appropriate places of the larger vector, and evaluates the objective.  Code is worth a thousand words, so please take a look at the SubObjective functor in the attached code.  This doesn't seem to go any faster than sub-rows of the full Hessian.  Presumablyt this is because it needs to evaluate the full objective with fvar datatypes in both cases?  Because it's not faster than getting the whole row, this doesn't seem to be a good way to go.

I can't think of a way to quickly get arbitrary off-diagonal strict sub-matrices without redefining the objective function to take as arguments an arbitrary combination of double and fvar types.  I can't think of a tidy way to do this in full generality, and I think to use Eigen matrix operations I'd have to promote everything to fvar types anyway.  Any other ideas?

I'm new to both C++ and STAN, so apologies in advance if I'm confused or need extra clarification for responses.  :)

Ryan

messages.body_plain:
You're right that we don't have a sparse Hessian operation.

And you're right as to why --- we don't have a way to call
a mixed double/var vector function.

I don't know of a better way of doing this than promoting,
which is tantamount to just computing the whole dense
Hessian.

I played around with trying to have two implementations of
our var and fvar types, one that's a "real" autodiff variable
and one that just wraps doubles to get around the type problem,
but it just pushes it down one level, and the run-time costs
of doing it with virtual functions or conditionals is too high.

I still have the feeling that it must be possible to engineer
such a thing with a clever use of something like the CRTP, but
I could never figure out how to do it.  I don't know if other
autodiff libs have reasonable solutions.  If you find out, I'd
like to hear more about what they do.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Apologies for sending another message, but I was hoping you could help me with something. I was watching Michael Betancourt's MLSS Iceland lecture (very nice) and was hoping to recreate the annulus sampling illustration he showed (comparing RW Metropolis vs Gibbs vs HMC) for a lecture series I'm giving on Bayesian statistics.

I was wondering how I could go about generating these series? I can generate an ''annulus''-type distribution, by taking a 1D normal, and essentially dragging it through 2 pi, to make a 2D ring. However, whilst this can be used to show RW Metropolis vs HMC sampling, it doesn't really lend itself to Gibbs sampling (well, it does, but it's trivial because the angle parameter is independent to the radial one.)

I can see how I could generate series that mimicked the distributions that Michael Betancourt showed, but not ones that actually did RWM, Gibbs and HMC properly using my framework. My question is, how can I recreate these?

Best,

Ben

> Your constraint is convenient because you're really

>
> data {

> }
> parameters {

> So you can just drop them.
